bullets: Real2SimLab is a new platform that runs simulation programs generated from real-world observations against multiple existing benchmarks while retaining each benchmark’s original scorer. Its common interface replaces separate method-to-benchmark integrations with one execution path. Why it matters: If you evaluate agents that turn videos into simulations, this changes the platform decision: one method implementation can be compared across benchmark-specific inputs and scoring rules without rewriting every integration, reducing engineering differences that could otherwise confound results. Evidence: E002. High confidence.

GlassGround is a new graphical user interface localization benchmark with 3,250 paired tasks that hold interface states, instructions, and targets fixed while switching between native screenshots and wearable-camera views. The authors report mean accuracy falling from 94.8% to 48.5% across ten open-source models. Why it matters: If you are selecting a model for smart glasses or camera-based assistants, screenshot benchmarks are not an adequate proxy. The paired design lets evaluators attribute performance loss to the observation channel rather than to different tasks or interfaces. Evidence: E021. High confidence.

MultiNet v2.0-Gridworld is a new preview benchmark designed to attribute agent failures rather than only rank success rates. Evaluators can independently vary mechanisms such as key-door dependencies, ordered actions, distractors, and decoys while keeping rendering, actions, and scoring fixed. Why it matters: If you are debugging a reasoning vision-language model, this design can separate failures caused by perception, learning environment rules, action ordering, or recovery. That distinction changes whether the next intervention should target visual understanding, planning, or error handling. Evidence: E025. High confidence.

The SimGlot Frozen Evaluation Dataset v1.1.0 is an update that archives inputs and supporting evidence for four agent-evaluation configurations, including a newly added versioned archive with a published SHA-256 file fingerprint. Why it matters: If you need to reproduce or compare SimGlot measurements, the frozen configurations make the benchmark setup itself inspectable. This matters where oracle behavior—the mechanism deciding whether an answer is correct—and configuration choices may change reported agent performance. Evidence: E001. Medium confidence.

μ-Bench is a new benchmark for voice agents serving several people in one shared session. Its 800 cases vary group size, acoustics, follow-up requests, tool access, and separate user permissions; joint success requires satisfying every user while respecting privacy and authority boundaries. Why it matters: If you are choosing a suite for shared-space voice products, single-user task completion misses failures where one person’s request conflicts with another’s permissions or privacy. This benchmark makes those coupled constraints part of the score rather than a separate safety check. Evidence: E010. High confidence.

JHealthBench-L is a new Japanese localization of an open-ended medical benchmark containing 79 consultations and 1,022 clinician-reviewed criteria. It adapts institution, medication, and care-pathway assumptions rather than relying on machine translation of foreign clinical rules. Why it matters: If you evaluate medical language models for Japan, translated prompts alone can penalize locally appropriate answers. This artifact offers a way to test against regional clinical practice, changing the choice between reusing an imported rubric and commissioning a locally reviewed evaluation. Evidence: E015. High confidence.

Trained Here, Tested There is a new evaluation of seven prompt-injection detectors across five public datasets. It contrasts same-source held-out testing with transfer to datasets collected from other sources, rather than treating one dataset split as evidence of general detection ability. Why it matters: If you are selecting a prompt-injection defense, this design tests whether performance survives a change in data source. It can prevent a deployment decision based only on a detector recognizing the wording and structure of its own training corpus. Evidence: E008. High confidence.
bullets_zh: Real2SimLab 是一个新平台，可针对多个现有基准运行根据真实世界观测生成的仿真程序，同时保留各基准原有的评分器。其通用接口以一条执行路径取代了各自独立的方法到基准集成。Why it matters: 如果你评估的是将视频转换为仿真的智能体，这会改变平台选型：同一个方法实现可以在不同基准特有的输入和评分规则下进行比较，而无需重写每项集成，从而减少可能干扰结果的工程差异。Evidence: E002. High confidence.

GlassGround 是一个新的图形用户界面定位基准，包含 3,250 个配对任务；在保持界面状态、指令和目标不变的同时，在原生屏幕截图与可穿戴相机视图之间切换。作者报告称，在十个开源模型中，平均准确率从 94.8% 降至 48.5%。Why it matters: 如果你正在为智能眼镜或基于相机的助手选择模型，屏幕截图基准并不足以充当代理指标。配对设计使评估者能够将性能下降归因于观测通道，而不是任务或界面的不同。Evidence: E021. High confidence.

MultiNet v2.0-Gridworld 是一个新的预览版基准，旨在归因智能体失败，而不只是按成功率排名。评估者可以独立改变钥匙与门的依赖关系、动作顺序、干扰项和诱饵等机制，同时保持渲染、动作和评分不变。Why it matters: 如果你正在调试推理型视觉语言模型，这种设计可以区分由感知、环境规则学习、动作排序或恢复能力导致的失败。这一区分会影响下一步干预应针对视觉理解、规划还是错误处理。Evidence: E025. High confidence.

SimGlot Frozen Evaluation Dataset v1.1.0 是一次更新，归档了四种智能体评估配置的输入和支撑证据，其中包括一个新增的版本化归档，并公布了 SHA-256 文件指纹。Why it matters: 如果你需要复现或比较 SimGlot 测量结果，冻结配置可使基准设置本身接受检查。当预言机行为——即判定答案是否正确的机制——和配置选择可能改变所报告的智能体性能时，这一点尤为重要。Evidence: E001. Medium confidence.

μ-Bench 是一个面向多人共享会话中语音智能体的新基准。其 800 个案例涵盖不同的群组规模、声学条件、后续请求、工具访问权限和独立用户权限；联合成功要求在尊重隐私和授权边界的同时满足每位用户。Why it matters: 如果你正在为共享空间语音产品选择评测套件，单用户任务完成情况会遗漏这类失败：一个人的请求与另一个人的权限或隐私发生冲突。该基准将这些相互关联的约束纳入评分，而不是作为单独的安全检查。Evidence: E010. High confidence.

JHealthBench-L 是一个新的日语本地化开放式医疗基准，包含 79 次问诊和 1,022 项经临床医生审核的标准。它对医疗机构、药物和诊疗路径方面的假设进行了适配，而不是依赖对外国临床规则的机器翻译。Why it matters: 如果你要评估面向日本的医疗语言模型，仅翻译提示词可能会惩罚符合当地实践的答案。该成果提供了一种依据地区临床实践进行测试的方法，从而影响是在复用引进的评分标准与委托开展本地审核评估之间作出选择。Evidence: E015. High confidence.

Trained Here, Tested There 是一项新的评估，覆盖七种提示注入检测器和五个公共数据集。它对比了同源留出测试与向其他来源所采集数据集的迁移，而不是将单一数据集划分的结果视为具备通用检测能力的证据。Why it matters: 如果你正在选择提示注入防御方案，这种设计可以检验其性能能否经受数据来源变化。它可以避免仅仅因为检测器识别出了自身训练语料库的措辞和结构就作出部署决定。Evidence: E008. High confidence.
briefing.caveat: This briefing reviewed 168 selected evidence records from a 694-record keyword-filtered corpus, so it does not represent the full captured feed or the wider AI field. Brave, OpenReview, and Semantic Scholar were unavailable, and several attention connectors carried stale observations because requests failed or hit rate limits. Claims describe source-authored releases and were not independently validated.
briefing.caveat_zh: 本简报审查了从一个经关键词筛选、包含 694 条记录的语料库中选出的 168 条证据记录，因此不能代表捕获到的完整信息流或更广泛的 AI 领域。Brave、OpenReview 和 Semantic Scholar 不可用，而且由于请求失败或触发速率限制，多个关注度连接器包含过时的观测结果。相关说法描述的是来源作者发布的内容，未经独立验证。

evidence_items.summary: We present OWE-Bench (OpenWorldEngineer-Bench), a benchmark of 26 long-horizon engineering tasks written by domain experts in software engineering, physical engineering, machine learning, and scientific computing. Tasks range from optimizing kernels and designing an aircraft, to identifying the faults responsible for an earthquake. Each task requires significant domain knowledge and engineering work, with models averaging hundreds of millions of tokens per task. Solutions are scored on practical measures such as speed, cost and accuracy, both on provided cases the agent could test against and on hidden cases that an engineer would expect from the task description. The best-performing frontier model so far, Claude Fable 5.2, scores 54.6% and averages 211 million tokens per task. We highlight two findings. First, when models are given more time, they use more test-time compute and achieve higher scores. Models also scale differently with test-time compute: GPT-6 Astra achieves higher scores at shorter time limits and at equal token use, while Claude Fable 5.2 uses more tokens at longer limits to achieve the highest overall score. Second, each model scores lower on hidden cases than on the provided cases, by an average of 18 points, which we call the deployment gap. Models also fail to predict the deployment gap, overestimating their performance on hidden test cases by an average of 21 points. We hope that OWE-Bench grounds progress toward agents whose engineering solutions perform as well in deployment as they do in testing.
evidence_items.title: OWE-Bench: A long-horizon benchmark for measuring real-world engineering

evidence_items.summary: Real-to-simulation transfer, which builds simulations from real-world observations, has long been studied in research and industry. Recently, coding agents have become capable of generating simulation programs from video recordings, and several benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate them. However, each individual benchmark defines its own inputs, deliverables, and scoring pipeline. This leads to $N \times M$ integrations when evaluating $N$ methods on $M$ benchmarks. To this end, we present Real2SimLab, a unified platform for real-to-simulation transfer. It evaluates a method by running its written program and scoring the output simulation with the original scorer of each benchmark. Moreover, Real2SimLab provides a pipeline to create training data and reward annotations for real-to-simulation methods. Our pipeline carefully avoids data contamination by filtering out the video recordings that exist in benchmarks. For each video recording, a program is first produced, and then our pipeline computes its reward with the same code that Real2SimLab uses for evaluation. So far, it supports 47 coding agents and 5 non-agent methods on 6 benchmarks. Both the platform and Awesome-Real2Sim, our research map of nearly 300 real-to-simulation papers, are open source, and we invite the Real2SimHub community to build them together.
evidence_items.title: Real2SimLab: A Unified Platform for Real-to-Simulation Transfer

evidence_items.summary: We present AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base, a mixture-of-experts language model with 80 billion total parameters and approximately 3 billion active parameters per token, trained from scratch at Yandex and released under the Apache 2.0 license. The model combines Kimi Delta Attention with full attention, uses Attention Residuals, and is trained with Muon. Training comprises general pretraining on 17.5 trillion tokens, two context-extension stages, and a dedicated stage for reasoning and agentic interaction. We describe the data collection and augmentation pipelines, evaluation protocols, architectural ablations, and scaling-law experiments. We identify the limitations of held-out training loss as a proxy for downstream performance and introduce an auxiliary loss on mixture-of-experts outputs to stabilize training at the predicted learning rate. Domain-specific data selection and augmentation improve factual knowledge, mathematics, and programming skills, while agent trajectories introduced during pretraining improve performance on agentic benchmarks after supervised fine-tuning. In zero-shot reasoning evaluation, the model achieves leading results among open base models of comparable size, with 88.7% pass@8 on IMO-AnswerBench and 82.9% pass@8 on LiveCodeBench v5-v6. To evaluate Russian-language factual knowledge, we introduce and release two benchmarks with their evaluation protocols: WikiWebFacts, which tests short factual questions drawn from encyclopedic sources and search queries, and HardMultiQA, which tests more demanding factual questions inspired by user interactions. Our model scores 86.5% on WikiWebFacts and 67.9% on HardMultiQA, compared with 83.2% and 65.4% for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base (284B total and 13B active parameters) and 72.8% and 54.5% for Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-Base (120B total and 12B active parameters), outperforming both larger models on these benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base

evidence_items.summary: Advances in deep generative modeling have made it increasingly plausible to train human-level embodied agents. Yet progress has been limited by the absence of large-scale, real-time, multi-modal, and socially interactive datasets that reflect the sensory-motor complexity of natural environments. To address this, we present PLAICraft, a novel data collection platform and dataset capturing multiplayer Minecraft interactions across five time-aligned modalities: video, game output audio, microphone input audio, mouse, and keyboard actions. Each modality is logged with millisecond time precision, enabling the study of synchronous, embodied behaviour in a rich, open-ended world. The dataset comprises 5525 hours of interactive gameplay from more than 232 participants. Alongside the dataset, we provide an evaluation suite for benchmarking model capabilities in object recognition, spatial awareness, language grounding, and long-term memory. PLAICraft opens a path toward training and evaluating agents that act fluently and purposefully in real time, paving the way for truly embodied artificial intelligence.
evidence_items.title: PLAICraft: Large-Scale Time-Aligned Vision-Speech-Action Dataset for Embodied AI

evidence_items.summary: Abstract. Consumer large language model (LLM) interactive-fiction products are marketed on narrative continuity but are almost always evaluated on prose quality. This preprint separates the two. We report a fixed-protocol, single-day, zero-dollar, zero-card benchmark of ten consumer web products conducted on 15 November 2026, built around a 15-turn retention probe: an identical fact ("My cat's name is Marmalade.") is planted at turn 2 and queried verbatim at turn 15. Four of ten products reached turn 15; three of those four (75%) recalled the fact, while one fluent, on-persona session silently lost it. Four further products were right-censored before the probe could be administered by signup walls, paid-trial gates, or non-persistent sessions, and two were untestable under the protocol. We argue that the dominant continuity risk in this category is not local prose quality but silent state drift — a failure that leaves the immediate utterance fluent while the narrative record is wrong — and we introduce a five-mode taxonomy of it. As a constructive response we document branching-story-kit, a 207-line, zero-dependency deterministic story-state kernel (JSON scene graph, additive/assigning reducer, guard predicates, invariant validator, and a turn-stamped memory log) released under MIT with a 21-test conformance suite. We close with preservation risk: in the companion late-2026 availability dataset, two companion applications were removed from the iOS App Store, decoupling reader continuity from reader investment. Data and code availability. All measurements, instruments, and code are open and persistently identified. Primary dataset: Harvard Dataverse, doi:10.7910/DVN/YEBHQR; CERN Zenodo mirror, doi:10.5281/zenodo.24511974. Software (branching-story-kit v1.0.0, MIT): doi:10.5281/zenodo.24514910; source at github.com/ouba-studio/branching-story-kit; JSR package at jsr.io/@ouba-studio/branching-story-kit.
evidence_items.title: State Drift in Consumer LLM Interactive Fiction: A 15-Turn Empirical Benchmark Across 10 Platforms and a 207-Line Deterministic Story-State Kernel

evidence_items.summary: 3D perception is shifting from task-specific pipelines to geometric foundation models: monocular depth networks, feed-forward 3D/4D reconstruction models, and vision--language models that predict geometry. However, their progress cannot be measured reliably. Published numbers are not comparable, because every paper samples frames, sets resolutions, and selects test splits differently. They are not robust because the alignment required for every up-to-scale prediction can outweigh the gap between models: fitting depth in the wrong space nearly triples its error, and standard trajectory alignment understates the error of failing methods by up to 2.6times. And they rarely cover long recordings, dynamic scenes, or aerial views. We present SpatialArena, an open arena that scores geometric models with the same metrics and rules, with robust and deterministic alignment. SpatialArena spans five tasks, from monocular depth to SLAM. It covers 23 public datasets with 418,929 images across indoor, outdoor, aerial, object-centric, and dynamic scenes, together with Spatial Arena, our own captures with accurate poses and depth. Evaluating 52 models, we find that single-image depth is close to saturation on public benchmarks but not on large, uncontrolled scenes, and that progress now comes from consistency across frames and views, where feed-forward 3D/4D models match or surpass monocular specialists and overtake video depth models. The benchmark, toolbox, and leaderboard will be publicly released.
evidence_items.title: mvp-ai-lab/SpatialArena

evidence_items.summary: Version 2.1 of the agent tool-policy benchmark: hidden instructions in invented physiotherapy-clinic notes, in English and Roman Urdu, tested on four small local models. What is new- Two more models with the same 40 tasks, prompts and settings: mistral:7b and qwen2.5:7b (1,280 replies in total, all valid JSON, model digests recorded).- pooled v2.py: comparisons pooled over models with the task as the unit (sign-flip permutation test and task-level bootstrap interval), by attack kind and framing.- Clearer chart labels (outputs v2/datamark.png).- paper/: LaTeX source and PDF of the paper on versions 2 and 2.1. Main results- With the plain prompt, the four models followed 19-22 of 40 hidden instructions in English and 21-29 in Roman Urdu.- Datamarking cut them from 83 to 40 of 160 in English and from 97 to 56 in Roman Urdu (p < 0.0001), but had no significant effect for qwen2.5:7b in English (19 to 16, p = 0.51).- After datamarking, out-of-scope attacks were followed 2 of 80 times in English and 26 in Roman Urdu (p = 0.0005).- A rule on tool names let 174 wrong-argument attacks through; checking the patient, recipient and date against the staff request let none through and blocked no correct action. All tasks, patients and addresses are invented. Research code; not a security evaluation of any product.
evidence_items.title: Agent tool-policy benchmark: permission rules and hidden instructions in a clinic

evidence_items.summary: Classifiers that flag prompt injections are a common first defence for LLM applications, and their reported accuracy usually comes from held-out data drawn from the same sources they were trained on. We test how well such detectors transfer. We evaluate seven detectors on five public datasets: a fixed keyword heuristic, four TF-IDF logistic-regression models each trained on one dataset, and two openly available fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3 classifiers. The datasets are deepset prompt-injections, safe-guard-prompt-injection, jailbreak-classification, SPML and Gandalf ignore-instructions. Every detector scored well on its own source, with AUROC between 0.955 and 0.999. On other sources, the TF-IDF models averaged an AUROC of 0.872 (range 0.727–0.987), and the deepset classifier fell from 0.997 on its own data to 0.666 and 0.789 on two others. Thresholds transferred worse than rankings. Thresholds set for a 1% false-positive rate on the training source gave false-positive rates of 26% or more in five of twelve cross-dataset cases (up to 79.7%), and recall fell as low as 3.5%. The ProtectAI v2 classifier was the most robust, with AUROC of at least 0.979 on three of the four labelled test sets and 100% recall on Gandalf. It still caught only 36.7% of injections in the deepset test set and flagged 12.0% of benign SPML prompts. The keyword heuristic never produced a false positive, but caught only 14–42% of injections. No detector reached 90% recall at 5% or fewer false positives on all four labelled test sets. Exact-text overlap between test and training sets was small, except that 108 safe-guard test prompts also appear in the jailbreak training set. Detector accuracy should be reported across datasets and at a fixed operating point, not only as in-distribution AUROC. Code, logs and derived data to reproduce every number are in the attached archive. Preprint, not peer-reviewed.
evidence_items.title: Trained Here, Tested There: A Cross-Dataset Evaluation of Prompt-Injection Detectors on Five Public Datasets

rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: We present MEMO (a Mesh for Every MOment), a method that reconstructs the geometry of complete dynamic scenes, captured by multiple synchronized cameras, and extracts a mesh at every frame. Existing dynamic Gaussian splatting methods either model appearance alone or target isolated objects segmented by foreground masks, and all of them recover meshes by TSDF fusion or Poisson reconstruction, whose fixed grids limit the detail they can capture. At the core of MEMO is a per-Gaussian motion model inspired by Gaussian processes, which represents each Gaussian's position and rotation over time as a combination of temporal Gaussian kernels. The model keeps every Gaussian a valid surface element throughout the sequence and carries an implicit representation of the dynamic geometry, so a mesh can be derived at any time from a field defined by the Gaussians. Although common in real captures, large and fast motion poses a challenge that dynamic Gaussian splatting methods usually overlook. To account for it, we design a track-based initialization scheme that fits each Gaussian's initial trajectory to point tracks in closed form. We evaluate MEMO on Blender-Moments, a new benchmark of nine animated scenes with ground-truth meshes at every frame, and on two real-world datasets. MEMO reconstructs the most accurate geometry among state-of-the-art methods, and remains competitive in novel-view synthesis and training time. Project page: https://memo-4d.github.io
evidence_items.title: A Mesh for Every Moment

evidence_items.summary: Voice agents in shared spaces must satisfy interdependent multi-user requests while upholding per-user authority, privacy, and task constraints. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage when participants react throughout a session. We introduce $\mu$-Bench, a benchmark for joint task completion in closed-loop, full-duplex multi-user voice interaction. Simulated participants act from isolated profiles of goals, knowledge, and permissions, adapting to the agent's speech and tool outcomes. Across 20 domains, 100 scenarios vary group size, acoustics, and follow-up demands to form 800 cases (408 tool-augmented, 392 tool-free). Joint Task Success (JTS) requires all user goals, privacy boundaries, and terminal states to hold jointly, while Pure JTS further disallows unauthorized tool calls; Attribution, Threading, and Coordination (ATC) diagnostics localize failures. Across 13 voice agents, proprietary systems peak at 62.24\% tool-free and 65.44\% tool-augmented success, while open-weight models remain below 20\%. ATC diagnostics show that open-weight models lag primarily in multi-turn attribution and threading, and controlled contrasts reveal that larger groups consistently degrade joint task success across capable systems. By coupling reactive multi-user simulation with verifiable session-level outcomes, $\mu$-Bench provides a rigorous testbed for shared voice agents.
evidence_items.title: $\mu$-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion in Shared Interaction Voice Agents

evidence_items.summary: Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.
evidence_items.title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents

rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: AI wearables, such as smart glasses, extend the context available to agents beyond digital environments to users' physical surroundings. With these devices, computer tasks can originate from users' ongoing activities rather than solely from explicit instructions. Through first-person observations, agents can identify objects and activities relevant to user requests and ground digital tasks in the surrounding context. We call this interaction paradigm Ego Use. However, first-person observations are limited by the wearer's viewpoint and may provide incomplete or ambiguous evidence of ongoing activities. As new observations arrive, agents may need to revise their understanding of the physical context and user intent, and reassess whether prior digital actions remain valid. Whether current agents can reliably handle these changes remains insufficiently evaluated. We introduce EgoUseBench, a benchmark for evaluating Ego Use across three interaction settings with different levels of first-person context. Computer-Use relies on explicit instructions, Offline Ego Use provides prerecorded first-person context before execution, and Online Ego Use provides continuous observations as user intent evolves. Based on over 74 hours of real-world first-person recordings, we construct 693 tasks across the three interaction settings. To capture task evolution, we track first-person observations, user requirements, and website state separately. We further group tasks by how information changes during execution, resulting in three types: Graft (revised user requirements), Refresh (new first-person observations), and Clarify (agent-initiated information seeking). We evaluate advanced models and find that average success rates in Online Ego Use are 26.3% lower than in Computer-Use. This result reveals the difficulty of keeping task execution aligned with evolving first-person context and user intent.
evidence_items.title: EgoUseBench: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agents under Evolving First-Person Contexts

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from passive chatbots into autonomous systems that operate continuously in dynamic environments. Such agents need not only solve current tasks but also learn from past interactions to improve future performance. However, existing streaming benchmarks often rely on short task sequences or largely independent tasks, providing limited evidence of whether agents can effectively reuse experience when later tasks depend on earlier outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{EvoLink-Bench}, a benchmark for evaluating self-evolving agents in long-horizon, interdependent task streams. It covers daily office work, multi-turn dialogue, and AutoResearch-style workflows, with persistent workspaces and dependencies across tasks. The benchmark includes two complementary levels: \textbf{L1}, which evaluates the acquisition and revision of language-expressible knowledge, and \textbf{L2}, which assesses the development of task-level capabilities through execution and feedback. Its evaluation further distinguishes within-task recovery, persistent-state updates, and experience reuse in later tasks. We evaluate five agent frameworks across three backbone configurations under three persistence conditions, covering 19,635 scored task slots from selected evaluation cohorts. Results show that no framework consistently performs best across both levels, retries recover only a limited proportion of failed tasks, and persistent-state updates do not necessarily improve subsequent performance. Furthermore, the effects of evolution differ between knowledge- and capability-level tasks, suggesting that these two forms of evolution require different learning mechanisms. Performance gains also vary across domains and task streams, with improvements on some tasks not necessarily extending to others.
evidence_items.title: EvoLink-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Self-Evolving Agents in Long-Horizon Interdependent Task Streams

evidence_items.summary: CrawlCheck: Agent safety benchmark A frozen suite of cases that tests whether an AI agent stops before it signs in on a lookalike domain, connects to a poisoned tool, pays on a revoked receipt, acts on a stale answer, or fetches a page whose robots.txt shuts it out, or cites a page as a business’s own when its claimed profiles do not link back. Each case carries its truth and the signed CrawlCheck answer it came from, so it can score an agent or serve as a checkable reward when… See the full description on the dataset page: https://huggingface.co/datasets/crawlcheck/agent-safety-benchmark.
evidence_items.title: crawlcheck/agent-safety-benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Satellite time series capture how land surfaces change over time. Pixel-wise temporal foundation models read a year of satellite observations per pixel, yet public benchmarks lack a temporal axis or subsample it to a few dates. We introduce Analemma, a temporal benchmark of six datasets that carry every 10 and 20 m Sentinel-2 band and a time series spanning a growing season, completed where their releases omit geometry, dates, or cloud masks. One frozen-encoder protocol evaluates all models across label ratios and three seeds, with two baselines without pretraining. The TESSERA model ranks first overall. A from-scratch model on monthly composites outranks every foundation model except OlmoEarth v1.3-Base, suggesting that temporal input explains most of the performance. Three evaluation choices left unstated by the source publications each shift TESSERA v1 by 7.6 to 18.6 mIoU, against top-two gaps of 0.6 to 2.8. Data, harness and leaderboard will be publicly released soon.
evidence_items.title: Analemma $\infty$: A Temporal Benchmark for Geospatial Foundation Models

evidence_items.summary: Rubric-based benchmarks such as HealthBench evaluate large language models (LLMs) on open-ended health consultations using case-specific physician criteria, many of which presuppose the healthcare institutions, medications, and care pathways of their source region. Under machine translation alone, these regional assumptions remain in the rubric, leaving responses appropriate in Japan uncredited or falsely penalized under foreign clinical rules. To adapt established clinical evaluation perspectives to Japan without authoring rubrics from scratch, we construct JHealthBench-L (79 patient-facing consultations, 1,022 criteria) through source-cited LLM drafting, single-specialist selection and revision, independent dual-physician review, and meta-review. Specialists rewrote only 4.4% of criteria from scratch, and independent reviewers approved 93.6% of Stage-2 criteria without issue. Comparing JHealthBench-L with a machine-translated baseline across 18 LLMs reveals that translation-only evaluation preserves coarse model rankings ($\tau = 0.817$, mean shift +0.027) yet flips verdicts on 17.7% of modified criteria (vs. 7.3% re-grading noise) and reduces false penalties on Japan-adapted negative criteria by 7.1 percentage points, masking item-level clinical mismeasurement behind stable leaderboards. Axis-level and paired analyses further show that context awareness and Japan-specific clinical criteria remain primary bottlenecks, whereas Japanese continual pretraining and reasoning post-training substantially improve locally grounded performance. Datasets, physician revision logs, and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/horshohei/JHealthBench-L.
evidence_items.title: JHealthBench-L: Clinician-Reviewed Localization of HealthBench for Rubric-Based Medical LLM Evaluation in Japan

evidence_items.summary: LLM Benchmarks — Current Top 100 & Local GPU Benchmarks Machine-readable mirror of https://llmbenchmarks.io and our first-party local GPU benchmark suite at https://llmbenchmarks.io/local-gpu-benchmarks/ (DE: https://llmbenchmarks.io/de/lokale-gpu-benchmarks/, alias https://llmbenchmarks.io/en/local-benchmarks), plus dedicated views for Coding & Agent Benchmarks and the AI & Open-Weight Model Directory, covering 100 selected global models, 56 benchmarks, 2570 visible table cells… See the full description on the dataset page: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Mausbiber/local-gpu-llm-benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: Mausbiber/local-gpu-llm-benchmarks

rationale: Matched: agent~benchmarks, benchmark, data collection, dataset, evaluat
evidence_items.summary: Benchmarks provide standardized measures for evaluating and advancing large language models (LLMs) and multimodal LLMs (MLLMs). As models improve, existing benchmarks can approach saturation, making it harder to challenge models and distinguish among them. While reusing annotated datasets can reduce data collection and labeling effort, constructing new benchmarks remains labor-intensive, and existing agent-based approaches often target specific tasks or automate only parts of the process. To address these challenges, we introduce BenchHarness, an autonomous harness for end-to-end benchmark customization. It coordinates multiple agents and tools to analyze user requirements, search for suitable datasets, and construct validated benchmarks, with support for refinement based on model performance. To evaluate BenchHarness, we construct 16 benchmarks spanning diverse tasks and modalities. Human review and LLM-as-a-judge assessments indicate high benchmark quality, while evaluations across multiple models reveal challenging tasks and meaningful performance differences. In comparisons with source benchmarks, the generated benchmarks yield lower scores and larger performance gaps, even when the originals approach saturation. BenchHarness thus provides a reusable approach to benchmark construction, supporting informative evaluation as model capabilities and user needs evolve. Our code and benchmarks are publicly available.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark Everything Everywhere All at Once

evidence_items.summary: Clinical spectroscopy has emerged as a powerful tool across biomedical research, with applications spanning from disease diagnosis and screening, to biomarker detection, therapeutic monitoring and intraoperative assessment. However, despite substantial progress, the analysis of spectroscopic data remains a major bottleneck, with current workflows still heavily reliant on trial and error, expert intuition and prior experience. Here, we introduce a multi-agent, large language model (LLM) framework for automated optimisation of preprocessing pipelines for spectral data. Our system combines a memory-derived information set, or \textit{dossier}, with LLM-based agents that reason over previously evaluated preprocessing pipelines in order to propose, rank, and iteratively refine preprocessing strategies by following a multi-reward rule. Unlike exhaustive, brute-force search over a parameter space, the agent constructs candidates sequentially, enabling more targeted exploration. We benchmark our approach across 18 scenarios on six public clinical datasets against seven baselines, including random search, established optimisation methods and grid search. Our agentic optimisation achieved the highest classification accuracy in four out of six datasets. Ablation across LLM backbones and dossier configurations further shows that access to optimisation history is a key contributor to performance. These results demonstrate the potential of history-informed agents to enable more automated, adaptive and reproducible preprocessing pipelines in spectroscopy.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models as Preprocessing Optimisers in Clinical Spectroscopy

evidence_items.summary: We introduce BOP-Refer, the first benchmark for monocular 3D and 2D grounding of everyday and industrial objects sourced from 9 diverse BOP datasets. We pair images from these datasets with VLM-generated and human-verified referring expressions, and derive accurate ground-truth 3D and 2D bounding boxes of the referred objects from their 3D models and 6DoF pose annotations. Our systematic evaluation of 17 frontier VLMs across the major proprietary and open-weight families (Gemini, GPT, Claude, Qwen, Gemma) shows that the best model, Gemini 4 Carbon, reaches 72.6% AP_IoU2D in 2D but only 12.4% AP_IoU3D in 3D, despite the more lenient IoU thresholds in 3D. The predicted 3D boxes are usually centered on the target objects in the image but often off in depth by more than the object's size, suggesting that metric scale estimation, which needs reliable object size priors, is currently by far the main source of error.
evidence_items.title: BOP-Refer: Benchmark for Monocular 3D and 2D Object Grounding

evidence_items.summary: This paper introduces Atunda, the first systematically collected video dataset of Afrogenic dance moves, designed for training and evaluating deep learning models for movement classification. The first phase of the dataset includes nearly 400 videos covering 13 distinct dance moves from African and African Diaspora performative culture, making it the first AI-ready resource of its kind. Using this dataset, we train and evaluate various configurations of temporal convolutional neural networks, achieving a classification accuracy exceeding 95%. The baseline results provide a benchmark for future studies in movement classification, especially in the understudied area of Afrogenic performative culture and tradition. This work lays the foundation for developing in the future digital metrics of similarity, automated attribution systems, and tools that preserve and promote the cultural heritage of Afrogenic dances.
evidence_items.title: Atunda: Building an Afrogenic Dance Movement Dataset for AI-Driven Classification

evidence_items.summary: Agentic software systems are increasingly used in development, where changes to the model, prompt, scaffold, tools, or execution environment require repeated testing. Test case selection (TCS) can reduce testing costs while providing estimates of agent performance or exposing failures early. Although TCS has been studied for deep neural networks and LLM code models, prior work does not directly address agentic systems and often requires model information unavailable for proprietary agents. We present the first empirical study of black-box TCS for agentic software systems. We treat each benchmark task as a test case and adapt black-box regression-testing techniques using selection criteria based on task descriptions, metadata, code fragments, and embeddings. We also propose strategies that estimate task difficulty using heuristic features or independent LLM-as-judge assessments. Our strategies select tasks without executing the target agent or using past results. We evaluate fourteen selection strategies, including random sampling, plus a historical-data baseline, across ten AI agent benchmarks with 12 to 101 agents per benchmark. We assess Success Rate estimation and early failure detection. No single strategy dominates both objectives. Adapted black-box regression-testing strategies are most effective for Success Rate estimation, with Category Partition obtaining the lowest median error on five benchmarks at the 20% task budget. LLM-as-judge selection is more effective for early failure detection. For GPT 5.2 Codex on SWE-bench Verified, Category Partition selects 100 instead of 500 tasks, reducing execution cost from \$225 to \$47, with a Success Rate estimation error of 0.8 percentage points. At the same budget, LLM-as-judge selection detects nearly twice as many failures as random sampling: 53.0% of selected tasks reveal failures, compared with 27.4% for random sampling.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating More with Less: Black-Box Test Selection for AI Agents

evidence_items.summary: Precise 9-DoF pose control is essential for visual content generation, enabling users to specify object location, size, and orientation in 3D space. However, existing methods typically focus on either text-to-image (T2I) or text-to-video (T2V) generation, with limitations in pose controllability and temporal coherence. We present SceneDesigner++, a unified framework for 9-DoF pose control across both T2I and T2V generation. We construct ObjectPose9D++, a dataset containing high-quality images and videos with accurate pose annotations. Trained on ObjectPose9D++, SceneDesigner++ combines absolute and relative pose encoding strategies to decouple frame-wise spatial grounding from inter-frame motion modeling. Specifically, absolute pose encoding leverages CNOCS map sequences to provide explicit, frame-wise 9-DoF pose guidance. Meanwhile, our relative pose encoding, termed VPRoPE, incorporates relative pose information into rotary position embeddings to explicitly model inter-frame pose transitions, thereby promoting temporally coherent object motion. A learnable orthogonal transformation is further introduced for each attention head, allowing different heads to capture complementary geometric relationships while preserving input feature norms to promote training stability. We further adopt a two-stage training strategy to learn the absolute and relative pose encoding mechanisms separately. Benefiting from this lightweight and decoupled design, SceneDesigner++ also supports integration with an independently trained camera-control module, enabling separate or joint control over object and camera motion. Finally, we introduce T2IVPoseEval, a benchmark for evaluating diverse object poses and motion patterns in both T2I and T2V tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SceneDesigner++ consistently outperforms same-backbone baselines in pose fidelity and motion quality.
evidence_items.title: SceneDesigner++: A Unified 9-DoF Pose Control Framework for T2I and T2V Generation

evidence_items.summary: Wearable assistants must localize interface elements from camera observations when direct screenshot access is unavailable, yet existing GUI grounding benchmarks primarily evaluate native screenshots. We introduce GlassGround, a new benchmark that pairs native screenshots with wearable camera observations while holding GUI states, instructions, and targets fixed. GlassGround contains 3,250 tasks across Android and iOS, captured using four wearable devices under four viewing conditions. Across ten open-source models, mean grounding accuracy drops from 94.8% on screenshots to 48.5% on camera images. Further analysis reveals that changes in target scale, screen geometry, and background cannot fully explain this performance degradation. We then study two ways to narrow this gap. At inference time, local zooming and screen rectification help but leave most of the gap. For training-time adaptation, we build on GlassGround's paired-view design and introduce PairDistill, a baseline that aligns target representations across views alongside coordinate supervision. Trained on independently collected data and using no screenshots at inference, it improves camera-image accuracy by 9.4 and 12.2 points on two backbones and transfers to unseen devices and operating systems. Combined with local zooming, it reaches 69.6% and 64.4%, but does not close the gap. The GlassGround dataset and code are available at https://github.com/yunnw/GlassGround.
evidence_items.title: GlassGround: GUI Grounding Beyond Native Screenshots with Egocentric Wearable Vision

evidence_items.summary: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) image registration under varying acquisition geometries is challenging because orbit direction, look side, and incidence angle affect backscatter, terrain-induced distortion, and feature visibility. However, large-scale geometry-aware benchmarks remain scarce. This paper presents MOVR-SAR, a multi-resolution dataset of 450,845 registered and quality-screened tile pairs derived from 2774 scene pairs from Capella, Umbra, Sentinel-1, and NISAR. It covers X, C, and L bands, ground sampling distances of 0.25-20 m, and diverse regions and land-cover types. A unified framework defines four imaging-geometry pair categories from orbit direction and look side, plus viewing-angle-separation labels for Capella and Umbra, enabling stratified evaluation under same- and opposite-direction illumination. Systematic evaluation of representative matching methods shows that official and cross-modal pretrained weights perform poorly on high-resolution X-band imagery. Fine-tuning on MOVR-SAR improves accuracy and reduces disparities across platforms, imaging-geometry pair categories, and viewing-angle separations. For example, fine-tuning increases FlexGlue AUC@5 from 3.06% to 89.79% on Capella and from 1.79% to 89.03% on Umbra, reaching 93.41% and 94.77% on Sentinel-1 and NISAR, respectively. Fine-tuning substantially reduces the official-weight same-orbit, same-look-side advantage and reverses the three-method average category ranking on Capella, suggesting that this bias reflects training-data coverage rather than an invariant limitation of cross-geometry matching. Land-cover effects remain platform- and method-dependent. MOVR-SAR provides a training resource and geometry-aware benchmark for robust SAR-SAR registration. The dataset and model weights will be released at https://github.com/fdhzhz5870/MOVR-SAR.
evidence_items.title: MOVR-SAR: A Multi-resolution SAR Registration Dataset under Orbit-crossing and View-variant Imaging Differences

evidence_items.summary: Embedding models increasingly inform how people search, recommend, and retrieve information, yet we lack credible ways to test whether these similarity judgments reflect how humans understand meaning. Existing benchmarks typically rely on static, expert-labeled pairs with coarse Likert-style annotations, limiting scalability and making it difficult to obtain consistent, high-confidence annotations. We introduce Aligned Machine, an interactive, public-facing platform that transforms broad participation into a continuously growing Human-Aligned Similarity Benchmark (HASB) for evaluating semantic alignment in embedding-based systems. Participants complete a cognitively-natural, forced-choice task, comparing two pairs of items (text or images) and selecting which pair is more similar. This comparative design is accessible to non-experts, yields clean preference data, and supports robust aggregation. We report results from an initial deployment with 115 participants contributing 2,875 total labeled pairs and 872 unique pairs. Using HASB, we evaluated 12 widely used embedding models and found only partial alignment between embedding similarity and human judgments. Text-only models consistently achieve higher overall agreement than multimodal models, while multimodal performance varies systematically by task type: alignment is strongest for image-image comparisons, weaker for image-text comparisons, and lowest for text-text comparisons. Aligned Machine is designed to evolve over time as participation grows, supporting longitudinal analysis, domain-specific studies, bias detection, and measurement of concept drift across model versions. By combining accessible public participation with rigorous comparative evaluation, HASB provides a scalable and accountable framework for auditing semantic alignment in embedding models.
evidence_items.title: Aligned Machine: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal Embedding Similarity via Human Comparative Judgements

evidence_items.summary: Frontier models are increasingly used to discover real-world security vulnerabilities, making it critical to systematically evaluate their cybersecurity capabilities. However, existing security benchmarks primarily focus on known vulnerabilities in open-source projects, largely overlooking closed-source binaries, which underpin much of the software industry. In this paper, we ask: how effective are frontier models at uncovering deep vulnerabilities in production binaries? To answer this question, we present DeepBinary, the first comprehensive benchmark for open-ended vulnerability discovery in Windows kernel binaries. Given a target binary, an agent analyzes it using a disassembler and kernel debugger in network-isolated VMs and reports each vulnerability with a crashing proof of concept (PoC). Unlike existing benchmarks, DeepBinary replays every report on fresh VMs and employs an LLM-based judge to assess its validity, uniqueness, and impact (estimated by bug bounty values). Beyond known vulnerabilities, DeepBinary also enables the discovery and validation of previously unknown (0-day) vulnerabilities. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of representative open- and closed-weight models (including GPT-6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) across diverse coding agents (including Codex and Claude Code) on 12 target binaries. In total, they discover over 200 vulnerabilities with an estimated aggregate bounty of $661,000, including 146 distinct previously unknown vulnerabilities across all experiments. Our results further reveal substantial differences in models' ability to analyze binaries, conduct experiments, and sustain vulnerability discovery over long horizons. Overall, DeepBinary makes long-horizon, open-ended vulnerability discovery in complex binaries measurable, revealing fundamental differences in how frontier models analyze and explore such systems.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Open-Ended Vulnerability Discovery in Windows Kernel Binaries

evidence_items.summary: Agentic benchmarks report a success rate that confounds distinct causes of failure: misreading the environment, never working out how components of the environment operates, operating the components in the wrong order, and failing to recover from a mistake, each of which calls for a different fix. We present an early preview of MultiNet v2.0-Gridworld - an interactive maze environment built for attribution rather than ranking. Four different types of mechanisms, namely key-door pairs, switch-gate pairs, distractors and decoys, and ordered combinations of these mechanisms, can be added, modified, or removed independently while the renderer, the action space, and the scoring function stay fixed. A breadth-first search over the joint state of position, facing direction, inventory, and mechanism state gives every instance an exact optimal action count, which sets its difficulty and grades unfinished episodes. We fix the evaluation protocol on 15 held-out mazes over 540 episodes, then evaluate three vision-language models on 50 mazes. They solve 6 of 150 episodes, 45 of the 50 mazes were not solved by any model, and no episode containing a switch-gate mechanism was solved.
evidence_items.title: Attributing Agentic Failure in Reasoning Vision-Language Models with Interactive 2D Environments

evidence_items.summary: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/
evidence_items.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake

evidence_items.summary: The development of autonomous machine learning (ML) agents capable of end-to-end data science workflows represents a significant frontier in artificial intelligence. These agents must orchestrate complex sequences of data analysis, feature engineering, model selection, and hyperparameter optimization, tasks that require sophisticated planning and iteration. While recent work on building ML agents has explored using large language models (LLMs) for direct code generation, tool-augmented approaches offer greater modularity and reliability. However, existing tool-use benchmarks focus primarily on task-specific tool selection or argument extraction for tool invocation, failing to evaluate the sophisticated planning capabilities required for ML Agents. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating tool-augmented ML agents using a curated set of 61 specialized tools and 15 tabular ML challenges from Kaggle. Our benchmark goes beyond traditional tool-use evaluation by incorporating an in-memory named object management, allowing agents to flexibly name, save, and retrieve intermediate results throughout the workflows. We demonstrate that standard ReAct-style approaches struggle to generate valid tool sequences for complex ML pipelines, and that tree search methods with LLM-based evaluation underperform due to inconsistent state scoring. To address these limitations, we propose two simple approaches: 1) using shaped deterministic rewards with structured textual feedback, and 2) decomposing the original problem into a sequence of sub-tasks, which significantly improves trajectory validity and task performance. Using GPT-4o, our approach improves over ReAct by 16.52 percentile positions, taking the median across all Kaggle challenges. We believe our work provides a foundation for developing more capable tool-augmented planning ML agents.
evidence_items.title: ML-Tool-Bench: Tool-Augmented Planning for ML Tasks

evidence_items.summary: The rapid advancement of reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs) has led to notable improvements on mathematical benchmarks. However, many of the most commonly used evaluation datasets (e.g., AIME 2024) are widely available online, making it difficult to disentangle genuine reasoning from potential memorization. Furthermore, these benchmarks do not evaluate proof-writing capabilities, which are crucial for many mathematical tasks. To address this, we introduce MathArena, a new benchmark based on the following key insight: recurring math competitions provide a stream of high-quality, challenging problems that can be used for real-time evaluation of LLMs. By evaluating models as soon as new problems are released, we effectively eliminate the risk of contamination. Using this framework, we find strong signs of contamination in AIME 2024. Nonetheless, evaluations on harder competitions, such as CMIMC 2025, demonstrate impressive reasoning capabilities in top-performing models. MathArena is also the first benchmark for proof-writing capabilities. On IMO 2025, top models achieve slightly less than 40%, demonstrating both notable progress and significant room for improvement. So far, we have evaluated over $50$ models across seven competitions, totaling $162$ problems. evidence_items.summary: Decision models are language models fine-tuned to return a probability for each option of a typed query, which routers and guardrails threshold directly. They are built on multilingual bases but ranked almost entirely in English. We evaluate 25 top-ranked open-weight decision models on 17 tasks in 14 languages, comparing each language with English on parallel items. Every model loses accuracy in every language, from about 2 points in high-resource languages to 8 in Tamil, while confidence falls only half as much: a threshold set for 95\% accuracy in English yields 90% in Tamil. The size of the loss is set by the language and the base model rather than by leaderboard rank. In 81 controlled fine-tuning runs, task skill learned in English transfers to other languages and a few thousand target-language items narrow large losses, but neither more data nor full-parameter tuning closes them. Finally, the same test items are answered more accurately in all 23 benchmark--language pairs we compare when an LLM rather than a person translated them, so LLM-translated test sets understate the gap.
evidence_items.title: Lost in Translation, Not in Confidence: Benchmarking and Calibrating Multilingual Decision Models

evidence_items.summary: When a household financial narrative is the input to an automated assessor, its assessment may differ from the assessment of the profile and financial snapshots the narrative was generated from. We present a task-specific study of these assessment differences in synthetic narratives under two generation conditions. A generator–jury framework links household simulation, the assembly of each household's profile and snapshots into a survey, narrative generation, and separate assessment of surveys and narratives by a two-tier large language model (LLM) jury. Each assessment gives a financial-health score from −5 to +5 and two ranked contributing factors; the survey-based assessment serves as the same model-derived reference for both conditions. Narrative assessment is blinded: the jury applies the same criteria to each narrative without access to its survey or reference. The baseline and candidate conditions differ in prompt instructions and thinking mode. Agreement between narrative-based and survey-based assessments, which we call assessment consistency, is compared across the two conditions on the same households, using the same generator and the same jury configuration. Across the narratives of 8,102 common eligible households, the candidate reduced mean absolute health-score discrepancy (MAE) from 1.775 to 1.202 score points, a 32% reduction relative to the baseline. Mean squared discrepancy (MSE) fell by 45%; the smaller squared mean discrepancy accounted for 75% of this MSE reduction, reflecting a smaller average downward score offset. Post hoc Spearman analysis showed less similar household ordering: rank correlation with survey-based scores decreased from 0.764 under the baseline to 0.728 under the candidate. Average gains concealed increased MAE among households assigned negative survey-based scores by the jury. A complementary numeric check found that traceable figures could coexist with substantial score disagreement.
evidence_items.title: Synthetic Household Financial Narratives: A Dataset and Evaluation Study

evidence_items.summary: This repository accompanies the manuscript entitled “Reflection Interference, Cross-Dataset Generalisation and Spatial-Support Constraints in Automated Pupil Localisation: An Empirical and Mathematical Benchmark”. The study comprises six experimental phases examining reflection restoration, resolution-dependent detection, multiscale geometric estimation, supervised coordinate regression, participant-separated evaluation, cross-dataset generalisation and spatial-support constraints using the MRL Eye Dataset and Labelled Pupils in the Wild (LPW). The repository contains research notebooks, a numerical replication script, 28 aggregate experimental tables, mathematical analysis results, numerical figures, software environment documentation, a data dictionary and reproducibility documentation. Numerical replication using privately retained prediction records successfully reproduced all nine final scientific tables and passed 17 principal numerical checks across 249,626 prediction records. No discrepancies were reported in recalculated localisation errors, detection-validity indicators, threshold-based accuracy or geometric lower-bound verification. The public archive excludes raw eye images, videos, frame-level prediction records and trained models pending confirmation of their redistribution conditions. Consequently, complete prediction-level numerical replication requires access to the corresponding research records. The investigation characterises pupil-localisation performance and failure mechanisms. It does not establish clinical diagnostic performance or claim superiority over state-of-the-art pupil detectors.

evidence_items.summary: Real-time autoregressive video generators stream minutes of video and accept new prompts on the fly, but struggle to keep people, objects, and places consistent over a long interactive story. Agent systems provide such memory for offline multi-shot generation, yet they read the whole script in advance, plan each shot before generating it, and regenerate failed shots, which a live stream does not allow. We present Agentic LongLive, an asynchronous agentic memory for long video generation. A memory agent on separate GPUs reads only the prompts revealed so far, never the generated video, and keeps a text state and evolving images for every person, object, and scene. From this entity memory it composes a global image and a per-shot memory image, which an auxiliary GPU prefills into the generator's attention sink before the next shot starts, and writes entity cards for the prompts that name them, so the video never waits for memory and video errors are not written back. A small language model, trained with reinforcement learning and an image reward calibrated using downstream video outcomes, decides what to remember before the next prompt is known. On LongStory-Online, a new benchmark of 25 stories (857 shots) revealed one shot at a time, Agentic LongLive improves persistent-state accuracy of LongLive-2.0, its base generator, by 26.3 points, protagonist identity by 44.9, and revisited-place consistency by 40.4, at about 1% extra generation time on H100. The full system streams faster than real time on one 8xB200 node with the generator in BF16 (34.3 FPS), keeps image quality stable over 14-minute stories, and improves identity on two MiniMax-H3 generators, one of which, LongLive-H3, also runs in real time with it. To our knowledge, it is the first real-time video generator with text and image memory kept by an LLM agent.
evidence_items.title: Agentic LongLive: Asynchronous Agentic Memory for Long Video Generation

evidence_items.summary: As agents based on vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly interpret social-media content, errors in their analysis may lend credibility to rumors and amplify their spread. In this paper, we study the problem of visual cognitive collusion, in which coordinated posts combine authentic images and locally faithful captions to induce VLM agents to infer and accept attacker-chosen target claims through their own reasoning. To enable systematic evaluation of this cognitive threat, we introduce a new benchmark comprising 544 target cases and 33.2K candidate images across eight application domains. We further propose VisualMontage, a multi-agent framework for simulating such attacks through narrative planning, image selection and ordering, and caption assignment under iterative review. We evaluate this threat through extensive experiments across 12 vision-language models, examining modality effects, production-team components, and downstream defenses. Using identical attack feeds across models without victim-specific optimization, we demonstrate cross-model transferability, achieving mean attack success rates of 61.93% for proprietary models and 68.71% for open-weight models. Moreover, 92.65% of generated feeds pass independent model-based validity auditing. Even after downstream review, residual attack success rates range from 35.3% to 76.7% across the evaluated configurations. Our additional controlled comparisons further reveal that captions can improve model-rated posting naturalness while reducing attack success. Together, these findings reveal a novel cognitive threat in social-media interpretation and motivate safeguards that assess how authentic posts jointly shape agents' reasoning and conclusions.
evidence_items.title: VisualMontage: Manipulating the Beliefs of Vision-Language Agents with Authentic Image Sequences

evidence_items.summary: Introduction Each donated organ creates an urgent coordination challenge because clinical evidence, allocation priorities, and institutional approvals must be brought together quickly, securely, and transparently. Existing approaches support parts of this process, but ranking, information review, record protection, and workflow governance remain separate. This fragmentation obscures how evidence informs a recommendation and the authorized actions that follow. Methods We present an integrated blockchain and large language model (LLM) decision support system connecting transparent ranking, constrained note review, deterministic safeguards, encrypted records, and authorized workflow actions. Structured attributes establish organ-specific reference rankings. The LLM only assigns predefined readiness states from notes, receives no rank information, and cannot select recipients. The safeguard excludes candidates on temporary hold and preserves the order of those remaining, while smart contracts govern the workflow. We evaluated the system using a synthetic dataset informed by public organ allocation guidance and clinically relevant compatibility, urgency, logistics, and readiness factors. The dataset comprised 1,600 training, 320 validation, and 400 independent test cases balanced across kidney, liver, heart, and lung workflows. Results Fine-tuned Qwen and GPT-4o mini returned valid and complete outputs in 93.0% and 97.0% of cases, with macro F1 scores of 99.3% and 99.6% among valid and complete outputs, respectively. When every candidate in an unsuccessful case was counted as incorrectly classified, the corresponding overall macro F1 scores were 95.3% and 98.0%. The selected primary recipient agreed with the synthetic reference in 372 and 387 cases, respectively. In a post hoc robustness analysis, all 20 scenarios produced the expected selection or stopped safely without creating a decision.
evidence_items.title: An integrated blockchain and large language model decision support system for organ donation and transplantation workflows

The experiments evaluate the impact of visual data compression and downsampling on communication efficiency and 6-DoF pose-estimation performance. Four image resolutions are evaluated: 1920×1080, 1280×720, 640×360, and 360×240. JPEG quality levels of 100%, 75%, 50%, and 25% are included in the compression experiments. The dataset also contains experiments performed at different marker distances and under moving-marker conditions. The recorded metrics include frame rate (FPS), received data rate, pose-estimation time, normalized pose-estimation accuracy, reprojection/pixel error, stability, and tracking accuracy. 2. Client-side performance logs (5 CSV files) These files contain additional runtime measurements collected on the client side during experimental sessions. The recorded metrics include capture time, encoding time, sending time, frame rate (FPS), CPU usage, and memory usage. These measurements provide additional information about the computational and communication overhead associated with the client-side processing pipeline. 3. Network monitoring logs (3 CSV files) These files contain network-level measurements collected during separate experimental sessions. The recorded metrics include round-trip time (RTT)/latency, jitter, packet loss, download bandwidth, and upload bandwidth.

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) connected biomedical devices, wearable sensing, medical imaging analytics, electronic health record (EHR) intelligence, genomics, smart home monitoring, and telehealth platforms have opened new possibilities for proactive detection. Yet their impact remains constrained by fragmented implementation, limited interoperability, insufficient clinical integration, and unresolved governance challenges. This paper develops global agentic healthcare intelligence (GAHI) as a sociotechnical framework for integrating AI-enabled healthcare intelligence technologies in ageing systems. It introduces the sociotechnical health intelligence transformation model (SHITM), which explains transformation as the alignment of technological intelligence, healthcare value creation, and societal legitimacy. Using comparative framework synthesis and integrative literature review methods, the article evaluates 30 healthcare intelligence technologies based on clinical relevance, early detection capability, AI maturity, scalability, governance risk, ageing applicability, and implementation readiness. The analysis proposes an early detection capability index (EDCI) and a governance risk score (GRS) to support structured evaluation. GAHI is then articulated as a six-layer architecture comprising data acquisition, intelligence processing, agentic decision systems, clinical intelligence, governance and compliance, and population health intelligence (HI). The framework advances biomedical engineering, health informatics, AI governance, gerontechnology, and sustainable health-system design by moving from isolated digital applications toward interoperable, explainable, privacy-preserving, and clinically actionable intelligence ecosystems.
evidence_items.title: Global Agentic Healthcare Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Modern deepfake methods can create fake faces that are very difficult to detect just by watching a video. Therefore, practical deepfake-detection systems must be accurate while using limited computing resources. CNN-based methods analyse individual frames and can identify visual signs of manipulation, but they may miss unnatural changes between consecutive frames. Video Transformers can analyse these changes over time, but they usually require substantial computational power. A more practical approach is to combine CNNs for analysing facial details with recurrent and attention-based models for studying changes across frames. However, only a limited number of studies have tested such combined methods on realistic videos containing multiple people, where some faces may be manipulated while others remain genuine. This paper describes and evaluates an integrated architecture for video-level deepfake classification. Spatial features are extracted by an EfficientNet-B0 backbone augmented with a multi-scale, attention-refined feature path; the resulting 1,280-dimensional frame embeddings are processed by a two-layer bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) network with an additive temporal attention mechanism that rescales each frame representation by a learned weight; and the weighted sequence is refined by a single-layer Transformer encoder with four attention heads before temporal averaging and binary classification. Training employs gradient accumulation, mixed-precision arithmetic, chunked frame processing, exponential moving averaging of parameters and differential learning rates, enabling 45-frame sequences to be trained on a single 12 GB consumer graphics processing unit. The architecture was evaluated on a subset of the FFIW-10K benchmark using a held-out evaluation set of 1,987 instances, comprising 998 real (50.23%) and 989 fake (49.77%).
evidence_items.title: An Integrated Spatio-Temporal Architecture for Deepfake Video Classification: An Evaluation on the FFIW-10K Multi-Person Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We develop the concept of bounded delegated agency to explain how AI shopping services reduce consumer effort while preserving decision authority. Drawing on delegation, self-determination and service-value perspectives, we analyse two respondent-level datasets (N = 1,920) using factorial regression models with HC3 robust standard errors and bootstrap-based indirect association analysis. Results indicate that greater AI autonomy increases perceived task offloading, while reversibility reduces perceived agency encroachment and strengthens continued delegation intention, without demonstrated improvements in preference congruence or recommendation discrimination. Under high autonomy and low reversibility, consumer-priority disclosure is associated with an 8.91-percentage-point increase in recommendation acceptance compared with commercial-objective disclosure. Measurement summaries satisfy conventional reliability and validity thresholds. However, unavailable execution logs constrain causal interpretation and verification of actual restoration. The findings distinguish psychological reassurance from effective consumer protection, extending AI service research by demonstrating that greater acceptance and perceived control do not necessarily translate into better decision outcomes. Practically, AI service providers should establish explicit execution permissions, reliable reversal mechanisms and transparent objectives while evaluating both consumer perceptions and actual decision protection.
evidence_items.title: Governing agentic AI in marketing: Bounded delegated agency and consumer decision authority in shopping services

evidence_items.summary: Many languages of instruction in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) are poorly represented in the data used to train language models. Before these models can support early-grade literacy in such languages, we need to know whether they hold the linguistic knowledge of each language that literacy teaching relies on. To test this, we present the Linguistic Knowledge Benchmark and the reproducible, largely automated pipeline that turns curriculum documents, teacher guides and pupil books into a vetted question set organised on a fixed grid of nine linguistic domains and seven grade levels. The pipeline combines LLM-driven source survey, feature consolidation, item generation and quality control with an item-selection step inspired by item response theory and a final expert review. We instantiate it for Kiswahili (Kenya; 135 items) and English (United Kingdom; 137 items) and evaluate 121 and 119 models respectively. Frontier models exceed 90% accuracy in both languages, but accuracy falls steeply for smaller and cheaper models, and more so in Kiswahili. The two best models under 10 billion parameters reach 91.7% and 73.0% in English but only 51.9% and 40.7% in Kiswahili, and the mean accuracy of models deployable on mobile and tablet hardware is 47% in English against 24% in Kiswahili. The models most practical for low-resource classrooms are therefore the least capable in the languages they would serve. We release a 20-item sample per language, all pipeline prompts, open-source code, and a public leaderboard. This is the first rung of a three-level evaluation ladder for measuring and generating decodable text to support foundational literacy.
evidence_items.title: The Linguistic Knowledge Benchmark: Do Language Models Know the Foundations of Early-Grade Literacy?

evidence_items.summary: Knowledge graph foundation models such as ULTRA achieve zero-shot link prediction on unseen graphs through dedicated architectures that hard-code a transfer mechanism. In this work we move that mechanism out of the architecture and into the representation, by \emph{reifying} the input graph: every fact becomes a node, connected to its subject, object, and relation type through a fixed vocabulary of six meta-relations, with relation types as anonymous shared nodes rather than model parameters. On this representation, five textbook GNNs (GAT, GINE with sum and with mean+max aggregation, GraphSAGE, R-GCN), each trained on a single knowledge graph of 4,245 triples for 30 minutes on one NVIDIA A100, transfer zero-shot to 40 inductive link-prediction benchmarks. The best of them, an off-the-shelf GAT, matches ULTRA, a dedicated foundation model pretrained on three graphs, across ULTRA's own evaluation suite. The same fixed vocabulary extends to relational databases, a row becoming an entity and a foreign-key column a relation type; a preliminary probe on two unseen databases, with no cell values, schema text or in-context labels, shows a model of this family pretrained on three knowledge graphs ranking foreign-key targets far above random-initialization and degree controls. We release the code, the checkpoints, and the evaluation pipeline for all 40 benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: Reification as a Transferable Vocabulary: Zero-Shot Link Prediction with Vanilla GNNs

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The Thai Textile Research Dataset (v2.4 Gold) is an open-access, calibrated, and audit-certified benchmark designed for machine learning, pattern recognition, and computational analysis of indigenous weaving traditions across Thailand. Curated under rigorous Q1 academic verification criteria, the repository encapsulates 308 master specimen images ($N = 248$ verified for supervised benchmark learning) and 655 standardized, non-overlapping $512 \times 512$ pixel patches divided into leak-free training ($N = 469$), validation ($N = 98$), and test ($N = 88$) partitions. The dataset integrates calibrated optical captures across two distinct modalities: high-resolution photographs of authentic handwoven textiles ($N = 272$) and reconstructed digital pattern structural charts ($N = 36$). Every specimen is annotated with rich mathematical, folkloric, and spatial metadata—including discrete mathematical symmetry classifications ($p1$, $pm$, $D 2$, horizontal frieze bands, and $p2$), 16-grid homogeneity indices, CIEDE2000 colorimetric scales, weaving techniques, geocoordinates, provenance, and original institutional attributions. The entire dataset adheres strictly to the FAIR Guiding Principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable), conforms 100% to international research ethics standards, contains zero personal identifiable information or human imagery (PDPA compliant / Object-Only), and operates under certified open redistribution agreements.
evidence_items.title: Thai Textile Research Dataset: A Calibrated Multi-Modal Benchmark for Geometric Symmetry, Motif Taxonomy, and Visual Feature Extraction (v2.4 Gold)
