evidence_items.summary: This repository contains the source code accompanying the manuscript “AI-enabled uncertainty-aware embryo ranking from time-lapse imaging for development-stage IVF decision support.” The code implements a reproducible research pipeline for uncertainty-aware embryo prioritisation from public time-lapse imaging data. The framework combines deep visual representation extraction, sequential latent-state modelling with an adaptive unscented Kalman filter, conservative uncertainty-penalised embryo ranking, and offline contextual-bandit evaluation using morphokinetic proxy rewards. The implementation supports multiple temporal sampling regimes, including the base, F15, F30, and F45 variants, and produces dataset indices, train/validation/test splits, ranking outputs, off-policy evaluation summaries, diagnostic tables, and publication-oriented figures. The archive also includes baseline evaluation code, figure-generation utilities, configuration files, run scripts, tests, and documentation intended to support transparent reuse and independent inspection. The code is provided for retrospective method-development and reproducibility purposes only. It is not a clinical device, does not perform validated implantation or live-birth prediction, and should not be used for autonomous clinical decision-making.
evidence_items.title: AI-enabled uncertainty-aware embryo ranking from time-lapse imaging for development-stage IVF decision support - Source Code

evidence_items.summary: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-to-multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) generators predict spatial protein expression from routine histology, yet pixel-level marker reconstruction does not establish downstream utility. We present HEmIF-Bench, evaluating five frozen generators across eight datasets spanning molecular, cellular, tissue, and patient scales. HEmIF-Bench decouples internal encoder features from generated outputs, benchmarking both against the pathology foundation reference UNI2. Mirroring the clinical workflow where pathologists rely on mIF to define cell phenotypes, delineate tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) and germinal centers (GCs), and stratify patient risk, we evaluate external CD3 recovery, single-cell classification, dense nuclear segmentation, TLS/GC segmentation, and patient survival prediction. Across the benchmark, foundation-model-based MIPHEI-ViT leads among the generators, while non-foundation models show task-specific strengths. Comparing the two routes reveals that internal encoder features generally outperform generated outputs, and larger output marker panels do not guarantee stronger downstream utility across datasets. Moreover, neither internal encoder features nor generated outputs consistently surpass frozen UNI2. These findings show that pixel-level stain fidelity does not equate to downstream utility, and that generators trained at current paired-data scales have yet to surpass large-scale pure-H&E foundation models. With the expansion of paired translation cohorts and the advancement of foundation-based generative architectures, HEmIF-Bench establishes a definitive benchmark for tracking when H&E-to-mIF generation crosses the threshold to deliver genuine value beyond routine histology for tumor microenvironment analysis and precision oncology.
evidence_items.title: HEmIF-Bench: Benchmarking H&E-to-mIF Models Beyond Virtual-Stain Fidelity

evidence_items.summary: Identifying and solving partial differential equations (PDEs) from sampled solution data often requires substantial expert effort in equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration, especially under noise and distribution shifts. Can large language model (LLM) agents automate this workflow accurately and efficiently? To investigate this question, we introduce RSI-PDEbench, a benchmark of 1,001 cases spanning 42 equation templates, including both classical and fractional PDEs. It provides three evaluation settings: Full evaluates performance on noise-free solution data; Noisy tests robustness to Gaussian noise with an RMS equal to 50\% of the clean-signal RMS; and Hard-OOD tests challenging out-of-distribution generalization to unseen equation templates and shifted coefficient ranges. We further introduce RSI-PDE, a recursively self-improving agent harness that shortlists candidate equations by residual loss, uses relative $L^2$ feedback to refine coefficients and numerical solvers, and applies a validation gate to policy and memory updates. We compare RSI-PDE with single-run baselines and native agent harnesses (Claude Code or Codex) across four frontier models. Across the three settings, RSI-PDE improves the pass rate averaged across the four models by 106.5--181.9\% relative to single-run baselines and by 3.0--19.6\% relative to native harnesses, while reducing total recorded model calls by 46.9\% across the 12 model--setting pairs. These results highlight the potential of validated recursive self-improvement in LLM agents to advance scientific computing.
evidence_items.title: RSI-PDEbench: A Benchmark for Self-Improving Agents in PDE Solving

evidence_items.summary: Large-scale text-to-image foundation models have achieved remarkable visual realism, yet generating human images with correct anatomical structures remains challenging. Existing approaches enforce anatomical constraints through part-specific modules or localized loss weighting during supervised fine-tuning on high-quality human photos, but such datasets are limited and often provide ambiguous optimization signals due to confounding factors such as lighting, pose, and background. Preference-based alignment offers an alternative, but standard Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) treats all pixels equally and therefore fails to exploit the localized nature of anatomical artifacts. To address this, we propose the framework of Alignment via Synthetic Anatomical Preference (ASAP), which constructs controlled preference pairs through a localized degradation mechanism applied to high-fidelity human images. This mechanism performs a controlled experiment on images by introducing explicit anatomical errors in targeted regions while preserving the remaining content. With this mechanism, we create the Human Anatomical Preference (HAP) dataset with over 10K curated pairs for effective anatomical alignment of text-to-image human image generative models. To better leverage the locality of these controlled preference pairs, we introduce a localized and margin-bounded variant of DPO that prioritizes optimization in targeted anatomical regions while enforcing a finite preference margin to prevent over-optimization and preserve global semantics. We further introduce HAF-Bench, a benchmark for systematic evaluation of anatomical fidelity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ASAP consistently reduces anatomical errors across multiple foundation models while maintaining overall image quality.
evidence_items.title: Towards Anatomically Plausible Human Image Generation via Synthetic Localized Preferences

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models have demonstrated remarkable reasoning capabilities in various visual tasks. However, their abilities in K12 scenarios are still systematically underexplored. Previous studies suffer from various limitations including narrow subject coverage, insufficient data scale, lack of diversity in question types, and naive answer-centric evaluation method, resulting in insufficient exploration of model capabilities. To address these gaps, we propose K12Vista, the most comprehensive multimodal benchmark for Chinese K12 subject knowledge understanding and reasoning to date, featuring 33,000 questions across five core subjects from primary to high school and three question types. Moreover, beyond the final outcome, we are also concerned with the correctness of MLLMs' reasoning processes. For this purpose, we meticulously compiles errors from MLLMs' reasoning processes and leverage an automated data pipeline to construct K12-PEM-800K, the largest process evaluation dataset offering detailed step-by-step judgement annotations for MLLMs' reasoning. Subsequently, we developed K12-PEM, an advanced process evaluation model that integrates an overall assessment of both the reasoning process and answer correctness. Moreover, we also introduce K12-PEBench, the first high-quality, human-annotated benchmark specifically designed for evaluating abilities of reasoning process evaluation.Extensive experiments reveal that current MLLMs exhibit significant flaws when reasoning within K12Vista, providing critical insights for the development of more capable MLLMs.We open our resources at https://github.com/lichongod/K12Vista.
evidence_items.title: K12Vista: Exploring the Boundaries of MLLMs in K-12 Education

evidence_items.summary: Visual context is a powerful cue for object recognition: scenes inform what, where, and at what scale objects are likely to appear. Yet over-reliance on context becomes a failure mode when models predict objects based on their typical neighbors rather than the objects' own visual features, which we call typicality bias. While extensively studied in the pre-Transformer era, it has often been assumed that architectural and scale improvements would naturally solve it, and a systematic diagnostic across the modern vision stack remains absent. We provide such a diagnostic framework. We measure typicality bias via normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI) over object pairs, and introduce STRANGE-Bench (Synthetic Typicality-RANked Grounded Evaluation Benchmark): a photorealistic, layout-controlled benchmark spanning 17 sub-tiers from typical to never-co-occurring object pairs. Across five model families (specialist detectors, open-vocabulary detectors, self-supervised, vision-language, and multimodal large language models) and three recognition tasks (supervised detection, open-vocabulary detection, and classification), the bias is prevalent: gaps of 5-11 p.p. persist when objects appear outside their typical company, and do not consistently shrink with scale. To mitigate it, we turn to data augmentation: existing augmentations are designed for visual diversity, not for breaking co-occurrence shortcuts, and sample from the very distribution that produces typicality bias. We propose Anchor-Atypicality Sampling (AAS), a simple sampling rule for paste-based augmentations that uses the NPMI signal to tilt the training-time co-occurrence distribution toward atypical partners. AAS reduces the typicality gap by up to 1.6 p.p. on natural-image COCO splits and 23.0 p.p. on synthetic STRANGE-Bench across three model families, without sacrificing overall performance.
evidence_items.title: Stranger Things: When Objects Appear Without Their Typical Neighbors

evidence_items.summary: Cross-modal place recognition (CMPR) matches natural language descriptions against databases of geo-tagged reference images, enabling localization without visual queries. Despite its potential for language-guided navigation, existing vision-language models lag far behind visual place recognition (VPR) baselines, even after task adaptation. Unlike general-purpose text-to-image retrieval, place recognition relies on subtle local cues to distinguish visually similar locations. We therefore hypothesize that a primary bottleneck in CMPR is capturing fine-grained correspondences between image regions and text details, which requires higher visual token granularity, strong text representation capacity, and local cross-modal matching. To address this challenge, we propose CrossPlace, a two-stage CMPR framework. Stage 1 performs global retrieval by pairing a jointly aligned DINOv2-B/14 visual backbone with a progressively fine-tuned BGE-Large text encoder, while Stage 2 refines top candidates using a lightweight token-level cross-attention reranker. Through systematic analysis, we isolate the drivers of retrieval accuracy and show that visual token density provides the largest performance improvement, while text encoder capacity and task fine-tuning offer complementary gains. To evaluate robustness under realistic conditions, we also extend CMPR evaluation to city-scale and severe weather and illumination settings. Across all existing and new benchmarks, CrossPlace achieves double-digit Recall@1 improvements over prior cross-modal methods, closes the gap to unimodal text retrieval, and narrows it to unimodal VPR. Code and benchmarks are available at https://github.com/oferidan1/CrossPlace
evidence_items.title: Towards Closing the Performance Gap in Cross-Modal Place Recognition

evidence_items.summary: To avoid the quadratic cost of dense attention over long contexts, models such as DeepSeek-V4 and Hy4 have turned natively sparse, and speculative decoding, which matters most where decoding is slowest, increasingly runs on them. Their drafters, however, still keep a context cache of their own, over the whole prompt or a sliding window. Beyond memory, such a cache costs prefill time, prefix-cache hits and decode concurrency. Drafters that read the target's cache avoid one of their own, but settle only which cache, not which positions, and still read everything or a recent window. Neither rule is made for the query at hand, and computing a selection per query in the drafter would cost more as the context grows. Yet a natively sparse target already picks positions for each query, over a cache it keeps anyway. Both of the drafter's choices are therefore already made, and paid for, by the target: its cache and its selection. We measure how far one selection carries: made a step early, it still covers close to nine tenths of what each later token selects on DS-V4.1-Flash. We present DFly2, a block-parallel drafter that shares the target's sparsity. Each draft layer reads the KV its paired target layer cached (KV sharing), at the positions that layer's indexer selected, a fixed number anywhere in the context (Index sharing). DFly2 thus runs no scoring pass and keeps no cache of its own. On DS-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Hy4~flash, whose sparse attention and architecture differ, it accepts more tokens per step than DFlash and DSpark trained on the same recipe, over general, long-context and agentic benchmarks. Its margin over the stronger baseline widens from 3.9%-10.5% on general workloads to 10.0%-31.5% on long-context and agentic ones. At high concurrency on DS-V4.1-Flash, at matched per-user decode speed, its throughput is 62% and 81% higher on two 64K sets.
evidence_items.title: DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target's Sparsity

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in video understanding, yet existing video question answering (VQA) benchmarks mainly evaluate models in offline settings. Real-world streaming scenarios instead require models to answer context-dependent queries by retrieving and reasoning over evidence distributed across the video history. We introduce StreamRecall, a benchmark for context-aware Multi evidence reasoning in streaming video QA. StreamRecall requires models to retrieve, associate, and reason over temporally scattered evidence to answer queries at the appropriate moment. It contains 4,983 questions over 462 videos, with context-aligned query times and fine-grained temporal evidence annotations. We further propose the Evidence Utilization Cascade to diagnose model reasoning through evidence localization, grounding, chain completion, and answer derivation. To enable efficient long-term streaming reasoning, we present EviStream, a training-free causal visual memory mechanism that preserves reasoning-critical evidence under a fixed KV budget. Experiments reveal substantial gaps between current VLMs and realistic streaming requirements, establishing StreamRecall as a foundation for developing evidence-aware streaming video intelligence.
evidence_items.title: Recalling the Past to Answer the Present: Context-Aware Multi-Evidence Reasoning for Streaming Video Question Answering

evidence_items.summary: Social intelligence in a robot requires interpreting a situation from the perspectives of the people involved and using that understanding to decide when and how to act. We introduce LUDIUS, a benchmark for evaluating how vision-language models exercise this judgment through a robot's verbal responses and actions, organized around 15 social intelligence skills drawn from social psychology, sociology, and cognitive science. LUDIUS comprises six editions, each a collection of episodes spanning one simulated week. Three editions each cover all 15 skills in a different household. The other three focus on interactions involving multiple people, safety, and context-specific norms, respectively. We evaluate frontier models and a smaller model finetuned on social-interaction data we generated, using a common evaluation harness. The harness supplies each model with the robot's camera views and residents' reactions, retrieves relevant interaction history, and converts the model's tool calls into robot verbal responses and actions. Models tend to perform worse when they must reason about what a resident saw or heard earlier, reconcile competing interests, or fulfill a request within safety constraints and household rules. Beyond the home setting, LUDIUS's design pipeline offers a way to construct social intelligence benchmarks by translating social intelligence skills into context-specific judgments and observable robot behavior.
evidence_items.title: LUDIUS: A Benchmark for Embodied Social Intelligence in Everyday Human-Robot Interactions

evidence_items.summary: World models are increasingly used in robotics to improve the performance of embodied models. Compared with general-purpose video generation, robotics places more stringent requirements on world models. Generated videos must satisfy fine-grained physical constraints on robot motion and object interactions. However, existing world model benchmarks can overlook robotics specific physical details and struggle to assess them accurately. To address this problem, we introduce WorldPhy, a world model benchmark for accurate, fine-grained evaluation of physical plausibility in robotics. Our benchmark contains 300 tasks, each consisting of an initial-frame image and a task instruction, covering diverse robotics scenes, task categories, viewpoints, and robot configurations. We further collect over 12K high-quality human annotations, and use them to train WorldPhyReward to accurately provide scores and reasons across six fine-grained physical dimensions and an instruction-following dimension. Comparisons with general VLMs and existing reward models show that WorldPhyReward better aligns with human ratings. We system- atically evaluate 13 frontier open and closed-source world models. The results reveal that current world models struggle to consistently maintain fine-grained physical plausibility across different robotics scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/chuziyuan139/ WorldPhy.
evidence_items.title: WorldPhy: Benchmarking Fine-Grained Physical Plausibility of World Models in Robotics

evidence_items.summary: Generating coherent and explorable 3D worlds from scattered images with little or no visual overlap is a fundamental and long-standing challenge in computer vision, which existing geometry-aware methods fail to address. Meanwhile, existing image- and video-based methods may generate unseen regions but produce inconsistent geometry across views. To bridge this gap, we present WorldBridge, a framework for coherent and controllable 3D world generation under scattered images with little or no visual overlap. WorldBridge encodes scattered references into a global scene context to guide geometry and appearance generation across views. Our temporal and spatial reference attention mechanism further enhances the fidelity of temporal references along the target trajectory and supports flexible spatial references outside it. A plug-and-play latent-reference consistency strategy improves reference fidelity through reprojection-guided test-time optimization. We also introduce the WorldBridge benchmark suite to evaluate 3D world generation from scattered, low-overlap references, which is rarely explored by current benchmarks. Both qualitative and quantitative results demonstrate that our method enables controllable and coherent 3D world generation, surpassing the existing state-of-the-art solutions. Our project page is available at https://davidyan2001.github.io/WorldBridge/.
evidence_items.title: WorldBridge: Bridging Scattered Views for Coherent 3D World Generation

evidence_items.summary: LLM-based user simulators are increasingly used to evaluate conversational assistants. Yet, these simulators can drift from their assigned goals or fail to exhaustively explore all specified options, causing evaluation errors incorrectly attributed to the assistant. Prior work has examined goal alignment in single-task settings, but many practical scenarios require simulators to execute multi-step workflows with sequential tasks, fallback logic, and cross-task dependencies, where simulator fidelity has not been measured. To close this gap, we introduce a benchmark of 500 workflows represented using the Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) abstraction. Our experiments reveal that the simulator's fidelity degrades sharply with workflow complexity, and that goal drift accounts for the majority of failures. Fidelity also depends on the assistant's response style, with the same simulator scoring substantially better or worse across styles. To address this, we propose ReUST (Reasoning + User State Tracking), a simple prompting strategy to maintain state information across dialogue turns. ReUST improves goal success rate by more than 12 points for mid-sized and large models, and reduces simulator sensitivity to the assistant's response style.
evidence_items.title: Reliable User Simulation in Complex Multi-Step Workflows

evidence_items.summary: Diagnosis of congenital heart disease (CHD) requires understanding the spatial relationships between cardiac structures, which clinicians assess by scrolling through CT or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) slices and rotating 3D reconstructions. Although automated methods have advanced cardiac segmentation, identifying congenital heart defects from volumetric scans remains an open challenge. The two existing approaches rely on handcrafted diagnostic rules limited to static anatomical abnormalities. We introduce CHD-Bench, the first benchmark for interactive CHD diagnosis, defining a multi-label task and evaluation protocol over 247 CT and MRI scans from three cohorts covering 38 CHD types. We also present CHD-Harness, open-source software that runs a VLM in a 3D Slicer environment through 22 tools, manages each examination, and records the resulting diagnosis and supporting views. We evaluate off-the-shelf medical, open weight, and closed weight VLMs and compare them with a 3D CNN classifier and published rule-based results. Gemini 4 Argon with CHD-Harness achieves the highest macro F1 across all three cohorts (0.63, 0.63, and 0.43). Allowing for interactive examination raises its macro F1 by up to 20 points over static views. These results establish CHD-Bench and CHD-Harness as a foundation for developing and evaluating VLMs for interactive CHD diagnosis.
evidence_items.title: CHD-Bench: Diagnosing Congenital Heart Disease through Interactive Examination

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can write and repair RTL, but successful compilation or testbench execution does not establish defect removal, behavioral preservation, security, or implementation feasibility. Existing LLM-based RTL repair methods often report a single repair rate without retaining separate evidence for these properties, limiting reproducible comparison and integration into hardware design flows. We present REFORGE, which, to our knowledge, is the first LLM-assisted RTL repair framework that maintains and accumulates structured repair evidence across iterations, allowing it to generate fixes that satisfy multiple objectives simultaneously, including functionality, behavioral equivalence, security, and cost efficiency. REFORGE profiles buggy RTL, identifies structural and security-relevant features, localizes failing behavior, and uses verification-guided diagnosis to generate complete RTL repair variants. Each variant undergoes syntax checking, simulation, formal analysis, off-trigger preservation, security re-scan, and synthesis-based power, performance, and area analysis. We implement REFORGE as a backend-independent repair-and-verification flow and evaluate it in 288 runs across three LLM backends and three benchmark suites. On CirFix, the proposed context and diagnosis increase runs delivering a checked repair from 32/63 to 51/63, while every configuration repairs the Hack@DAC OpenTitan defect. Evidence records also show that a testbench-only criterion reports 3.9 times more repairs than the full set of applicable checks, security-clean outputs may lack functional verification, and different RTL repairs can implement equivalent hardware. These results show that LLM-generated RTL repairs require explicit multi-stage verification evidence rather than a single pass/fail outcome.
evidence_items.title: REFORGE: LLM-Assisted RTL Bug Repair with Structured Context and Verification Feedback

evidence_items.summary: Visual language models (VLMs) have demonstrated exceptional capabilities across various multimodal tasks, but they remain susceptible to hallucinations, undermining their reliability. Existing hallucination benchmarks primarily focus on identifying hallucinations and describing their manifestations, often neglecting their underlying causes. Specifically, multimodal hallucinations can stem from two distinct failure modes: text modality bias (TMB), reflecting an over-reliance on misleading text input; and language prior (LP), reflecting a reliance on previously learned knowledge. To differentiate these failure modes, we propose VTK-Bench, a benchmark that explicitly separates three information sources: visual information (V), textual information (T), and prior knowledge (K). By establishing mutually exclusive answers corresponding to V, T, and K, VTK-Bench enables fine-grained attribution analysis of model responses. Furthermore, we introduce discrete attribution and soft attribution metrics to characterize information source preferences. Extensive experiments on 11 representative open-source VLMs show that LP is more prevalent than TMB in most evaluated models. Notably, TMB decreases substantially with model scaling, whereas LP exhibits relatively limited improvement and remains the dominant failure mode. These findings highlight the importance of different information source preferences for a deeper understanding of multimodal hallucinations.
evidence_items.title: VTK-Bench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Distinguishing Language Priors and Text Modal Bias in Visual Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Dental caries assessment is a structured clinical process requiring lesion localization, identification of the affected tooth and surface, and severity grading rather than simple image-level recognition. 3D intraoral scans (IOS) preserve detailed dental geometry and surface morphology and support standardized rendering from complementary viewpoints, enabling fine-grained visual assessment while introducing a distinct need for anatomically grounded multi-view reasoning. Despite recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and dental vision-language benchmarks, existing evaluations do not jointly assess hierarchical arch-to-tooth-to-surface reasoning, cross-view evidence integration, and surface-level caries assessment. To address this gap, we introduce CariesBench, a hierarchical benchmark constructed from 5,932 3D IOS, comprising 85,455 standardized multi-view renderings and 133,994 clinically grounded visual question answering instances with expert quality control. CariesBench comprises three complementary task families: Arch-level Clinical Screening (ACS), Tooth-level Diagnostic Reasoning (TDR), and Structured Clinical Decision-Making (SCD). Using the CariesBench training set, we further fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct to obtain IntraoralGPT. Extensive evaluation of 24 representative baseline MLLMs reveals a substantial benchmark-level performance disparity between arch-level screening and tooth-level diagnostic reasoning, with higher accuracy on ACS than on TDR. CariesBench-specific supervision substantially improves the Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct baseline, increasing the 19-task macro-average clinical accuracy from 52.7% to 69.5% and TDR Overall from 34.4% to 44.7%.
evidence_items.title: CariesBench: A Hierarchical Multi-view Benchmark for Dental Caries Screening and Diagnostic Reasoning from 3D Intraoral Scans

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) evaluations provide two response types: probabilities assigned to correct answers and binary indicators of correctness. Restricting evaluation to one type narrows the range of available models or discards probability information. We propose a method to integrate both types through a common two-parameter logistic item response model and fractional-response quasi-maximum likelihood estimation. The framework includes binary-only models in common-scale evaluation without discarding available probabilityinformation; broader measurement coverage does not by itself ensure greater precision or measurement equivalence. Simulations evaluate statistical efficiency when both response types have the same expected value. Moreover, adding probability respondents improves item calibration more efficiently than adding binary respondents. However, adding noisier binary responses to an already precise probability sample can increase estimation error under equal observation weights. An application to Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) combines probability response data from the Open LLM Leaderboard with binary response data from Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) and reveals model-family response patterns, differences in item characteristics, and systematic ability shifts between evaluation protocols. The proposed framework extends common-scale IRT evaluation to models with different response formats while highlighting the roles of observation variability and evaluation-protocol comparability in statistical efficiency and interpretation.
evidence_items.title: Joint Estimation of Abilities and Item Parameters for Large Language Models Using Probability and Binary Responses: A Fractional-Response IRT Framework

evidence_items.summary: An RGB-D camera that films an object being moved, often from one viewpoint, sees one side of it and how its parts move. We present ArtKit, which takes such a video as input to create an articulated model with complete parts, a kinematic tree, and typed joints. Our central idea is generating the hidden geometry and verifying it against what the camera sees. A generative part prior proposes complete, part-decomposed geometry based on the first frame. Point tracks, grouped into rigid trajectories, split and merge the generated parts into links. We then fit revolute and prismatic joints, with a visibility-aware energy ensuring that the articulated model explains the depth observed across the video. A rule checks against the video to choose between synchronous group fits and per-frame chain fits, so that one pipeline serves a diverse range of articulated objects, such as household items and robotic hands. Finally, we regenerate each link of the chosen fit as one part and keep it wherever it agrees better with the observations. We evaluate on Articulate-100 and on HArt, a new benchmark of 60 PartNet-Mobility objects and 8 robotic hands and grippers rendered as RGB-D videos with ground-truth parts and joints. ArtKit reduces the axis and part motion errors of the strongest baseline by more than half on the objects, as well as the axis error on the hands. ArtKit also runs on real recordings and generated videos.
evidence_items.title: ArtKit: Motion-Driven Re-Segmentation and Link Re-Generation for Articulated Objects from RGB-D Video

evidence_items.summary: AI systems are increasingly capable of producing machine-checked Lean proofs of advanced mathematical results. Real mathematical formalization, however, is not isolated theorem proving: it requires building the definitions and intermediate lemmas that connect a result to a formal library. Existing evaluations often provide isolated theorem statements in settings where much of this supporting theory is already available in Mathlib. We introduce AutoformBench, a benchmark of 341 Lean 4 formalization tasks drawn from 24 advanced mathematical sources. Lean-experienced mathematicians formalized and audited each target statement, leaving the corresponding Lean proof to the evaluated agent. Each problem is embedded in a broader mathematical development: agents receive the informal proof but must translate it into Lean while constructing the missing definitions, intermediate lemmas, and supporting infrastructure. We compare the performance of frontier models on these problems. We find a largely shared difficulty frontier: success depends less on mathematical domain than on models' ability to construct missing formal infrastructure. Data and code at https://github.com/facebookresearch/autoformbench
evidence_items.title: AutoformBench: A Lean Formalization Benchmark for Advanced Mathematics

evidence_items.summary: Continuous bedside waveforms record rapid physiological changes that can inform clinical decisions. Existing benchmarks examine selected prediction conditions, but it remains unclear how model advantages depend on signal duration, warning time, and available inputs across care settings. We introduce Actionwave, a benchmark for waveform-centric clinical prediction across intensive-care, operating-room, and emergency-department settings. Actionwave uses a common decision-time prediction interface and groups clinically grounded tasks by what is inferred and when. It varies conditions relevant to clinical use, including the warning required before an intervention. We compare diverse architectures and pretrained biosignal encoders under specified model-size and compute budgets. The protocol requires patient-level splits, strict information cutoffs, and comparisons that isolate individual modeling factors. Across 20 tasks and 1.4M task-labelled windows from source datasets, the experimental grids account for over 87,000 model fits. These comparisons identify task-specific choices and show why matched cohorts, unimodal controls, and explicit timing are necessary when interpreting waveform model performance.
evidence_items.title: Actionwave: A Systematic Benchmark for Waveform-Centric Clinical Prediction Across Care Scenarios

evidence_items.summary: Existing benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) in hardware design evaluate downstream artifacts such as generated RTL, assertions, or testbenches. When a model fails, it may have misread the specification or understood it and failed to write the code. We present SpecRead, a benchmark that isolates specification comprehension from generation ability. SpecRead v2.2 contains 383 questions over 10 open-source OpenTitan IP blocks in four types: exact retrieval, cross-section reasoning, contradiction detection in mutated specifications, and spec-RTL consistency checking, plus 41 distractor controls and 41 consistent-RTL controls. Type-4 items use real RTL mutations retained only when Icarus Verilog simulation shows a behavioral change. A with-spec vs. without-spec ablation suggests the questions require the excerpt rather than training recall alone, though it does not rule out memorization of the unmutated source text helping a model spot mutations. Ministral-3B scores 33.7% overall (129/383). On t3, verdict-plus-location accuracy is 48.0% with a 51.2% distractor false-positive rate. On t4, the violation-vs.-compliant decision is effectively degenerate (MCC -0.06, balanced accuracy 49.5%), flagging all 41 consistent-RTL controls; location accuracy remains measurable at 79.2%. Layered scoring suggests, as a hypothesis, that the fine-grained violation taxonomy is the hard part, though the category labels are not independently validated. A rule-table prompting intervention on a 60-question sample lowers accuracy on every type except t2 (tied). SpecRead is automatically scorable by deterministic checks, with gray-zone cases counted wrong under the conservative main scoring, regenerable for type-3 items via mutation injection, and built exclusively from public sources.
evidence_items.title: SpecRead: A Benchmark for Measuring Whether Language Models Understand Hardware Specifications

evidence_items.summary: Reasoning models produce long traces of intermediate decisions and tool calls, making test-time verification important for ensuring correctness. Existing approaches either verify only the final answer, which misses early errors, or rely on branch-and-verify strategies that explore multiple trajectories. We introduce interwhen, a single-trajectory verification framework that steers model behavior by providing feedback on intermediate reasoning traces. It addresses two key challenges. First, given a set of verifiers, obtaining verifiable states from the reasoning trace typically requires prompt engineering or external task decomposition into fixed steps. Instead, we propose a monitoring system that periodically polls the reasoning trace and forks inference of the reasoning model to recover intermediate states. Verifiers are run asynchronously alongside generation, adding negligible overhead on correct executions and intervening only when violations occur. Second, beyond math and code, a central challenge for process verification is the scarcity of verifiers. interwhen addresses this through automatic verifier synthesis from natural-language policy documents. Given a policy, it can generate code-based verifiers, including provably correct verifiers in Lean and z3. Together, these contributions yield a plug-and-play test-time verification system that can improve task completion and policy compliance of any reasoning agent. On reasoning benchmarks where policies encode mathematical or logical constraints, interwhen achieves near-perfect accuracy for reasoning models using a fraction of the tokens of baselines. On agentic benchmarks with policy-based verifier generation, it enables improvements in task quality for SLMs without any finetuning, e.g., task completion rate of Qwen3-30B jumps from 32% to 87% on the telecom domain in tau2-bench. Code at https://github.com/microsoft/interwhen.
evidence_items.title: interwhen: A Generalizable Framework for Steering Reasoning Models with Test-time Verification

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable multimodal information processing and reasoning ability. When equipped with tools through function calling and enhanced with retrieval-augmented techniques, compound LLM-based systems can access closed data sources and answer questions about them. However, they still struggle to process and reason over large-scale graph-structure data. In this technical report we introduce the GDS (Graph Data Science) agent. The GDS agent introduces a comprehensive set of graph algorithms as tools, together with preprocessing (retrieval) and postprocessing of algorithm results, in a model context protocol (MCP) server. It is accompanied by a skill that guides the LLM through graph analysis. The agent can be used with any modern LLM out-of-the-box. GDS agent allows users to ask any question that implicitly and intrinsically requires graph algorithmic reasoning about their data, and quickly obtain accurate and grounded answers. We introduce new benchmarks that evaluate intermediate tool calls as well as final responses, and the results indicate that the GDS agent solves a wide spectrum of graph tasks. We also demonstrate how the GDS agent can perform open-ended analyses at the level of domain experts, on tasks such as money laundering tracing and pattern mining in biology. Finally, we discuss the remaining challenges and the future roadmap.
evidence_items.title: GDS Agent for Graph Algorithmic Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Clustering algorithms are fundamental tools across many fields, with density-based methods offering particular advantages in identifying arbitrarily shaped clusters and handling noise. However, their effectiveness is often limited by the requirement of critical parameter tuning by users, which typically requires significant domain expertise. This paper introduces a novel density-based clustering algorithm loosely inspired by the concept of selective attention, designed to minimize reliance on parameter tuning for most applications. The proposed method computes an adaptive threshold to exclude sparsely distributed points and outliers, constructs an initial cluster framework, and subsequently reintegrates the filtered points to refine the final results. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate the robustness, accuracy, and ease of use of the proposed approach, establishing it as a powerful alternative to conventional density-based clustering techniques.
evidence_items.title: SACA: Selective Attention-Based Clustering Algorithm

evidence_items.summary: Poetry-to-video generation requires more than translating text into visual scenes. Poetic language is highly compressed, often depends on historical and cultural knowledge, and frequently conveys meaning through metaphor, imagery, and other non-literal expressions. We introduce PoVi, a benchmark and agentic framework for grounded poetry-to-video generation, evaluating semantic grounding, discourse coherence, and audiovisual realization. PoVi reconstructs poem semantics into an evidence-bounded representation and progressively transforms them into narration, interpretation, character assets, and shot-level visual plans, followed by narration-aligned video generation. Across three planning backbones and four video generators, PoVi consistently improves over single-call generation, with the largest gains on implicit background knowledge and metaphorical relations. PoVi provides a testbed for studying knowledge-grounded, long-horizon multimodal generation beyond direct text-to-video synthesis.
evidence_items.title: PoVi: Agentic Poetry-to-Video Generation with Knowledge Grounding and Figurative Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Autonomous research agents are emerging as a promising approach to scientific problem-solving across disciplines, owing to their growing ability to improve a solution through repeated experiments. Evaluating this ability requires benchmarks that pose open-ended research problems and measure improvements over established scientific methods. We introduce REE (Research Entrance Exam), a benchmark that tests AI agents on scientific research. It consists of 100 open-ended research problems spanning five broad scientific areas and 23 domains. To ensure high quality, every problem is drawn from active research in its field and individually reviewed by domain experts. Each problem is posed as a task of iterative improvement: an agent has up to 12 hours to improve a working starter solution, and REE scores the result on a common scale against an established expert solution evaluated under comparable conditions. By this measure, two of the four frontier agents we evaluate, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, outperform the expert solutions on 86% and 81% of problems, across all five scientific areas. Their runs also show how they do so: both agents surpass the expert solutions within the first two hours on average, and their best solutions mostly tailor or combine established methods of the field. REE thus provides a unified framework for evaluating autonomous scientific research, capturing both improvements over established methods and the research processes behind them.
evidence_items.title: REE: A Scientific Research Entrance Exam for AI Agents

evidence_items.summary: This dataset provides a heterogeneous collection of network traffic and system-level security data acquired in a controlled, enterprise-like network environment. It was developed to support research into intelligent cybersecurity applications, including network anomaly detection, attack classification, behavioral analysis, and the analysis of application-layer payloads and system logs. The collection combines realistic benign activities, nine controlled attack scenarios, and supplementary records representing potentially suspicious behavior. Data were acquired from multiple sources and processed into formats suitable for cybersecurity analysis and machine learning. Dataset Contents The dataset includes: Benign network traffic: 93 packet capture files and 1,114,057 extracted unidirectional network flows. The flow records contain network communication metadata and extracted application-layer payloads, where available. Malicious network traffic: 20 packet capture files and 241,619 extracted unidirectional network flows, representing nine controlled attack scenarios. The flow records include network communication metadata and extracted application-layer payloads, where available. Suspicious activities: A supplementary collection of 4,410 CSV records covering eight categories of potentially suspicious network behavior. These records contain only information derived from network packet headers, without application-layer payloads or associated packet captures. System and service logs: Approximately 596,000 Windows and Linux log events, providing host-level observations. The availability of both raw packet captures and structured flow records in the benign and malicious traffic collections enables analyses at different levels of granularity, including statistical traffic analysis and application-layer content analysis. The suspicious activity collection provides additional header-derived information for investigating potentially unusual network behavior.

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have offered a new path for misinformation detection, but the reliability of model-generated auxiliary information and the applicability of detection results in new scenarios have yet to be verified. Some representative studies and related methods have been classified into three types in this paper: content-driven, context- and relation-driven, and knowledge- and evidence-driven methods. Factual reliability, generalisation reliability and the reliability of explanations and evidence are introduced. According to the comparison of previous experiments, semantic augmentation, simulation of user behaviour and logical reasoning can all improve the detection rate in specific circumstances; however, the level of improvement differs depending on the dataset and model parameters. This suggests that method selection should depend on the available information and the specific detection scenario, rather than classification scores alone. Based on the above results, this article analyzes and evaluates issues such as data contamination, synthetic data bias, and external evidence reliability, providing reference for the selection and evaluation of detection methods.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model-Driven Misinformation Detection: Methods, Trustworthiness Evaluation, and Challenges

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Heart-sound denoisers are often judged by reconstruction fidelity under artificial noise, leaving diagnostic preservation after transfer insufficiently characterised. We built a multi-corpus benchmark rather than proposing a new architecture. Criterion-based panel construction defined an executable panel of ten learned denoisers trained on a common source corpus, four classical filters and an identity control. We evaluated five 300-recording arms from four phonocardiogram corpora (1,333 unique recordings). Paired comparisons covered 18 artificial-corruption conditions and their no-added-noise passthroughs in three arms, plus two original-recording arms without paired clean references, using four fixed classifiers. Uncertainty used patient clustering where identifiers were available, recording clustering otherwise, and a parent-recording sensitivity analysis for PaHS. Mean AUROC change was +0.014 on the denoiser-development corpus but -0.085 and -0.081 on two external corpora. On external no-added-noise inputs, some learned denoisers reduced AUROC by up to 0.380 and attenuated approximately 91\% of magnitude within detected cardiac-event regions on BMD-HS. On original BMD-HS recordings, the largest AUROC reduction was 0.387, with a 0.767 sensitivity loss at the pre-denoising threshold. Development-distribution benefit therefore did not establish diagnostic preservation after transfer. Target-corpus task effects, no-added-noise behaviour and fixed operating points should be evaluated before integration into a diagnostic pipeline.
evidence_items.title: A multi-corpus benchmark reveals limits of diagnostic preservation in heart-sound denoising

evidence_items.summary: This dataset accompanies the preprint “CoCoFlex: steering a pretrained structure generator with cryo-EM particle images to model continuous conformational variation,” available on Langtaosha Preprints . It provides atomic conformational ensembles, reconstructed density maps and numerical source data for two simulated benchmarks (CAHRA Challenge 2 and an MD-derived TGFBIp ensemble) and four experimental systems (MSP-1, HER2, TRPV1 and PfCRT). The structural files include benchmark ensembles, conformations sampled along latent principal directions, initial predictions, coordinate-guidance targets, and models after guidance and canonical refinement. A separate archive contains PULCHRA-completed and restrained-relaxed benchmark structures, including the two map-aligned relaxed MSP-1 models used in Fig. 4d. The four original map collections contain particle-group reconstructions, half maps and masks. The refined map archive contains 12 HER2 and TRPV1 full maps obtained through focused 3D classification and local refinement, together with four refinement masks. Numerical source data include ensemble metrics, stereochemical assessments, wing-centroid distances, Fourier shell correlations, model–map correlations, regional motion measurements and local-resolution summaries. The deposit contains eight ZIP archives and a README. Extract all archives into the same directory, with cocoflex results source data.zip last, to assemble the cocoflex results folder. The README and source-data indices identify the models, maps, masks and processing stages used in the manuscript. Coordinate-frame information is provided in the README and map frames.json .
evidence_items.title: Data for CoCoFlex: steering a pretrained structure generator with cryo-EM particle images to model continuous conformational variation

evidence_items.summary: Gradient-flux (GF) approaches present an important chance to expand ecosystem-atmosphere observations beyond the gases routinely measured using eddy covariance (EC) alone. We developed a dataset to explore when and where gradient-flux approaches work across diverse ecosystems. We utilized standardized observations from 47 terrestrial sites within the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) to develop this continental benchmark dataset for evaluating the performance of three GF approaches, the modified Bowen ratio (MBR), aerodynamic (AE), and wind-profile (WP) methods, against co-located EC measurements of CO2 and H2O. This multi-site benchmark dataset comprises EC and GF fluxes by method and sampling height pair, along with corresponding micrometeorological data. Additional data include: storage fluxes, gradient-flux ensembles, site-level canopy complexity and metadata for tower geometry and sensor heights, ustar thresholds, metadata for validation sites, site canopy attributes, site concentration profiles, and site sampling height pairs.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark dataset for comparing eddy covariance measurements and gradient flux calculations across 47 National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) flux towers, August 2021 - August 2026

evidence_items.summary: This repository contains the supplementary materials and experimental data supporting the research article "Conversational Retrieval of System Dynamics Models by Feedback Structure Using Signed Causal Graphs". The corpus of 63 System Dynamics models is published separately (doi:10.5281/zenodo.18047724), and the 37 topical scenarios of Set 1 with their relevance judgments are part of the dataset of the previous study (doi:10.5281/zenodo.22164313). The dataset is divided into four components: the structural query set (Set 2), the aggregated run outputs, the per-block checkpoints, and the run manifest. 1. Structural Query Set (Set 2) File graphrag-set2.csv: The 40 structural scenarios. Each row contains the scenario number, the domain, three phrasings of the same request (a broad intent, a refinement and an expert query) and the identifiers of the relevant models (GoldenUuids). Scenarios with the domain Theory are structural requests without a topical anchor (scenarios 19, 20, 23 to 29, 32 and 35). File graphrag-set2-goldspec.jsonl: The gold structural specification of each scenario, one JSON object per line. A specification can contain loop constraints (polarity R or B, involves terms, minimum length), constraints on archetype, behaviour mode, external forcing and model size, a strength (must or should) for each constraint, and curated synonym lists for the involves terms. The relevant models in graphrag-set2.csv were computed from these specifications by the independent oracle. File set2-archetype-scenarios.txt: The scenarios that carry an archetype constraint (21, 22 and 23), used for the descriptive comparison of H with H-noarch. 2. Aggregated Run Outputs All runs used .NET 10.0 on Windows 11 (AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 7840U, CPU only), with five sampling seeds (42, 7, 123, 1234 and 2026), giving 120 blocks and 4,620 scenario executions. All CSV files are semicolon-delimited and UTF-8 encoded. Numeric values use a decimal point.

evidence_items.summary: Computer-using agents are increasingly expected to complete realistic user goals rather than isolated GUI actions. However, existing benchmarks typically isolate web, mobile, or desktop environments, leaving it unclear whether a single generalist agent can execute long-horizon workflows that span multiple operating systems and persistent application states. We introduce OS-Omni, a live cross-platform benchmark and execution environment for evaluating computer-using agents across Windows, Ubuntu, macOS, iOS, Android, and Web environments. OS-Omni is released in versioned waves of 300 tasks each; this paper focuses on the first release, v1, which contains 48 tasks per platform and 12 cross-platform workflows that pair a desktop with an Android phone. OS-Omni provides reproducible initialization, platform-specific adapters, trajectory logging, and executable final-state evaluators, and includes controlled service-backed applications for workflows involving account, cart, budget, calendar, message, and other persistent state. Human studies show that OS-Omni tasks require 67.54 interaction steps, substantially exceeding OSWorld references of 15.0 steps. On v1, the strongest evaluated agent, Claude Opus 5.5, reaches 68.5% average success, trailing the 77.3% human reference by 8.8 points; the gap is uneven across platforms, with frontier models exceeding humans on Linux but trailing them by more than 25 points on iOS and macOS. These results indicate that current agents remain far from platform-robust, long-horizon computer use, especially when success requires sustained state tracking and durable final-state changes.
evidence_items.title: OS-Omni: Benchmarking Generalist Computer-Using Agents on Long-Horizon Workflows Across Platforms

evidence_items.summary: In-context learning (ICL) lets agents acquire new rules from context and adapt to user-specific requirements at inference time. The same frontier agents now operate both computers and robots, yet their ICL remains insufficiently assessed: existing benchmarks are largely offline, rely on text or static images, and risk training-data contamination, while robot evaluations are limited to method-level ablations. We present ICLWorld, an online benchmark that evaluates the ICL of agents from digital to physical worlds, covering computer use and robot use, together with UIverse, a unified harness that turns every environment into a user interface. We build 30 environments, record 630 demonstration videos (10+ hours), and design 160 tasks with customized, often counter-intuitive rules that cannot be satisfied without learning from the context. Each task comes with three rule versions, given as text or video, and we test generalization at three levels, from replaying the demonstration to new instances and unseen environments. Across six frontier models, the strongest agents, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, succeed on 82% and 76% of computer-use runs but only 27% and 26% of robot-use runs, and a no-rule control reduces success to at most 8%. GPT-6 Astra succeeds under all three rule versions on only 38% of computer-use tasks, half its rate under a single rule, and answers 98% of robot rule questions correctly yet completes only 20% of these tasks. Frontier agents learn rules comparably well from video and from text and transfer them across environments, whereas weaker agents rely on text and lose most of their video-based success once the demonstrated situation is resampled. These findings reveal substantial gaps between the digital and the physical world and between identifying a rule and acting on it.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for clinical decision support, yet scalable and specialty-specific methods for evaluating their performance and safety remain limited. We developed RheumBench, the first rubric-based LLM benchmark in rheumatology, providing a specialist-validated framework for open-ended evaluation. We evaluated ten systems, comprising three frontier proprietary general-purpose LLMs, one frontier open-weight general-purpose LLM, and six clinical retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems, including two certified medical products and one rheumatology-specific RAG system. RheumBench comprised 100 clinical cases (70 diagnostic and 30 diverse clinical management) and 1,020 case-specific rubric criteria independently reviewed and weighted for clinical appropriateness and potential harm by two board-certified rheumatologists. Systems were evaluated for answer quality, prompt sensitivity, potential harm, diagnostic accuracy, and system confidence. Responses were scored by a three LLM judge panel, yielding 50,553 rubric-level LLM evaluations, with high agreement with rheumatologist consensus (Cohen’s κ = 0.91). Overall system performance (0-100%) varied substantially, with a maximum RheumBench score of 54.0% (Claude Fable 5), and frontier general-purpose LLMs generally outperformed clinical RAG systems, including certified Prof. Valmed and DR.INFO. Management case performance varied widely, with thorough prompting improving mean management scores in 9 of 10 systems and yielding a peak score of 72.9% with GPT-5.6 Sol. Potentially severe errors occurred with all systems and were predominantly omission errors. In predominantly rare-disease cases, top-1 accuracy reached 57.1% (GPT-5.6 Sol) and top-3 67.1% (Claude Fable 5). Self-reported system confidence was generally high and diagnostic calibration analyses showed systematic overconfidence for all systems, with the lowest Brier score of 0.203 (Claude Fable 5).

evidence_items.summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are increasingly used for structured prediction, yet their suitability for healthcare applications remains uncertain because predictive performance alone does not establish fairness, probabilistic reliability, or robustness. We developed a multidimensional benchmark to compare four TFMs: TabFM, TabPFN, TabDPT, and TabICL, against Logistic Regression and XGBoost across a curated, standardized suite of ten WHO-aligned healthcare classification datasets across diverse disease domains. Additionally, we harmonized clinical schemas, standardized protected sex attributes and outcome targets, and released both balanced-scale and natural-prevalence variants of the datasets to establish a benchmarking resource in healthcare machine learning. All models were evaluated using identical five-fold stratified cross-validation partitions and standardized preprocessing. Performance was assessed using 20 metrics spanning predictive discrimination, sex-based fairness, probability calibration, and robustness to Gaussian feature perturbations. A composite Clinical Model Evaluation Score (CMES) was used to summarize performance across these dimensions. Google TabFM achieved the highest mean CMES (0.8811), followed closely by TabDPT (0.8796), TabICL (0.8775), TabPFN (0.8756), XGBoost (0.8650), and Logistic Regression (0.8549). The Friedman test indicated significant differences among models (χ2F (5) = 24.914, p = 1.45 × 10^−4; Kendall’s W = 0.498). However, post-hoc comparisons revealed no statistically significant differences among the four TFMs after Holm correction. TFMs generally demonstrated stronger discrimination and probabilistic calibration than conventional baselines, with TabFM achieving the highest mean Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (0.9327) and the lowest expected calibration error (0.0674).
evidence_items.title: Tabular Foundation AI Models in Healthcare: A WHO-Inspired Benchmark for Responsible AI and Trustworthiness

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in spatial omics have enabled tissue atlases spanning serial sections, donors, and experimental technologies. Aligning these datasets is essential for comparing spatial organization, reconstructing three-dimensional tissue architecture, and registering sections to a common coordinate framework. However, systematic comparisons of alignment accuracy, computational efficiency, and usability remain limited. Here, we benchmarked 15 tissue alignment and registration algorithms using experimental and simulated spatial transcriptomics datasets across pairwise alignment, three-dimensional reconstruction, cross-resolution alignment, and atlas registration tasks. We assessed spatial-domain and cell-type correspondence, spatial gene-expression similarity, computational scalability, and usability. Simulated datasets with known spatial coordinates additionally enabled direct evaluation of geometric accuracy and reconstruction stability. No single method performed best across all settings: performance depended on the task, spatial resolution, and tissue characteristics, and strong pairwise alignment did not necessarily translate into reliable three-dimensional reconstruction. Evaluation metrics captured complementary aspects of alignment quality, highlighting the importance of using multiple criteria for comprehensive assessment. These findings provide practical guidance for method selection and identify priorities for improving the accuracy, scalability, and accessibility of spatial omics alignment.
evidence_items.title: A systematic benchmark evaluation of algorithms for 3D tissue alignment and registration with spatial omics

evidence_items.summary: This study presents an exploratory benchmark of object-detection architectures and explainability methods for dermoscopic skin lesion images. It compares model performance and explanation properties under a controlled, dataset-specific protocol, without assessing clinical effectiveness or screening readiness. Thirty-two model variants spanning seven detector families (YOLOv8, YOLOv9, YOLOv10, YOLOv11, YOLOv12, YOLOv26, and RT-DETR) were evaluated on four lesion classes—basal and squamous cell carcinoma (BCC + SCC), invasive melanoma (MI), melanocytic nevus (N), and pigmented benign keratosis (PBK)—as well as negative images of healthy skin. Models were filtered by recall, mAP@50–95, and inference time, then prioritized using a study-specific per-class score that emphasized malignant-lesion recall. This descriptive procedure selected a common reference detector for paired XAI comparison and was not subject to statistical inference. YOLOv8m was designated as the reference (recall 79.3%, mAP@50 81.9%, inference time 4.2 ms; BCC + SCC recall 69.4%). Because each detector was trained once and selection used test-set results, these findings neither provide an independent post-selection estimate of YOLOv8m’s generalization nor establish its superiority. A paired comparison with instance-segmentation models trained on the same data found no significant differences in recall or mAP@50 across 22 architecture variants, whereas detection was significantly faster on the study hardware. Seven XAI methods were compared using 337 true-positive detections from the reference detector. Under the original evaluation protocol, LayerCAM achieved the strongest localization and robustness at low computational cost, whereas LIME and D-RISE showed the strongest faithfulness. Additional evaluations confirmed the high localization performance of LayerCAM using polygon annotations but revealed the influence of detection geometry, feature level, and architecture-related factors.
evidence_items.title: An Exploratory Technical Benchmark of Object Detectors and Explainability Methods for Malignancy-Prioritized Skin Lesion Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Occupancy detection from indoor-environment sensors often exceeds 95% accuracy, but mostly when models are trained and tested in the same room. We rebuilt five public datasets (29 office, lecture, library, and residential rooms in four countries, 128,902 fifteen-minute intervals) from their official releases and evaluated models with chronological splits, within datasets and with the target dataset held out (leave-one-dataset-out, LODO). With temperature and CO2, the mean AUROC fell from 0.900–0.927 to 0.809–0.844, and F1 at the default threshold fell from 0.68–0.76 to about 0.50. With illuminance, the AUROC fell only from about 0.97 to 0.92–0.96, but F1 still fell from 0.80–0.84 to 0.64–0.70. A CNN-LSTM and domain adaptation did not close the gap. Over 54 cases, the F1 loss split into ranking and operating-point components of similar median size (0.109 and 0.105). Unsupervised label-shift correction did not raise F1, whereas a threshold set on the labeled day before each test day raised the mean F1 from 0.50 to 0.61 (logistic regression, no illuminance) but lowered it in 16 of 50 cases. We also found that the indoor-environment data of one public dataset were time-stamped 8 h early, which inverted its illuminance cue. Studies report LODO results and check time alignment, and deployments need a short labeled commissioning period.
evidence_items.title: Can IoT Occupancy Sensors Work in an Unseen Room? A Cross-Dataset Benchmark Using Environmental Sensors

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Accuracies approaching 100% have been reported for fundus disease classification on the ODIR-5K dataset, including 98.2% in our unpublished preliminary pipeline. We quantified how labelling and evaluation shape such figures. Methods: Each image was classified as normal or as one of seven disease categories using eye-level labels from ophthalmologists’ per-eye keywords (5990 images, 3263 patients). Four convolutional neural networks were fine-tuned, tested externally on RFMiD and locally recalibrated. Results: With eye-level labels and patient-level splits, the reference model (EfficientNetB0, 384 pixels) reached a test macro-F1 of 0.659 (95% CI 0.609–0.702) and an accuracy of 70.8% (67.3–74.0%). The preliminary pipeline was trained and evaluated on the same images; its reproduction reached a macro-F1 of 1.000 and 100% accuracy on training images but 0.499 and 53.2% on held-out images. Propagating patient labels to eyes altered 16.4% of labels, and adding fellow eyes to training raised macro-F1 by 0.032 (95% CI −0.004 to 0.068). On four categories shared with RFMiD, macro-F1 and accuracy were 0.815 and 74.9% internally and 0.663 and 75.3% externally. Recalibration raised RFMiD macro-F1 from 0.657 to 0.735 but lowered diabetic retinopathy sensitivity from 0.925 to 0.775. Conclusions: Near-perfect accuracy came from evaluation on training images; fellow-eye leakage inflated performance far less.

README.md describes the generator, the file format and the columns of results.csv.  This version supersedes version 1, whose 2880 instances were generated with the demand scheme of Boctor et al. evidence_items.summary: Preprint (under review). 35-page main article accompanied by Appendices A–G. Software re-engineering is the process of analyzing, transforming, and modernizing existing systems to improve quality, maintainability, and adaptability while preserving critical behavior. Because organizations depend on long-lived software infrastructure, re-engineering plays a fundamental role in sustaining and evolving these systems. Large language models (LLMs) are opening new opportunities across reverse engineering, forward engineering, and assurance, attracting rapidly growing interest: 92.4% of included studies appeared in 2024–2026. We present a systematic mapping study of 1,284 primary studies organized along three facets: re-engineering goals, technological enablers, and automation and interaction strategies. Research concentrates on bounded, code-level tasks, with test generation and code translation accounting for 33.9% of studies, whereas architectural recovery and system generation remain underexplored. Prompting without weight updates dominates (76.4% of adaptation codings), and procedural pipelines outnumber agentic workflows, though this pattern warrants caution given moderate coding reliability. Most studies (87.3%) use benchmarks or open-source repositories; only 10.0% report operational evidence (mainly industry-authored) and 0.8% report longitudinal evidence. Overall, current work advances isolated techniques more than integrated, system-level modernization. We contribute a unified taxonomy, an empirical map, an analysis of evidence limitations, and a replication package, and identify priorities in architectural reasoning, integrated workflows, and operational evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Code Translation: A Systematic Map of LLM-Powered Software Re-engineering

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence promises to help states detect revenue leakage, select tax audits, identify procurement anomalies and administer public resources more consistently. Yet when a predictive score or opaque model influences a tax assessment, the exclusion of a tenderer, or the suspension of a supplier, an apparent gain in administrative efficiency can conceal a transfer of public power from accountable officers to technical systems and private vendors. This article examines that tension in South Sudan through doctrinal analysis of the Transitional Constitution, the Taxation Act 2009 as consolidated in 2021, the South Sudan Revenue Authority Act 2016 as consolidated in 2024, and the public procurement legislation and regulations of 2018 and 2024. It situates those instruments alongside the African Charter, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and carefully delimited comparative scholarship. The central finding is not that South Sudan lacks all procedural protections: tax law requires assessment notices and grants statutory appeals, while procurement law imposes published evaluation criteria, record keeping and administrative review. Rather, these mechanisms require adaptation where machine-generated inferences, training data and vendor-controlled code become material to public decisions. The article develops a legality–intelligibility–contestability framework, distinguishes decision support from automated legal determination, and proposes risk-tiered authorization, disclosure, explanation, human reconsideration and auditable records. Its principal contribution is a practicable, South Sudan-specific model under which AI may assist revenue and procurement functions but cannot displace the public official's statutory duty to decide, give reasons and answer for error.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Revenue Administration and Public Procurement: Due Process, Explainability and Human Oversight in South Sudan

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly participate in political discussions, making it important to understand which positions they support or oppose. We propose a framework for assessing LLMs' political stances through simulated social media interactions. The framework uses politicians' posts and multiple prompting methods to identify consistently expressed stances. Using this framework, we construct WorldPOLL, comprising 4,600 political posts from X/Twitter collected from approximately 200 politicians representing ruling and opposition blocs across 23 countries. Our quantitative analysis shows how support and opposition vary across models, countries, and political directions, while our qualitative analysis identifies the political views and policies models support or oppose. Together, these analyses reveal shared positions across models and differences across national contexts. We also examine whether models express consistent stances across prompting methods, investigate the reasons for disagreement, and assess the effects of model size and instruction tuning in stance inconsistency. WorldPOLL offers a practical way to measure LLM political tendencies, identify the views behind them, and assess their consistency in real-world political discussions.
evidence_items.title: Whose Side Are You On? A Framework and Benchmark for Assessing LLM Political Stances through Politicians Social Media Posts

evidence_items.summary: Autonomous specification engineering requires coding agents to translate functional requirements into executable tests and use the results to discover and validate defects. However, existing benchmarks evaluate coding agents on explicitly specified test generation tasks, commonly providing an issue description, a designated test entry point, or files to inspect, leaving the ability to determine what to test and where to investigate insufficiently evaluated. Relying on such clues bypasses the challenge of mapping requirements to implementations and proactively uncovering unknown defects. We propose SpecEngineeringBench, comprising 100 instances from 78 open-source Python repositories across 16 application categories, with multiple recorded defects in each instance. Two independent tasks evaluate complementary capabilities: generating test suites and discovering defects through execution analysis. The evaluation combines test validity, defect detection, and coverage with localization precision and recall. Across seven frontier coding agents, results reveal that test validity and coverage decouple from defect exposure: agents achieve a 91.47% Head Pass Rate and 80.48% Change-focused Coverage alongside a 26.36% Fail-to-Pass Rate, while localization recall drops from 78.11% at the file level to 51.29% at the function level. Autonomous test generation improves file, function, and hunk localization recall by 4.99, 2.77, and 2.69 percentage points over relying solely on existing repository test suites.
evidence_items.title: SpecEngineeringBench: Evaluating Coding Agents as Autonomous Specification Engineers

authors: Shiying Zhang, Yuxia Zhu, Huaze Xue, Shengqi Dang, Yizhen Wu, Yijie Li
evidence_items.summary: Video recasting aims to transform the entities and environments of existing videos into new visual worlds while preserving their essential actions and interactions. However, achieving coherent transformations remains challenging, as coordinated edits can disrupt the original event structure. In this paper, we introduce RecastAgent, an experience-guided agentic framework for source-conditioned video recasting that operates under frozen model weights. Our framework employs an Experience-Guided Planner to choose edit prompts and input video states under qualitative visual critique, allowing the agent to build upon partial progress or backtrack to preserve source structure. Across tasks, an Experience Accumulation module distills completed trajectories into conditional, evidence-linked principles that record both an editing strategy and its scope of validity. We additionally construct a benchmark of 67 source videos with 134 paired-specification tasks across six creative categories for evaluation. Experiments demonstrate that RecastAgent outperforms single-pass and agentic rewriting baselines across Bernini and Ditto. Furthermore, accumulated experience improves performance on held-out test videos and transfers zero-shot to external benchmarks like FiVE-Bench and VE-Bench.
evidence_items.title: What to Change, What to Keep: Experience-Evolving Agents for Video Recasting

evidence_items.summary: Abstract A random split of a single public dataset is used to score the majority of nutrient-deficiency classifiers. That is only effective if every photograph is a unique specimen. Frequently, it isn't. The score partially assesses recollection of previously seen content because augmented copies are often published alongside their originals, and duplicates of one leaf are randomly dropped into training and test alike. Using two perceptual hashes and a grouping strategy based on seeds that prevents unrelated photos from being chained into a single cluster, we audited all 10,600 images of a banana deficiency collection. Outcome: 4,155 photos, 2,005 groups, and 39.2% of the release. No group held more than six images, and 1,882 of them bridged the raw and augmented folders. That headline number turns out to describe the dataset badly. Every image in the healthy class and every image in the sulphur class sits inside a duplicate group; the other seven classes average 11.0%. Contamination under the 70:10:20 split used for training reaches 27.1% of test images overall—71.6% in healthy, 66.4% in sulphur, and below 11% everywhere else. Six matched runs of MobileNetV3-Large gave 88.45% (SD 0.57) on the random split against 82.73% (SD 0.85) on the group-aware one, a shortfall of 5.72 points (Welch t = 13.7, p < 0.001, 95% CI 4.8 to 6.7). Per-class recall locates it. Sulphur falls 14.3 points and healthy 10.0; no other class loses more than 3.5, while three classes improve, potassium by 9.0. Scoring one trained model separately on the contaminated and clean halves of its own test set gave 92.87% against 85.05%, a 7.82-point gap (p = 1.7 × 10⁻⁶). Balanced accuracy went the other way, 83.42% against 85.40%, because 79% of the contaminated half comes from the two affected classes. Contamination here is real, and it costs accuracy, but it belongs to particular classes rather than to the dataset, and a single percentage is a poor guide to it.
evidence_items.title: Near-Duplicate Contamination Is Concentrated, Not Uniform: A Class- Level Audit of a Public Banana Nutrient-Deficiency Image Dataset and Its Effect on Benchmark Accuracy
