evidence_items.summary: Abstract Reservoir models underpin field development decisions that involve substantial capital investment, yet their quality assurance prior to simulation remains a largely manual process. Experts inspect property histograms, production curves, and parameter files across three heterogeneous data modalities: spatial fields, well level time series, and tabular parameters. This workflow is time consuming, subjective, and structurally blind to defects that arise at the interfaces between modalities. Here we present a quality control framework that decomposes reservoir model inspection into four modality specific detection tasks, then fuses their outputs for integrated assessment. Four specialized algorithms each target a single data type: Isolation Forest identifies statistical outliers in well point residuals, a convolutional autoencoder flags anomalies in geological property planes, an LSTM autoencoder detects contextual anomalies in production time series, and XGBoost evaluates simulation parameter validity. Structured detection outputs are fused through a weighted scoring scheme into component scores, and a large language model guided by a domain knowledge base organizes the evidence and recommends a final quality decision in an evidence traced assessment report. All automated judgments are confirmed by a human expert. Evaluated on the 10 held out test sub-regions of the Baoqing-1 fault block model (partitioned from 50 sub-regions into 35 training, 5 validation, and 10 test) under a blind test protocol, the framework achieved a sub-region level final decision F1 score of 0.89 (9 of the 10 held out test sub-regions correctly decided, with no defective sub-region passing undetected), compared with 0.50 for the industrial rule based baseline and 0.67 for an end to end XGBoost classifier on the same 10 sub-regions. At the parameter judgment level, it achieved a defect detection F1 score of 0.90, reported as a secondary consistency metric.
evidence_items.title: A collaborative multi-model framework with large language model fusion for automated reservoir model quality assurance

evidence_items.summary: Computational reproducibility checks are essential to scientific credibility, yet few published papers are ever independently verified, largely because manual checking is labor-intensive and time-consuming. We tested whether an agentic large language model (LLM) could perform computational reproducibility checks at scale. We benchmarked computational reproducibility checks performed by an LLM analyst (Claude Opus running in the Claude Code harness) against results from expert-led reproducibility audits in the social and behavioral sciences and found that LLM accuracy was comparable to that of human experts. Agentic LLMs can now perform high-quality reproducibility checks relatively cheaply, quickly, and easily, putting large-scale audits within reach for journals, granting agencies, organizations, and individual researchers.
evidence_items.title: Automating Reproducibility Checks Using Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objectives This study aimed to evaluate the agreement between bone age (BA) assessments performed by large language model (LLM)-based applications and BA determined by clinicians using the Greulich–Pyle (GP) atlas, as well as artificial intelligence–based automated bone age assessment systems (ABAAS), in healthy children. Methods A total of 105 children aged 5–14 years, without chronic disease or treatments affecting bone maturation, were included. Left hand–wrist radiographs were evaluated by two clinicians using the GP atlas (Clinician-GP) and subsequently assessed by ABAAS-BoneXpert, RAD Sherpa, SMR-BAM- and LLM-based applications (ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot). Differences (Δ) between LLM and other assessments were analyzed, and intermethod agreement was evaluated using Bland–Altman analyses. Results Of the study participants, 55 were female (51.9 %), and the mean age was 9.42 years. Mean differences between LLM predictions and clinician GP assessments were minimal, particularly for ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot. Agreement analyses demonstrated close concordance between LLM outputs and automated systems, with the smallest discrepancies varying by sex and platform. Overall, the observed differences between the methods were relatively small. Conclusions LLM-based applications can provide results highly consistent with automated systems and clinician-based bone age assessments when appropriate parameters, such as sex and the reference atlas type, are correctly specified.
evidence_items.title: Agreement of automated and clinician Greulich–Pyle bone age assessment with large language model applications in healthy children

evidence_items.summary: In today’s dynamic manufacturing landscape, Flexible Manufacturing Systems (FMS) encounter significant challenges arising from unpredictable disruptions and growing demands for customization. Despite the fact that FMS scheduling issues as a whole have attracted a lot of attention, the scheduling of RFACs has received very little attention. To address this gap, this study employs the notion of the intuitionistic cubic linguistic fuzzy set to manage uncertainty and vagueness inherent in linguistic assessments. To optimize task scheduling efficiency, this study proposes artificial intelligence (AI)-driven fuzzy multicriteria decision making techniques to create an efficient schedule for RFACs. Novel Frank aggregation operators are developed to effectively process uncertain information within the fuzzy environment. Based on these developed operators, an advance AI-driven multicriteria decision making technique is developed to solve uncertainty in decision making problems. In addition an AI-enhanced TODIM method is developed to comparatively assess the performance of RFACs across multiple criteria. Comparative experiments with existing approaches demonstrate that the the proposed AI-enhanced fuzzy decision making models provide reliable and efficient solutions for complex scheduling and evaluation tasks in manufacturing systems, while offering improved decision-making performance under uncertainty.

evidence_items.summary: In the course of an additional investigation campaign for Snowy 2.0, in situ direct shear tests were performed during an early construction stage to validate design parameters which had been, until then, derived from results of laboratory testing. Since the shear strength of pre-sheared discontinuities had been identified as a governing factor regarding the stability of the Power Station Complex, which comprises two large underground caverns, it was considered as indispensable to test relevant features also under in situ conditions. After potential shear features had been identified in the process of geological mapping of a construction tunnel, probe holes were drilled and OTV inspections performed to trace potential features outside the tunnel perimeter. Based on the OTV imagery and the determined orientation of an identified shear feature, a test niche was planned and excavated. Within the niche, two blocks (0.5 m x 0.5 m) were prepared and tested under multistage loading conditions. The tested shear feature, a slickensided bedding parting, exhibited a dip angle between 38° and 40°. The paper describes all required work steps for block preparation and outlines the test execution. The results suggest friction angles between 26° and 29° with negligible cohesion, consistent with expectations for pre-sheared features. The successful execution of these tests under challenging site conditions established a new benchmark for in situ shear testing and provided robust design values for the large underground caverns of Snowy 2.0.
evidence_items.title: In situ direct shear tests on slickensided bedding partings – new benchmark for testing

evidence_items.summary: Background and Objectives: Monetary and physical indicators can yield different assessments of forest-product trade recovery. We examine Russian sawnwood imports into China. Materials and Methods: Annual Base pour l’Analyse du Commerce International (BACI) data for 2017–2024 support fixed supplier groups, four baselines and detailed-product composition checks. Separate United Nations (UN) Comtrade calculations retain original quantity units and use records reporting both weight and volume. Results: From the 2019–2021 baseline to 2024, coniferous unit values, in US dollars (USD) per tonne, rise from 236.70 to 372.29 for Russia and from 385.48 to 392.32 for the matched pool. Russian tonnes retain 62.31% of their baseline, compared with 55.95% for the pool, giving relative retention of 1.114. With a 2021 baseline, the proportions are 74.06% and 75.90%, giving 0.976. In the broad 28-supplier comparison, relative unit-value growth remains 1.514 under fixed baseline product weights. On the same three returned Comtrade records, 2024 unit value rises 14.20% per tonne and falls 2.61% per cubic metre relative to 2021. Conclusions: Recorded unit-value gaps narrow, while absolute physical imports contract. Relative mass assessments depend on benchmark choices; fixed product weights affect the magnitude of relative unit-value growth in broad sawnwood.
evidence_items.title: Russian Sawnwood Imports into China: Narrowing Unit-Value Gaps and Benchmark-Sensitive Mass Comparisons

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Accurate density functional theory descriptions of layered materials require exchange–correlation approximations that remain reliable as the nature of interlayer bonding changes with thickness. Here, we use diffusion quantum Monte Carlo (DMC) to benchmark density functional approximations for bilayer, few-layer, and bulk arsenic. DMC predicts equilibrium interlayer separations near 3.4–3.5 Å for three bilayer arsenene stackings, whereas bulk gray arsenic adopts a substantially more compact structure despite sharing the same nominal adjacent-layer registry with one of the bilayers. This contrast reveals a nontrivial thickness-driven evolution from a large-spacing, weakly coupled bilayer to the compact, chemically bonded structure of bulk gray arsenic. Among the tested approximations, SCAN+rVV10 most consistently reproduces the DMC equilibrium structures and relative stacking energies, while LDA, PBE+D2, and vdW-optB86b generally favor overly compressed geometries and overstabilize the bulk-like A1B–1 stacking. Based on this benchmark, SCAN+rVV10 predicts a thickness-dependent sequence from A1A1 to A1B1 and finally to bulk-like A1B–1 stacking. The structural evolution is accompanied by a stacking-dependent closure of the band gap associated with increasing interlayer As pz hybridization. These results demonstrate that the accuracy of density functional approximations for arsenene depends on the interlayer-bonding regime and establish DMC benchmarks for describing its evolution from the bilayer to the bulk limit.

evidence_items.summary: Automated readings of pennation angle, fascicle length and muscle thickness from B-mode ultrasound depend on the geometry of the stored frame and on how fascicles that leave the image are extended, and challenge entries add settings chosen on a small public leaderboard. This study measures all three in one entry of the UMUD Challenge, which scored 309 frames from six screen layouts, 103 on a public and 206 on a private leaderboard. The pipeline applies layout-specific values of scale and pixel aspect, resamples each frame to square pixels, segments aponeuroses and fascicle fragments with U-Nets and measures the three readings geometrically; the submitted entry blended its angle and length with public notebooks. Because the score is additive, 65 single-change contrasts from 13 base entries measured each decision on both splits. The primary selected entry scored 0.27608 on the private split, the 69th reported position of 690 teams. Reading every frame with square pixels cost 0.029 public and 0.037 private. Of 20 late-stage corrections, 9 kept the sign of their effect on the private split. An audit of the UMUD expert benchmark found that 26 of its 35 frames share their tissue with training images of both DL_Track_US and the challenge. On the 9 frames with no detected match in either set or orientation, the recipe scored 0.213, two experts against two others 0.218 and DL_Track_US 0.263 (0.209, 0.196 and 0.259 when both raters of a reference pair are required), with no difference established. Frame geometry and the extension rule moved readings as much as the choice of model, and small corrections tuned on about 100 public frames did not carry over.
evidence_items.title: Frame geometry, fascicle extrapolation and leaderboard overfitting in muscle ultrasound

evidence_items.summary: Reduced model output, analysis code and ParFlow input files for a controlled modelling experiment that determines the threshold depth for coupling between groundwater and evapotranspiration in the alluvial aquifer of Faryab-e Sharqi, southeast Iran.  Nine one-year ParFlow-CLM simulations differing only in the initial water table depth, from 1 to 30 m, were used to isolate the effect of depth from vegetation and soil. The package reproduces the reported threshold of 2.80 m and all robustness tests. Version 2 adds the scripts and data for every result in the article, including the spin-up evaluation (Table 2), the block bootstrap, the leave-one-out test, the search-setting sensitivity (Appendix A.2) and the figure script, and corrects the cluster bootstrap so that a cell drawn twice enters the resample twice.

evidence_items.summary: We introduce Puzzling-Bench, a benchmark of 23,777 puzzles with community-verified answers drawn from the Puzzling Stack Exchange archive (2014-2026): riddles, ciphers, logic grids, lateral-thinking problems, wordplay and recreational mathematics, a third of them with images. Every puzzle carries the answer accepted by its author, a short reference answer taken from it (LLM-extracted for the evaluation sets and checked on a 50-puzzle human review), the author's own hints, community tags and a creation date, so that the benchmark supports hint ablations, category analysis and a rolling post-cutoff slice (254 puzzles posted after the training cutoff of six of the nine models we evaluate, including the best one) as a contamination check. We evaluate nine frontier and open models with a two-tier scorer (normalized exact match, then an LLM judge) and validate the judge with three judges from two model families: they agree on 95-97% of verdicts (kappa 0.82-0.96), move no model by more than 1.6 points, and show no own-family preference. The best model, GPT-6.1, reaches 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set; a hard core of 17 puzzles defeats all nine models; model failures are strongly correlated, and the second-best model contributes a single puzzle to a greedy ensemble, yet an oracle over all nine reaches 91%. On a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, withholding the question's image costs the two best models 24 and 35 points. We release the dataset, the scoring pipeline and all per-row provenance.
evidence_items.title: Puzzling-Bench: Evaluating Language Models on 23,777 Human-Written Puzzles with Community-Verified Answers

evidence_items.summary: Embodied agents operating around people must not only recognize social cues, but also decide when the available evidence is sufficient, whether to intervene, and how to respond without violating social norms. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate these abilities in isolation or with access to completed videos, obscuring where an online social decision fails. We introduce AIRIS, a causal streaming benchmark that formulates social embodied intelligence as a time-anchored chain of Attention, Intention, Reaction, and Interaction (A-I-R-I). AIRIS contains 8,000 expert-curated questions grounded in 357 egocentric clips across 11 context categories and 36 capability dimensions. At each query, models receive only the observation prefix available at that time; decision-aware metrics reward calibrated waiting and complete reactions while penalizing premature commitment. Evaluating 45 proprietary and open-source general-purpose, embodied, streaming-video, and omni-modal models reveals fragmented and temporally miscalibrated competence. General-purpose VLMs excel at passive cue grounding and intent recognition, whereas embodied specialists lead on isolated reaction sub-decisions; yet across all families, models frequently guess intents before sufficient evidence emerges and fail to jointly align intervention timing, action domain, and concrete execution within the same episode. AIRIS thus provides a diagnostic foundation for bridging the gap between passive social perception and reliable embodied interaction.
evidence_items.title: AIRIS: Benchmarking Social Embodied Intelligence in Egocentric Streaming Videos

evidence_items.summary: World action models (WAMs) adapt pretrained video generators for robot control by jointly predicting future camera frames and actions, transferring physical priors learned from video into manipulation policies. However, generating future frames before every action makes test-time inference too slow for closed-loop control, while most existing policies remain restricted to short observation histories. Building on Fast-WAM, which showed that video prediction shapes policy representations during training so that future frame synthesis can be skipped at deployment, we present G0.7, a generalist world action model scaled along two axes: extending the context window from a single observation to up to five minutes of history, and scaling pretraining to a large-scale corpus of robot teleoperation and human egocentric (ego) video. Across public simulation suites and real-robot deployments, direct action decoding (Fast mode) matches imagine-then-act (IDM) inference from the same checkpoint while running in 60 ms per 16-step action chunk on a single RTX 5090 (7.6x faster than IDM) and supporting pause-free real-time chunking. Performance scales consistently with pretraining data, with human ego video driving the largest gains in out-of-distribution generalization: G0.7 achieves a 70.8 mean score across five simulation benchmark suites, 48% and 54% zero-shot pick-and-place success on Galaxea R1 Pro and R1 Lite, 96.7% in-distribution and 93.3% out-of-distribution success on video-conditioned in-context learning tasks, and 86.9% mean task progress across seven real-world post-training tasks including multi-minute box folding, drink preparation, and product bagging. Project page: https://www.galaxea-ai.com/model-g07.html
evidence_items.title: G0.7: Scaling Up a Fast World Action Model with Long Context

evidence_items.summary: We introduce HumanPhys, a human-centric benchmark for real-world physical perception, and a training corpus emitted by the same pipeline. Each question targets a physically grounded quantity related to people, including depth, inter-person distance, gaze angle, displacement, velocity, heading-step trajectory, blink count, and contact-deformation strength. The rendered probes additionally test illumination inference from body and face cues and camera ego-motion, both with and without a person in the frame. All labels are derived programmatically from sensor calibration, source metadata, or renderer state, rather than written by annotators or produced by estimators on the benchmark frames. HumanPhys systematically probes six dimensions of human-centric physical perception: spatial state, kinematics, blink events, deformation, illumination, and camera pose. To the best of our knowledge, no existing MLLM benchmark-and-training corpus jointly supervises this set of human-centered physical quantities under direct metadata- or renderer-derived labels. The six dimensions appear only partially dissociable across the tested MLLMs. We benchmark a range of open- and closed-source MLLMs on HumanPhys and find that all six capability dimensions remain challenging for current models. We hope HumanPhys will support future research on multimodal systems that perceive and reason about people in the physical world.
evidence_items.title: HumanPhys: A Human-Centric Physical-World Perception Benchmark for Real-World Visual Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: As large language models and AI agents become the primary consumers of search results, document set quality determines the upper bound of downstream generation. Yet existing evaluation systems remain confined to scoring documents independently and aggregating via nDCG, ignoring inter-document interactions (redundancy, conflict, complementarity) and unable to answer what makes one document set better than another. To address these issues, we propose a complete evaluate-diagnose-optimize framework. We design SetwiseEvalKit, a three-level, nine-dimension document set evaluation benchmark covering both short-form and long-form scenarios, comprising approximately 28K high-quality evaluation rubrics. We systematically evaluate 12 rerankers: even the best method achieves no more than 45% coverage, cross-document coordination dimensions are universally weak, and no single method maintains top performance across both settings. Building on this, we propose Rubric4Setwise, a training-free method that converts rubric-based evaluation criteria into document set selection signals, achieving the best downstream generation performance with fewer documents and search rounds. It is the only method that maintains state-of-the-art results across both scenarios, validating the effectiveness of closing the loop from evaluation to optimization.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Relevance-Centric Retrieval: Rubric-Oriented Document Set Selection and Ranking

evidence_items.summary: Explainable AI (XAI) helps users interpret model behavior and identify potential faults. Agentic XAI systems use Large Language Models (LLMs) to make explanations more accessible through natural-language interaction, but they can also produce plausible yet unfaithful explanations. This risk arises because unreliable XAI outputs for complex models can be amplified by LLMs and mislead users. We propose Faithful Agentic XAI (FAX), a verification method that improves the faithfulness of Agentic XAI explanations. FAX decomposes draft explanations into claims and tests them with inherently faithful tools that query the target model directly, filtering unsupported or contradicted claims before final generation. We also introduce CRAFTER-XAI-Bench, an open-world reinforcement learning benchmark with complex policies, diverse goals, and challenging scenarios for assessing model-specific faithfulness. On CRAFTER-XAI-Bench, FAX improves simulation faithfulness from 0.20 for the strongest baseline to 0.46 while maintaining high informativeness, relevance, and fluency. On three tabular benchmarks, FAX performs competitively with prior Agentic XAI baselines, but our analysis shows that these settings can conflate task accuracy with model-specific faithfulness. These findings show that explicit verification is essential for faithful Agentic XAI and that faithfulness benchmarks must be designed to test explanations against the behavior of the target model itself.
evidence_items.title: Towards Faithful Agentic XAI: A Verification Method and an Open-World Benchmark for Better Model Faithfulness

evidence_items.summary: Competent pretrained LLMs are often locked into architectures that mainstream tooling no longer supports, which strands their knowledge. The conventional remedy, uptraining, needs heavy compute plus a corpus covering everything the model knows. We study a common class of such conversions, architecture standardization, converting a model's normalization layers and interface to the Llama-family template while preserving dimensions, tokenizer, and attention layout. Our KEPT combines direct parameter copying, a training-free LayerNorm-to-RMSNorm initialization (OPM) that is near-optimal under activation assumptions we verify on three models, and standard equal-size distillation from the frozen source, without access to the source model's pretraining corpus. Converted from Orion-14B with ~123M tokens in four A100-days, Llamion stays within one point of the source's H6 average and MT-Bench score, shows no significant difference on Korean MMLU, HumanEval, or MBPP, and enters a Korean leaderboard closed to the custom-loader source, where its 66.87% KoMMLU accuracy exceeds the next-best similar-size entry by more than seven points at submission time. In controlled runs, the default normalizer initialization fails to recover the model under the same budget, and both FLOPs-matched uptraining and sequence-level distillation trail on MT-Bench.
evidence_items.title: Knowledge-Preserving LLM Architecture Standardization: Analytic Normalizer Mapping with Equal-Size Distillation

evidence_items.summary: Intracranial aneurysms (IAs), characterized by unpredictable growth and risk of rupture, are a major cause of stroke and can lead to life-threatening hemorrhages with high mortality and long-term disability. With aging populations, the incidence and overall burden of cerebrovascular diseases are expected to increase, highlighting the need for scalable approaches to analyze complex medical data and improve population-level understanding of these conditions. While digital twins and deep learning offer promising avenues for improving diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment, their effectiveness is limited by the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality medical data and corresponding labels. We present Synthetic VAsculature (SynVA), a modular toolkit for vascular mesh generation and anatomically consistent aneurysm synthesis. SynVA combines novel flow-matching-based methods for generating healthy vessel meshes with learning-based approaches for anatomy-conditioned aneurysm mesh generation; it computes aneurysms from pre-existing vascular geometries rather than generating them in isolation. In addition, we introduce the SynVA procedural model for vascular and aneurysm synthesis based solely on physiological principles and statistical priors, which enables the generation of large-scale datasets. To this end, we release a dataset of 50,000 fully labeled mesh samples for a variety of downstream vision tasks. Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations show that SynVA generates realistic vessel geometries and anatomically plausible aneurysms, with only minor trade-offs between expert-perceived realism and similarity to real aneurysms. Moreover, pretraining on SynVA data improves point-cloud segmentation and morphological parameter estimation on real data. Code will be released upon acceptance.
evidence_items.title: SynVA: A Modular Toolkit for Vessel Generation and Aneurysm Editing

evidence_items.summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive performance in mathematics, existing math benchmarks come with significant limitations. Many focus on problems with fixed ground-truth answers, and are often saturated due to problem simplicity or the viability of guessing or memorization. Crucially, they capture only a narrow subset of relevant math problems. To address this research gap, we introduce MathConstruct, a new benchmark of 121 challenging problems sourced from various math competitions, which targets constructive proofs, a widely encountered problem type requiring the construction of mathematical objects with specific properties. These proofs are particularly suitable for LLM evaluation, as solution correctness can be easily verified. Our automated verifiers also enable MathConstruct to generate problem variations, used to evaluate robustness. State-of-the-art LLMs solve only 60% of MathConstruct problems, highlighting its complexity and importance for LLM evaluation.
evidence_items.title: MathConstruct: Challenging LLM Reasoning with Constructive Proofs

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Purpose To evaluate the performance of large language model (LLM) ‘Deep Research’ agentic systems for writing systematic reviews (SRs) in ophthalmology. Methods Structured prompts were submitted in September 2026 to Deep Research tools powered by GPT‐6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 to produce SRs on the topics of 50 human‐authored SRs published between May and August 2026 in ophthalmology journals (2025 Journal Impact Factor ≥ 3). Main outcomes included literature coverage (recall and precision against the studies included in the human‐made SRs on the same topics), data extraction accuracy (discrepant numerical findings against cited sources), percentage of valid references and PRISMA adherence. Results One hundred SRs were produced, 50 for each LLM. Both LLMs showed limited overlap with the human‐made SRs, with similar recall (38.0% vs. 38.3%; p = 0.859) and higher precision for GPT‐6 Astra (53.2% vs. 36.8%; p < 0.001). GPT‐6 Astra achieved a lower data reporting error rate (0.2%) compared to Claude Fable 5.1 (0.9%) ( p < 0.001). The percentage of valid references was lower for GPT‐6 Astra (79.2% vs. 91.4%; p < 0.001). PRISMA adherence was suboptimal for both models (50.2% vs. 55.2% of items fulfilled; p < 0.001). Conclusion GPT‐6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 showed low data reporting error rates in evidence synthesis; however, incomplete literature coverage, bibliography management issues and poor adherence to reporting guidelines mandate human oversight, especially in study selection and quality appraisal.
evidence_items.title: Automating systematic reviews in ophthalmology with the use of large language model deep research tools

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background. Public protein-production records offer a potential resource for predicting experimental failure, but their labels reflect heterogeneous experimental procedures and reporting practices. Sequence redundancy and laboratory-specific conventions may therefore complicate evaluation. We examined whether predictive associations in these records transfer between structural genomics centers after controlling sequence similarity and visible construct-related features. Results. We harmonized 2380297 records into six stage-specific label categories, representing 98617 sequence clusters at 30% identity. Affinity-tag usage, tag position and recorded failure rates varied substantially between centers; pooled and within-center associations with sequence length also differed. On identical test subsets, the frozen ESM-2 model achieved a median prevalence-normalized precision-recall area under the curve of 1.85 with same-center training and 1.01 with training from other centers, despite the latter containing 4.0-17.7 times more homology groups. For expression failure, the four held-out center groups showed appreciable enrichment, weak enrichment, performance compatible with the random baseline, and performance below that baseline. The below-baseline result persisted after low-rank adaptation and the tested adversarial intervention. A model using only amino-acid composition remained competitive with the protein language model. Opposite directions relative to baseline were observed between expression and soluble-expression tasks in one center group with the frozen model, but this comparison was inconclusive after low-rank adaptation. Conclusions. In these public records, sequence-based prediction of experimental failure was strongly dependent on the evaluation center and task. Homology control and removal of visible construct features did not ensure transfer to held-out centers.
evidence_items.title: Center-dependent generalization in public protein-failure data: a benchmark with homology-controlled and laboratory-held-out evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Reliable national emissions forecasting requires evidence that model complexity improves prediction beyond transparent benchmarks. We analysed Ghana’s fossil carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions for 1970–2024 using EDGAR data. We compared retrospective expanding-origin evaluations at horizons of 1–10 years for persistence, drift, damped trend, ARIMA, elastic net, random forest, support vector regression, and a guarded ensemble. Preprocessing used past-only reconstruction of missing sector values, and inner validation respected horizon-specific target availability. Drift achieved the lowest RMSE among the primary specifications at 1, 3, 5, and 10 years, with gains of 2.4%, 7.0%, 13.7%, and 15.6% over persistence; none was significant after small-sample correction and Holm adjustment. Supervised models predicting emissions levels underperformed. However, diagnostic models predicting changes improved RMSE by 19.6% for elastic net at five years and 23.4% for support vector regression at ten years. These gains were not significant after adjustment across the diagnostic comparisons. The findings implicate target representation and extrapolation alongside sample and predictor limitations, rather than general algorithmic inferiority. An error-calibrated ensemble projects 0.748 t CO₂ per person in 2025 and 0.996 in 2034. Its empirical 2034 95% error band is 0.925–1.095, but sequential historical checks show undercoverage at several horizons. Transparent benchmarks, chronological validation, and explicit calibration checks are essential when interpreting forecasts from short annual inventories.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark-aware multi-horizon forecasting of carbon dioxide emissions in Ghana

evidence_items.summary: BACKGROUND: In severe traumatic brain injury (sTBI), intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring detects and directs management for intracranial hypertension. ICP monitoring is recommended for sTBI patients and is included as a benchmarked quality metric by the American College of Surgeons Trauma Quality Improvement Programs (ACS-TQIP), which reports annual ICP monitor usage across all participating trauma centers. We evaluated whether greater institutional ICP utilization was associated with lower center-level mortality. METHODS: For this retrospective observational study, adult patients aged 18 years and older meeting the ACS-TQIP definition of sTBI admitted to Level I or II trauma centers from 2013 to 2023 were identified. Patient data were aggregated by trauma center and calendar year to mirror the ACS-TQIP benchmarking framework. Annual institutional ICP monitor utilization and in-hospital mortality rates were calculated for each center-year combination. Multivariable generalized linear mixed-effects models evaluated whether centers with higher ICP monitor utilization had lower mortality after adjusting for patient demographics, injury severity, neurological status, operative intervention, injury mechanism, and hospital length of stay. RESULTS: Among 191,686 sTBI patients, 29,224 (15.2%) underwent ICP monitoring. ICP monitor utilization ranged from 11% to 21% during the study period with a notable increase in 2017, whereas overall mortality remained largely unchanged. Year-specific analyses demonstrated a protective association between greater ICP monitor utilization and mortality in 2015 and an association with increased mortality in 2023. After adjustment for differences in patient and institutional characteristics, higher institutional ICP monitor utilization was not associated with lower center-level mortality (odds ratio=0.99, 95% CI=0.97–1.00; P =0.128).
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of the ACS Trauma Quality Improvement Program benchmark for intracranial pressure monitoring across trauma centers

evidence_items.summary: An agentic AI simulator was built to advance our understanding about how the human brain and cognition change with age. The simulator generates worlds based on hypothesized age-linked cascades and then simulates studies across varied experimental designs and selection criteria. Each simulated world begins with 120,000 individual lives initiated by baseline parameters (e.g., genetic risk, birth year) and then changed by age-dependent cascades (e.g., amyloid-dependent, cardiovascular). Examples illustrate how the simulator predicts distinct data patterns in cross-sectional versus longitudinal designs, how alternative participant selection strategies emphasize baseline differences versus age-related decline, and how variable levels of association emerge between brain and cognition dependent upon design choices. Simulations of clinical trials provide information about design, power, and outcome considerations. Experiments on alternative simulated worlds evaluate how well hypothesized cascades accommodate real-world data patterns, capturing the insights and open puzzles inside the application. Most critically, the application is built to evolve. Its code contains a complete description of how to construct and update itself so that any person or AI agent can explore a new finding, recalibrate to emerging data, or build and simulate a novel future study. The simulator is offered as a tool for understanding data patterns, teaching, and generation of hypotheses to be tested in future studies using real-world data collection.
evidence_items.title: An Open, Evolving Brain and Cognitive Aging Simulator Enabled by Agentic Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: RESEARCH COLLECTION / FLAGSHIPS 71–80 OF 90 Meridian Metrology, Chronobiology &Multiscale Physiological Modeling at the Limit STARLI Acupuncture Trilogy | F71–F80 of 90 | Author 33 | Research Design Working Edition v1.1 This ten-volume research-design collection investigates classical meridian claims as testable spatial labels, acupoint microenvironment sensors, peripheral neural signal propagation, fascial transfer, quantum versus classical magnetometry, environmental associations, historical timing categories, seasonal adaptation, personalized scheduling and multiscale physiological digital twins. Traditional language is a research motivation, not evidence of distinct physical conduits, energies or treatment efficacy. Two five-theme research units contain ten English 777-page working editions: 300 conditional mathematical model plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 separately paginated investigations, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The proposals require calibrated reference measures, matched conventional baselines, concealed challenges, competing explanations and explicit refusal decisions. No experimental benefit or clinical outcome is asserted. Research Unit I · F71–F75 / Meridian Hypotheses & Physical Controls F71 MERIDIAN THEORY AND SPATIAL MAPPING OF HUMAN BIOELECTRICITY AT THE LIMIT — Tests whether predeclared route-versus-off-route skin impedance contrast persists after matching anatomy, temperature, pressure and hydration. Concealed route-label swaps and multifrequency four-electrode comparisons challenge sweat gland density and electrode-contact artifacts. Nonreproducible blinded contrast or calibration failure stops the claim. F72 ACUPOINT MICROENVIRONMENTS AND NANOBIOSENSING AT THE LIMIT — Compares biochemical and physical surface sensor signals at predefined point coordinates with nearby controls. Blinded pressure, moisture, perfusion and coordinate changes challenge apparent specificity against ordinary skin biology.
evidence_items.title: RESEARCH COLLECTION / FLAGSHIPS 71–80 OF 90 Meridian Metrology, Chronobiology & Multiscale Physiological Modeling at the Limit STARLI Acupuncture Trilogy  |  F71–F80 of 90  |  Author 33  |  Research Design Working Edition v1.1 This ten-volume research-design collection investigates classical meridian claims as testable spatial labels, acupoint microenvironment sensors, peripheral neural signal propagation, fascial transfer, quantum versus classical magnetometry, environmental associations, historical timing categories, seasonal adaptation, personalized scheduling and multiscale physiological digital twins. Traditional language is a research motivation, not evidence of distinct physical conduits, energies or treatment efficacy. Two five-theme research units contain ten English 777-page working editions: 300 conditional mathematical model plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 separately paginated investigations, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The proposals require calibrated reference measures, matched conventional baselines, concealed challenges, competing explanations and explicit refusal decisions. No experimental benefit or clinical outcome is asserted. Research Unit I · F71–F75 / Meridian Hypotheses & Physical Controls F71  MERIDIAN THEORY AND SPATIAL MAPPING OF HUMAN BIOELECTRICITY AT THE LIMIT — Tests whether predeclared route-versus-off-route skin impedance contrast persists after matching anatomy, temperature, pressure and hydration. Concealed route-label swaps and multifrequency four-electrode comparisons challenge sweat gland density and electrode-contact artifacts. Nonreproducible blinded contrast or calibration failure stops the claim. F72  ACUPOINT MICROENVIRONMENTS AND NANOBIOSENSING AT THE LIMIT — Compares biochemical and physical surface sensor signals at predefined point coordinates with nearby controls. Blinded pressure, moisture, perfusion and coordinate changes challenge apparent specificity against ordinary skin biology. Independent reference uncertainty and drift limits govern interpretation; no implanted sensors or diagnostic performance is claimed. F73  MERIDIAN PROPAGATION HYPOTHESES AND PERIPHERAL NEURAL NETWORK VALIDATION AT THE LIMIT — Contrasts observed latency maps with anatomically known nerve routes and classical path labels using safe surface electrophysiology and phantoms. Concealed electrode relocation, matched filtering and common-impedance controls test whether passive volume conduction or neural pathways fully account for apparent propagation; nonidentifiable timing is a stop condition. F74  MERIDIAN THEORY AND FASCIAL BIOMECHANICAL COUPLING AT THE LIMIT — Investigates rotation-to-strain transfer in matched fascial and non-fascial mechanical analogs. Masked tissue-layer substitutions, reversed rotation and a no-rotation sham challenge nonspecific traction and fixture friction. Kelvin-Voigt and layer-agnostic models are explicit comparators; no therapeutic needling claim follows. F75  QUANTUM-SENSING-ASSISTED VALIDATION OF MERIDIAN PHYSIOLOGICAL HYPOTHESES AT THE LIMIT — Tests whether quantum magnetometry improves signal-to-noise ratio beyond optimized classical sensing at equal bandwidth, observation time and sampling volume. Hidden instrument-label swaps and a null-field phantom confront calibration, optical-power and geometry confounds. No quantum-meridian hypothesis or treatment effect is established.   SECOND RESEARCH UNIT / ENVIRONMENTAL TIMING & CROSS-SCALE EVIDENCE Research Unit II · F76–F80 / Timing & Systems Models F76  HUMAN-NATURE UNITY PHILOSOPHY AND HUMAN-ENVIRONMENT COUPLING AT THE LIMIT — Evaluates held-out environmental-exposure and physiological-state interactions after sleep, activity and clock adjustment. Concealed reshuffling of temperature and light records tests whether apparent coupling is due to seasonal and circadian confounding. Calendar-matched distributed-lag regression provides a conventional benchmark. F77  ZIWU LIUZHU THEORY AND MODERN CHRONOBIOLOGY AT THE LIMIT — Compares traditional timing categories with multiharmonic cosinor and ordinary circadian-phase models. Masked shifts in social-clock and time-zone labels, while biological phase stays fixed, test whether any added predictive fit survives sleep and light covariates. A generic 24-hour oscillator remains the null account. F78  FOUR-SEASON HEALTH PHILOSOPHY AND HUMAN PHYSIOLOGICAL ADAPTATION AT THE LIMIT — Studies within-person seasonal physiology under matched photoperiod, indoor temperature, sleep and activity conditions. Blinded contrasting-season, temperature-matched comparisons separate adaptation from work schedules, daylight exposure and sampling imbalance. Claims stop without multi-season overlap or sustained matched contrasts. F79  HUMAN-NATURE UNITY AND PERSONALIZED TIMING OF INTELLIGENT ACUPUNCTURE AT THE LIMIT — Tests offline scheduling-policy decision regret against fixed-time and physiology-only timing policies. Concealed calendar permutations and held-out light/sleep phase changes challenge expectation, fatigue and appointment-selection confounds. Only retrospective or simulated policies are evaluated; no automated intervention is authorized. F80  CLASSICAL HOLISTIC LIFE PHILOSOPHY AND MULTISCALE PHYSIOLOGICAL DIGITAL TWINS AT THE LIMIT — Tests independently calibrated state transfer across tissue, autonomic and cognitive proxy layers. Masked twin-layer removal and external-site holdouts challenge high-dimensional overfitting and common sensor ancestry. Regularized physiology-only predictions are the comparator; no patient-facing clinical decisions follow. Physical Scope, Falsifiability & Evidence Status The proposed work is confined to ethics-approved non-invasive measurements, bench phantoms, authorized ex-vivo mechanical analogs, archival records, synthetic models and offline simulation. There is no completed acupuncture trial, new clinical procedure, verified anatomical meridian conduit or demonstrated quantum treatment effect. Source identity, calibration, negative controls, balanced comparators and non-negotiable stop conditions must be preserved. The documented research lineage is the STARLI 90 Flagship Master v1.3 and the source-supplied methodological DOIs 10.5281/zenodo.23480803, 10.5281/zenodo.23486020 and 10.5281/zenodo.23318840. The citations establish editorial ancestry, not independent verification. External source metadata and formula-to-claim fit require specialist review before using these proposals as validated evidence. Research Gates & Quality Assurance Boundary The source batch report records ten 777-page PDFs and zero exact duplicate Gate questions or full six-part annotations. Cross-volume lexical screening reports a maximum nearest score of 0.8761, with 59 matches at or above 0.80 and none at or above 0.90. Formula-domain fit, causal mechanism independence, empirical novelty and clinical safety have not been established by these automated checks. authors: Richmond Sin Jing Xuan, Peilin Feng, Wenbin Wang, Soujanya Poria
rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: AI agents working on long tasks often commit to an answer before they have enough evidence, a behavior called laziness. In our evaluations, they frequently commit even while their stated belief still names several possible answers. An outcome reward at the end of the episode scores only the final answer, so it cannot teach the agent when to commit, because a lucky guess receives the same reward as an answer backed by evidence. During training, however, the simulator can compute the exact posterior over the answer at every step and tell whether the evidence is already enough. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB), which rewards the agent for taking further steps while this posterior still allows several answers and for committing once the evidence is sufficient. The reward needs no judge, critic or reward model, and it never reads the belief line the agent writes before each action. We also introduce Pro Worlds, a benchmark of visual puzzles where the agent views a large world through a small window. We evaluate three vision-language models on three benchmarks, two of which are never seen in training. RLVB improves the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average. Under the outcome reward, GRPO and PPO fall below the base model on average. RLVB also outperforms PPO with a process reward from an LLM judge by 9.3% on average while using 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours. The trained agent answers with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12% and 74% of the episodes on the three benchmarks, against 8%, 0.4% and 36% for the base model. Its accuracy gain therefore comes from answering more often at high levels of evidence. The belief line shows how the agent reaches this evidence: it acts on its own belief. It commits at only 0.1 to 2.2% of the turns at which the evidence is insufficient and its line still names several answers, against 3 to 68% for the base model.
evidence_items.title: Lazy Agents Answer Against Their Own Beliefs: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs Teaches Them to Act on What They Believe

authors: Shifang Zhao, Haoyu Wang, Yuyang Yin, Dong Chen, Xingyilang Yin, Yunkang Tao, Honghao Chen, Guangzhi Wang, Yiran Wang, Junfu Pu, Cheng Cheng, Xiaodong Cun, Ying Shan
rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: Games, especially modern AAA games, challenge language models to perceive complex scenes, control actions, and make decisions over long horizons. Existing game benchmarks primarily test language models as computer-use agents that query a language model throughout play, incurring repeated inference cost and, in real-time games, acting while the environment continues to evolve. We ask whether coding agents can learn from game interaction to develop standalone game-playing programs that run without language model inference. We thus introduce Coding4Games, a benchmark for evaluating whether coding agents can develop standalone programs that play modern games through visual observations and standard game inputs. Coding4Games has three defining features: 1) Diverse Modern Games, covering 15 games with diverse visual, strategic, and control demands; 2) Development-Test Separation, in which a coding agent uses a sandbox and the standard player interface to iteratively develop a program, after which the selected program is frozen and independently tested without language-model inference; and 3) Outcome and Process Evaluation, which measures not only game performance and reliability but also how agents use feedback, revise programs, and resolve problems during development. Across 15 games, the best program per game outscores the strongest GUI baseline on 13 and ties it on one. The human player outscores all agents on 10 games. We additionally examine the effects of development budgets. Coding4Games evaluates whether coding agents can turn their understanding of complex interactive environments into programs that work reliably on their own.
evidence_items.title: Coding4Games: Can Modern Coding Agents Play Modern Video Games?

authors: Parsa Nilforushan, Gemmin Sugiura, Kourosh Hashemi, Peiman Zhiani, Mohammad A. Tayebi
evidence_items.summary: AI web agents can autonomously navigate websites and complete various tasks. As their capabilities and adoption expand, evaluating bot defenses requires adversarial stress tests. Although prior work demonstrates that existing agents can remain detectable, it remains unclear how effective bot defenses are against adversaries that coordinate evasion across browser fingerprints, automation controls, and interaction behavior. To investigate this threat, we introduce DarkAgent, an autonomous web agent that combines a forked Chromium browser that conceals automation artifacts and generative models that produce human-like mouse and keyboard traces. To address the limitations of existing keyboard mimickers, our keyboard model jointly generates realistic key events and their timings while reliably reproducing the target text. Released agent detectors accept our generated behavior as human, and trained classifiers find it substantially harder to distinguish from human traces than existing mimickers. DarkAgent achieves an 89% page-access bypass rate across a third-party stealth benchmark, exceeding the strongest published baseline by 12 percentage points. To further enhance the measurement of agents, we introduce a benchmark that measures browser fingerprints, interaction behavior, and network activity to assess each channel's contribution to detecting adversarial agents such as DarkAgent. On this benchmark, browser and behavioral modifications are complementary: either alone remains detectable, and only their combination evades all tested checks. Together, our findings expose the gap between passing existing bot defenses and reproducing human behavior, and point to timing between actions as a remaining signal for defenders.
evidence_items.title: Are Web Agents Still Detectable? Stress-Testing Bot Defenses with Coordinated Evasion

evidence_items.summary: Detailed knowledge of a user's persona is valuable for personalizing generative AI models and agents, yet such details are difficult to obtain and change over time. We address the task of inferring persona attributes from a single day of mobile activity logs. No suitable publicly available benchmark exists for this task, so we introduce a synthetic benchmark of 1,600 persona-log pairs. We target on-device inference so that raw logs never leave the phone, which makes memory rather than speed the limiting constraint: a day of activity yields roughly 30K tokens, whose key-value cache alone exceeds the INT4 weights of a 4B-parameter model. We therefore propose a log filtering method that retains only behaviorally distinct entries. Filtering reduces the memory footprint by up to 39% across nine models from four families and more than halves prefill time, while maintaining or improving prediction quality. For Qwen3-4B it removes 2.5GB, bringing the model from well beyond a realistic per-process budget to a manageable one. Within our benchmark, these results indicate that preserving diverse behavioral events matters more for persona prediction than retaining every semantically similar log entry.
evidence_items.title: LogToPersona: New Benchmark and Efficient Persona Prediction through Semantic Log Filtering

evidence_items.summary: Human gaze provides a rich window into attention and intent, making its understanding essential for applications ranging from social signal analysis to human-robot interaction. Existing methods typically employ highly customized architectures relying on auxiliary inputs like head crops or depth maps, causing cascading errors and inference overhead. Trained on single domains and confined to isolated gaze following with heatmap outputs, they lack flexibility and generalization for diverse interactive scenarios. To bridge this gap, we present LookAnything, a foundation model that unifies diverse gaze-centric tasks for holistic gaze following. Benefiting from large-scale multi-task and cross-domain training, LookAnything flexibly adapts to various settings, generating diverse outputs (points, boxes, heatmaps, and language) and supporting broad gaze-centric localization, description, and reasoning. At its core, we introduce learnable gaze-prior queries to promote gaze-aware representation learning, eliminating the need for auxiliary external inputs. To facilitate this paradigm, we construct HoliGaze, a comprehensive corpus and benchmark comprising 311K question-answer pairs across 5 capability dimensions and 9 distinct tasks. Experiments demonstrate that LookAnything consistently outperforms 33 leading vision-language models on holistic gaze following, while remaining highly competitive with dedicated specialists across 5 conventional target detection benchmarks. Evaluation on unseen datasets and deployment on a real robot further validate its strong out-of-domain generalization and flexible adaptation in real-world scenarios.
evidence_items.title: LookAnything: A Foundation Model for Holistic Gaze Following

evidence_items.summary: Learned image captioning metrics are trained and tested on human judgments, so their reported correlation is a claim about generalization. We audit this claim for the three most recent collections of such judgments, Polaris, Nebula, and Spica, matching images at the pixel level. First, test samples reappear in training sets: the Spica training set contains about two-thirds of the Polaris test set, with identical human ratings. Second, controlled retraining shows that duplicates can inflate a metric: for Pearl, the gain is confined to the duplicated samples and grows with every epoch; for DENEB, it stays below one point. The gain depends on the learner and on how often a training set repeats a sample. Third, Kendall's τ over all samples is the sum of two terms, detecting captions with the lowest human score and ranking the others; the first supplies most of the reported correlation and is nearly saturated. The recent test sets cannot order Polos, DENEB and Pearl consistently, and a ridge regression on frozen features matches or exceeds all three. Fourth, we propose a protocol that ranks a learned metric only with a model trained without test samples, reports both terms, and compares metrics by paired tests. Under it, zero-shot vision--language judges rank first on the three recent test sets, and a fine-tuned judge ranks first on the three earlier benchmarks. The same analysis applies to any evaluator learned from human judgments; filter lists and code are released at https://github.com/morninghut/ic-dataset-audit .
evidence_items.title: Do learned image captioning metrics generalize? Auditing duplicated samples in human-judgment benchmarks

evidence_items.summary: Audio-visual deepfakes can spread misinformation and enable impersonation, undermining trust in digital media. However, existing datasets provide limited coverage of forgery operations and their combinations, constraining detector development and systematic evaluation. We introduce Mega-MMDF, containing 100,000 real and 1.2 million forged clips across 22 pipelines spanning modality-specific manipulations, stacked forgeries, and joint audio-video generation. To assess its training value and enable fair comparisons, we develop DeepfakeBench-MM, which standardizes training and evaluation across 8 datasets and 10 detectors. Training-based detectors achieve their highest mean AUC when trained on Mega-MMDF, with gains of up to 0.0784 over the best alternative training dataset for each detector. Experiments on data scale and pipeline coverage further support the value of large, diverse training data. Cross-pipeline evaluations reveal bidirectional and asymmetric generalization. Training on composite forgeries does not necessarily enable detection of their constituent operations in isolation. Our analysis of altered inputs shows that modality masking can increase false alarms and missed detections, and temporal misalignment can raise mean predicted forgery probabilities. Together, these resources provide a foundation for understanding and improving multimodal deepfake detection, with publicly available code and dataset access subject to application and usage terms.
evidence_items.title: Mega-MMDF and DeepfakeBench-MM: Benchmarking Multimodal Deepfake Detection Across Diverse Forgery Pipelines

evidence_items.summary: SynAM-E is the dataset of the paper "Event Cameras for Melt-Pool Monitoring in Metal Additive Manufacturing: A Multi-Machine Benchmark and Experimental Analysis" (under review). It holds 85 simulated event-camera streams rendered with calibrated v2e from 15 public melt-pool video datasets recorded on 8 machines (3,923,454,180 events after 2-px guard-band filtering). Each shard ships events.h5 and a manifest with full provenance; the task splits hold out one machine at a time (leave-one-machine-out) or one dataset at a time (leave-one-dataset-out). Source frame video: Melt-Pool-Kinetics (DOI 10.1038/s41597-025-05597-2). License CC BY 4.0. What changed in 1.1. Labels, flags, names and documents only; all 85 event files are byte-identical to version 1.0. (1) BAM's two infrared shards carry swapped band and alloy labels in the compilation metadata: source7 MWIR is the SWIR camera's 316L-Si run and source7 SWIR the MWIR camera's AISI 2205 run (Altenburg et al., Quantitative InfraRed Thermography Journal 19(2), DOI 10.1080/17686733.2020.1829889). The alloy task now uses source7 MWIR as BAM's 316L clip, and LABEL CORRECTIONS.json lists public and corrected labels. (2) The shard manifests no longer carry pilot only = true. (3) The split files and documents describe the held-out units as machines and datasets, with a machine map in every machine-held-out split file. (4) The README, datasheet, reproducibility notes, class-count table and CITATION.cff follow the revised paper. CHANGELOG.md lists every change; SHA256SUMS.txt covers every file.

evidence_items.summary: As LLM agents increasingly learn from their own experience, the tasks they learn from and are evaluated on are almost always in English. We ask whether self-evolution transfers from English to Urdu, and release IRTIQA, a benchmark of aligned English, Urdu-translated, and Urdu code-switched variants of DROP, SNIPS, AppWorld, and SkillsBench, built with a matrix-language code-switching pipeline and human verification. Using IRTIQA, we evaluate three self-evolving frameworks, Tool-R0 (self-play RL), AgentEvolver (experience-guided RL), and Autogenesis (protocol-level evolution), against their unevolved backbones. Self-evolution often raises capability: AgentEvolver lifts AppWorld goal completion from near zero to 20-36% across all conditions, and Autogenesis improves SkillsBench pass rate from 16.48% to 22.22%. But it rarely closes the language gap. Evolved systems remain stronger in English, by up to 0.26 DROP F1, the gap is largest on multi-step tasks, and code-switching behaves as a distinct condition rather than degraded translation. On a shared Gemma-4 31B backbone, the gap exists before evolution, and RL-based evolution can hurt Urdu reasoning more than English. Language parity must therefore be an explicit design target, as it does not emerge from self-improvement alone.
evidence_items.title: IRTIQA: Evolving in English, Evaluated in Urdu -- Does Agent Self-Evolution Transfer from English to Urdu and Code-Switched Input?

evidence_items.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) distribute reasoning across specialized agents that must exchange messages and invoke tools reliably. Existing evaluations typically couple communication with open domain tasks, making it difficult to determine whether a failure arises from reasoning, malformed tool use, lost messages, or forgotten requests. Prior benchmarks do not isolate communication execution or measure routing redundancy against a known optimal path. We introduce CypherMAS, a synthetic benchmark that isolates communication and routing in fixed multi-agent graphs. Agents in chain, star, bipartite, or ring graphs route cyphered messages to remote peers holding the matching decoders; since the optimal route is known, redundant LLM calls can be measured and routing failures may be easily tracked. Across eleven open-weight models from 4B to 753B, small models fail at routing and tool use, dense models above 27B degrade with diameter, and successful runs exceed minimum LLM calls. These findings identify communication reliability as a distinct scaling bottleneck for multi-agent systems and provide a controlled diagnostic for complex multi-agent systems. The source code is freely available: https://github.com/Andoree/CypherMAS.
evidence_items.title: CypherMAS: Benchmarking Routing Reliability in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems

evidence_items.summary: Panoramic cameras capture nearly the entire spherical field of view in a single frame. However, the mismatch between this panoramic coverage and the field of view of LiDAR poses a substantial challenge for panoramic Gaussian splatting SLAM that relies on LiDAR depth priors. We introduce GOLD-SLAM, a Gaussian-splatting Omnidirectional LiDAR-Depth SLAM system that combines high-quality rendering with accurate geometric reconstruction. It performs tracking and mapping in the spherical domain and uses tracked visual features in regions without LiDAR coverage to improve pose estimation. To address insufficient coverage of newly observed surfaces and floating artifacts during incremental mapping, we introduce Depth-Aware Map Extension and Pruning (DAEP). To enable broader evaluation, we collect a new dataset, WHOLE, using a UAV platform across Weak-geometry, High-dynamic, Omnidirectional, Low-light, and Easy scenarios. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks and WHOLE demonstrate competitive rendering quality and improved geometric accuracy relative to perspective systems. Compared with existing panoramic baselines, GOLD-SLAM improves mean PSNR by 5.56-9.10 dB and reduces mean Depth-L1 by 71.9-83.9%. To assess deployment feasibility on resource-constrained platforms such as UAVs, we evaluate an embedded configuration of GOLD-SLAM on a Jetson Orin NX (16 GB), demonstrating online operation at the cost of reconstruction quality.
evidence_items.title: GOLD-SLAM: Gaussian-splatting Omnidirectional LiDAR-Depth SLAM

evidence_items.summary: Embodied spatial intelligence requires agents to gather information through exploration and interaction, then use it to reason and act. Existing benchmarks insufficiently distinguish correct outcomes from completion of these task requirements. We introduce ROAM-Bench to evaluate these abilities under robot motion and collision constraints. Independent checks use simulation state and episode records to assess outcomes and task requirements, with stronger checks of geometry, coverage, or placement. It comprises 250 manually validated tasks across 11 types in five groups and 27 indoor environments, covering object and room search, counting, geometric judgments, direction reasoning, and relocation. Human evaluators achieve 84% strict task success on 100 sampled tasks, with every correct outcome satisfying the required checks. Across seven frontier vision-language models, we identify two complementary failure modes: correct outcomes with unmet task requirements, and incorrect outcomes despite passing stronger checks. Oracle-input diagnostics show that more complete target observations and calibrated feedback improve final spatial judgments.
evidence_items.title: ROAM-Bench: Evaluating Embodied Active Spatial Intelligence through Evidence Verification

evidence_items.summary: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are rapidly improving, yet their evaluation remains largely static. Existing benchmarks provide a strong foundation, but fixed difficulty ceilings, limited feature coverage, and coarse aggregate scores progressively weaken their discriminative and diagnostic value. We introduce CUA-SEE, a closed-loop evaluation environment that co-evolves tasks and executable verifiers from rollout evidence. It disentangles three objectives: benchmark evolution expands evaluation scope through cohort-calibrated difficulty and coverage growth; diagnostic evolution increases resolution through agent-conditional capability-boundary probes; and verifier evolution improves precision by translating changing requirements into state-grounded checkpoints with adversarial validation. Across multiple agents, applications, and rounds, CUA-SEE generates challenging, measurable tasks while preserving process-level evidence. Our results position adaptive evaluation as a scalable counterpart to self-evolving agents, continuously tracking what agents can do, where their boundaries lie, and how reliably progress is measured.
evidence_items.title: Self-Evolving Evaluation Environments for Computer-Use Agents

evidence_items.summary: Recent self-improving coding agents have achieved strong benchmark performance by iteratively modifying their own executable implementations. A common pattern uses downstream task-derived evidence to decide which candidates or lineages continue evolving, which we term evaluate-and-select. Obtaining this signal requires repeatedly executing evolved agents on downstream tasks, so broader exploration incurs increasing evaluation cost, while repeated optimization against a fixed evaluation distribution may encourage benchmark-specific adaptation. We ask: can coding agents self-improve without downstream task evaluation inside the evolution loop? We introduce Explore-then-Integrate (ELITE), which integrates implementation mechanisms rather than selecting a single exploratory child to continue the lineage. At each generation, ELITE proposes diverse focused improvements, implements them independently from the same parent, and inspects the resulting programs to identify complementary, redundant, and conflicting mechanisms before reimplementing a compatible subset as one coherent descendant. No downstream task outcomes or task-solving trajectories of evolved candidates are used to guide evolution; only deterministic checks of structural and operational validity are used inside the loop. On SWE-bench Pro, ELITE improves the initial agent from 60.0% to 85.6%, compared with 86.7% for the Darwin Godel Machine (DGM) and 88.3% for the Huxley-Godel Machine (HGM), while using zero candidate task evaluations and reducing observed wall-clock evolution time by 8.8x and 3.2x, respectively, under the evaluated configurations. In cross-benchmark transfer without further adaptation, ELITE averages 73.3% on SWE-bench Verified and 69.3% on Polyglot. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of coding-agent self-improvement without downstream candidate task evaluation in our setting.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation-Free Recursive Self-Improvement for Coding Agents

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains first-order transition flattened matrices of browser interaction events, recorded while students worked on online assessment tasks. Each row is one participant working on one task (phase) in one assessment. It describes how likely each interaction event was to be followed by each other event. Data were collected across 15 assessments between November 2023 and February 2026. In total there are 8,329 participant–phase records from 1,832 anonymized participants. Files: ·         data.csv: the main dataset (8,329 rows × 259 columns) o    user: hashed participant ID o    assessment: hashed assessment ID (A01–A15) o    phase: the task within an assessment [hashed ID/task name] o    256 transition columns: all pairs of 16 event types (Copy, Download, Keystroke, LinkClick, PageClose, PageFocus, PageOpen, Paste, Scroll, TabClose, TabFocus, TabOpen, TextMarked, WindowClose, WindowFocus, WindowOpen) ·         assessment supplementary .csv: assessment ID with its active period (active from, active to, in UTC) Transition values: The column (A, B) gives the probability that event A is directly followed by event B. For each source event A, the values across all B add up to 1. If event A never occurred in that record, they are all 0. Values range from 0 to 1, and there are no missing values. Column naming Event transitions follow a tuple notation (A, B) (e.g., (Copy, Paste)) where the first element is the source event and the second is the target event. Pseudonymization ·         Participant IDs were replaced with keyed hashes (HMAC-SHA256, truncated, prefix U ). ·         Assessment IDs were replaced with sequential IDs (A01–A15), ordered by the original assessment number.
evidence_items.title: Students' Browser Event Transations During Online Task Solving

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to extract information from electronic health records (EHRs). Given the rapid pace of LLM development, robust scenario-specific benchmarks are essential to evaluate clinical usefulness and support safe deployment. Objective This study aimed to compare contemporary LLMs for structured data extraction from real neurosurgical EHRs written in Czech. Methods In a prospective single-center cohort, 172 hospitalized patients provided informed consent for the use of anonymized EHRs. For each patient, predefined records were collected and concatenated. Ground truth for 35 data points was established by dual extraction with consensus. A standardized prompt requesting JSON output was submitted to 19 LLMs. The primary outcome was overall accuracy; secondary outcomes were category-level accuracy and the proportion of complete machine-readable outputs. Results A total of 6264 documents were collected (median 33, IQR 25-41 per patient). Ground truth was established with 92.6% initial interrater agreement before consensus. Several models produced complete JSON outputs for 100% of cases (Claude 4.1 Opus, Grok 4, and Gemini 2.5 Flash); GPT-4.1 (DeepSearch) and GPT-5 completed 99.4%. The highest accuracy was achieved by GPT-4.1 (87.6%), followed by GPT-4.5 (85.6%), Claude 4.1 (84.8%), and Grok 4 (84.2%). Accuracy declined by data type: binary (up to 95%), numeric (~89%), multiple-choice (~75%), and short text (~78%). Conclusions Current LLMs can reliably extract structured clinical information from full, non-English EHRs, while older or smaller models show major limitations. A hybrid workflow—automated extraction with targeted validation—appears practical for research use.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model Performance in Structured Data Extraction From Neurosurgical Electronic Health Records: Comparative Benchmark Study
