evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Poland has 17 designated adult trauma centres but no national trauma registry. This study assessed which trauma data elements required by the American College of Surgeons (ACS) are available in Polish public data sources and what these sources reveal about the care of injured patients. Methods In this cross-sectional gap analysis, 17 verifiable requirements from the ACS Trauma Systems Consultation Guide, the 2022 Resources for Optimal Care of the Injured Patient, the National Trauma Data Standard, the Trauma Quality Improvement Program and the Utstein template were mapped against Polish sources and graded on a five-level scale. Sources were National Health Fund portals and open hospital data (2017–2025), Police, Statistics Poland and air rescue reports. In-hospital mortality in injury-related diagnosis-related groups was analysed; trauma centres were compared using indirect standardisation and funnel plots. Five established trauma registries served as comparators. Results Of 17 requirements, one was fully available in public data; the gap was small for one, moderate for one, large for four and critical for nine; one was not applicable. No source contained Abbreviated Injury Scale codes, physiological parameters, process times or linked 30-day outcomes. In injury-related groups the share of patients aged ≥ 65 years rose from 31.3% (2017) to 47.8% (2025); they accounted for 75.7% of in-hospital deaths in 2025. Multiple-injury groups (1002–1466 stays per year) were billed by trauma centres in 99.1–99.8% of cases. Standardised mortality ratios of centres ranged from 0.49 to 2.10; six of 17 lay outside 95% control limits. In operative severe head injury, the observed-to-expected mortality ratio was 0.89 (95% CI 0.85–0.92) in trauma centres and 1.05 (1.03–1.07) in other hospitals, but trauma centres transferred more patients onward (17.8% vs 11.9%).
evidence_items.title: No registry, no benchmark: a nationwide cross-sectional gap analysis of trauma care data in Poland against American College of Surgeons standards

evidence_items.summary: Smart parking systems guide drivers to free spaces through mobile interfaces whose usefulness depends on the accuracy and lead time of the underlying occupancy forecasts. We benchmark seven models—random forest (RF), XGBoost, LightGBM, a feed-forward neural network (NN), an LSTM, a temporal convolutional network (TCN), and a transformer—on a full year of real data: 112,830 observations from five LoRaWAN-instrumented spaces at the University of Prishtina, Kosovo (June 2024–June 2025). Departing from single-horizon nowcasting, we predict at 15-minute, 1-hour, and 2-hour lead times for both binary occupancy classification and continuous occupancy-ratio regression, under a leakage-free chronological split, with deep models trained to convergence and every result averaged over ten seeds with significance testing. The value of machine learning proves strongly horizon-dependent: because occupancy is highly autocorrelated, a zero-cost persistence baseline matches the best learned model up to one hour ahead, and only at two hours do six of the seven models beat it significantly (best long shortterm memory (LSTM) 79.82% vs. 76.32%, p < 10-10). For regression the sequence models lead at every horizon (R2 = 0.686 at one hour) and the gradient-boosted trees outrank RF. An ablation shows historical (autocorrelation) features supply almost all of the signal, corroborated by SHAP and permutation importance. A resource analysis is counterintuitive: RF trains fastest yet yields the largest model (165 MB), while the compact sequence models (~0.2 MB) are far more deployable. These results give realistic, persistence-aware guidance for smart-parking services.
evidence_items.title: Machine Learning for LoRaWAN Smart Parking: A Multi-Horizon Occupancy Prediction Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Fixed Benford conformity bands classify every unit as nonconforming when each observation rests on a few figures, and ratios built from the tested amounts can be associated with a digit statistic through arithmetic alone. We propose a panel-based benchmark that builds a bank-year index of first-digit deviation from five reported amounts and judges conformity and regression coefficients against a rotation reference, which preserves each bank’s ratios and growth path and randomises its scale. In simulations without departures, the benchmark flagged 3.7% to 3.9% of units at the bank level and 5.6% to 7.2% pooled, but its power against altered leading digits was at most 0.07 for a single bank and 0.26 pooled. We illustrate it on twelve Indonesian banks with four fraud hexagon proxies. The pooled deviation lay at the 67th percentile of the benchmark, and one of 13 units exceeded its 95th percentile. In fixed-effects models the benchmark reproduced about 17% of the leverage coefficient, and the remainder could not be distinguished from zero; the other proxies were indistinguishable from zero, with minimum detectable effects 1.7 to 3.6 times the estimates, so the illustration shows the limits of such a panel. The extracted amounts do not satisfy the balance identity within 1% of assets in 33 of 72 bank-years, and the proxies are unvalidated, so results are exploratory. Restricting the panel to the 39 bank-years that reconcile within 0.1% left these conclusions unchanged. Digit-based studies using ratios built from tested figures should benchmark associations against arithmetic dependence.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Benford’s Law: A Rotation Benchmark for First-Digit Screening in Small Bank Panels
MedShift-SFDA: A Difficulty-Graded Benchmark for Source-Free Domain Adaptation in Medical Image Segmentation

evidence_items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) requires sequential decisions about evidence acquisition, query reformulation, generation, verification, and abstention under resource constraints. A fixed workflow does not adapt its acquisition cost to observed evidence, while fully optimal partially observable control generally requires unknown stochastic models. We present Feedback-Greedy Agentic Orchestration (FGAO), a training-free controller for budgeted RAG. FGAO represents the state by externally assessed goal conditions and action preconditions, estimates state-normalized gain and harm rates by combining declared effects with within-query feedback, and scores actions by predicted deficiency reduction, cost, and bounded continuation value. We establish multi-action, budget-feasible source escalation; finite-horizon concentration for adaptively sampled feedback with explicit within-class heterogeneity; a continuation-aware action-selection error bound; and stopping and dependency-depth results under stated assumptions. We also characterize what verification can and cannot guarantee. On a matched 100-question SQuAD 2.0 evaluation using the same Sonnet-based serving path, FGAO v2 attains 76% exact match versus 72% for a CRAG-style implementation (exact paired p = .39); the difference is not statistically significant. FGAO v3 reaches 77% exact match at a higher mean cost (11.36 versus 8.48 declared units per question). In 1,000 synthetic episodes, the unlock-lookahead variant reaches 94.3% completion, comparable to a tuned verified planner (92.5%), whereas removing feedback or lookahead reduces completion to 72.9% or 2.6%, respectively. Beyond the mathematical analysis, FGAO is released as an open-source Python framework with reusable controller and RAG interfaces and a publicly deployed Docker-based HTTP API on Hugging Face Spaces.
evidence_items.title: FGAO: Feedback-Greedy Agentic Orchestration for Budgeted Retrieval-Augmented Generation

evidence_items.summary: Autonomous AI agents that read email, browse the web, call tools, and delegate to other agents turn a model's text-following behaviour into real-world actions. This makes prompt injection, where attacker-controlled content is mistaken for instructions, a direct route to data exfiltration, record tampering, and privilege escalation. Defences that try to make the model itself resistant are probabilistic and have been shown to fail against adaptive attackers. This paper takes the complementary position that an agent should be secured by the enforcement layer around the model, on the assumption that the model can be manipulated. It proposes a threat model and an attack taxonomy for agentic workflows, defines six defence designs from prompt-level filtering to a layered architecture of scoped capabilities, plan-locking, information-flow labels, and targeted human confirmation, and evaluates them in a simulated agent environment with eight tasks, fifteen tools at four privilege levels, and eight attack classes. The model is represented as a stochastic policy that follows an injected instruction with a given probability, and the defences are deterministic policy code. Without defences, attacks succeeded in about 60% of episodes at a follow probability of 0.6 and 77% for persistent memory poisoning. Prompt-level defences reduced this to 3% to 4% for tool-output injection but not for memory poisoning, and their effectiveness fell as detector recall fell (3.6% to 23.9% mean success from recall 0.85 to 0). Tool allowlists blocked out-of-scope tools but left in-scope abuse at 60%. Plan-locking with information-flow labels reduced every attack to zero except in-scope record tampering (30%), whereas scoped capabilities alone left exfiltration to a compromised known contact at 60%.
evidence_items.title: Securing Autonomous Agentic AI Workflows Against Prompt Injection and Privilege Escalation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Archaeology has many competing theories but, at the meso-scale where most interpretation occurs, few sound tests. We advance an agentic agent-based modelling (agentic-ABM) framework in which an AI research agent works with an archaeologist throughout testing. The AI agents stay outside the model, whose simulated agents follow fixed rules. The research agent synthesises literature, formalises published positions as rules, labels every parameter as cited or assumed, executes scenarios, runs sensitivity analyses, and docks the model: two independent AI agents on different large language models re-implement it blind. The archaeologist directs research, approves rules, tests code and evaluates outcomes. The case is a long-standing debate: the labour and cooperation behind Bronze Age Sardinia's 7,167 nuraghi (Nurnet data); 26 of 29 scenarios draw on published work, 13 directly. We develop a protocol for testing theory with agentic-ABM, extending docking to AI agents. Both re-implementations reproduce the labour results in sampled runs of both engines; construction-time differences trace mostly to specification ambiguities, and the second arm falls just short of the time criterion. Docking verifies implementation, not historical validity; results are bounds under stated assumptions. Agentic-ABM turns speculative theory into auditable, replicable, comparative tests of which pasts are more likely, not which happened.
evidence_items.title: Testing Archaeological Theory Using Agentic-ABM: A Case from Nuragic Sardinia

evidence_items.summary: Artificial Intelligence is evolving from the passive content generation of Generative AI (GenAI) to Agentic AI (AgAI) systems which are increasingly characterized by autonomy, adaptability, and goal-driven reasoning. Unlike traditional GenAI, AgAI systems are capable of perception, planning, and independent action. This shift introduces a unique class of sociotechnical risks, including goal misalignment, cascading operational errors, and security vulnerabilities. This paper reviews the AgAI landscape, examines its architectural components (planning, memory, action, and multi-agent collaboration) and its transformative potential across key sectors such as healthcare, education, manufacturing, robotics, and software development. By analyzing existing corporate and regulatory governance frameworks, the paper identifies gaps in accountability, liability, and real-time intervention. We argue that establishing trustworthy AgAI requires a shift from regulating content to constraining autonomous consequences, and propose seven research and governance challenges focusing on dynamic alignment, responsibility attribution, verifiable specifications, and standardized benchmarks, to ensure AgAI systems remain aligned with human values.
evidence_items.title: Trustworthy agentic AI systems: navigating the risks and governance of autonomous AI

evidence_items.summary: AI agents powered by large language models are beginning to initiate, authorize, and execute financial transactions on behalf of users and institutions. Between 2024 and 2026 the industry shipped the first payment infrastructure purpose-built for this shift: Google's Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), Coinbase's x402, Visa Intelligent Commerce, and Mastercard Agent Pay, while central banks began experimenting with agentic systems inside wholesale payment infrastructures. Yet the academic literature has not synthesized this transition: existing surveys cover LLM agents generally and financial applications of LLMs broadly, but none examine the specific problem of agents that move money. This survey provides a structured review of agentic AI in payments and financial transactions. We analyze 54 primary works spanning agent architectures, production payment protocols, central-bank research, agent identity frameworks, adversarial security literature, and liability scholarship. We propose a four-axis taxonomy (autonomy level, transaction authority, guarantee mechanism, and failure surface) and use it to map every surveyed system. We find that transaction-integrity guarantees such as idempotency, settlement finality, and reconciliation are enforced largely by convention rather than by structure; that machine-verifiable mandates and agent identity remain immature; and that liability allocation for agent-initiated transactions is unresolved across jurisdictions. We conclude with a research agenda covering bounded-autonomy mechanisms, payment-aware agent benchmarks, machine-verifiable mandates, and systemic-risk modelling. A living bibliography accompanies this survey.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI in Payments and Financial Transactions: A Survey of Architectures, Safeguards and Open Problems

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in video generation have made automated advertising production increasingly feasible. However, an effective advertisement must faithfully represent the product and communicate its selling points through compelling visual storytelling, which requires more than visual synthesis: it calls for deeper product understanding and strategic decisions about how to present product value. Crucially, product research and creative design are closely intertwined, as the information gathered about a product determines which features can be faithfully demonstrated and how they should be presented. In this paper, we introduce AdProducer, the first end-to-end agentic framework for advertising video creation, transforming concise creative briefs into finished advertisements. Our multimodal agent autonomously researches products through web and image search and translates its findings into selling-point-driven storyboards that guide a frozen video generator. To achieve this, we develop a dedicated data construction pipeline that yields two training datasets, AdProducer-SFT and AdProducer-RL, and train the agent through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning with joint optimization of storyboard- and video-level rewards. We further introduce AdCreation-Bench, comprising 305 advertising briefs across eight domains, with two complementary metrics: PG-Score for product correctness and creative execution, and Ad-Score for overall advertising effectiveness assessed by an independent judge. Experiments demonstrate that AdProducer improves the PG-Score of MiniMax H3 from 17.3 to 51.3 and generalizes to Veo 3.1 without additional training, improving its score from 28.0 to 35.9, with consistent gains in Ad-Score, VideoScore2, and human evaluations. Code, models, and data are released.
evidence_items.title: AdProducer: Towards Agentic Advertising Video Generation

evidence_items.summary: Conventional neural networks store synaptic parameters as explicit tensors whose persistent Flash footprint scales linearly (O(W)) with parameter count, constraining resource-limited edge microcontrollers. We formulate and systematically evaluate Fractal Neural Synthesis (FNS), a procedural weight derivation architecture that replaces hidden-layer matrices with a constant 24-byte coordinate seed Theta = (c_x, c_y, ell) in F_64^3 anchored near the complex quadratic bifurcation boundary dM of f_c(z) = z^2 + c. We introduce a large-bailout (R = 256) smooth escape kernel, four zero-overhead geometric sampling apertures--Cartesian Grid, coprime 3x3 Rule-of-Thirds (Z/9Z), phi-Vogel spiral, and multi-scale Harmonic Tripod--and prove conditional Kolmogorov (K_Kolm <= 192 + c_0 bits) and Shannon entropy bounds. Across magnifications zeta in [10^0, 10^8], C^1 Fourier and lattice-noise bases collapse to post-standardization rank ~2.25 and SHA-256 PRNG exhibits avalanche discontinuity (rho ~ 0.019, 50.6% micro-step retention), whereas dM uniquely sustains both rank (~10.0) and local continuity (rho in [0.81, 0.97], 89.2% retention). Under leak-free 10-fold CV across four zero-scaler-byte non-linear benchmarks, FNS with an INT8 readout surpasses 0-hidden Linear-INT8 by +3.6 to +10.8 pp while delivering 10.7x-129x total Flash reduction (725x-2,773x hidden reduction) relative to converged Float32 MLPs (90.30% Ionosphere in 285 B; 97.22% Optical Digits in 2,598 B; 97.90% PenDigits in 2,598 B; 87.00% Satimage in 1,570 B).
evidence_items.title: Fractal Neural Synthesis: Constant-Storage Procedural Weight Derivation via Complex Quadratic Boundary Dynamics

evidence_items.summary: Despite strong performance on standard benchmarks, video reasoning models remain vulnerable to visual degradation, raising concerns about their reliability in safety-critical scenarios. Existing benchmarks address this concern in part by simulating visual degradation or probing model reasoning with challenging questions, leaving open how well models handle naturally degraded video and whether they can make the simpler judgments that matter for safe driving. To this end, we introduce GRAPE-Bench, which jointly evaluates video reasoning across visual degradation conditions and question difficulty. It combines a synthetic set spanning twelve corruption types across daily-life and driving videos with real-world footage of driving at night or in rain, snow, or fog. Each video is paired with three progressively challenging questions, from fundamental judgments with potential safety implications to demanding reasoning stress tests. Across open-weight and frontier models, we observe ranking reversals between synthetic and real-world conditions and level-specific weaknesses obscured by overall accuracy. Synthetic-data fine-tuning improves Qwen3.5-9B's real-world accuracy from 76.7% to 81.1%, while clean-privileged on-policy distillation reaches 80.4% in a separate reasoning-enabled setting. Through preference steering, we further demonstrate continuous control over a frozen model's trade-off between safety-relevant judgments and challenging reasoning, with little change in overall accuracy. Together, GRAPE-Bench provides a unified testbed for evaluating, improving, and controlling video reasoning under degraded visual conditions.
evidence_items.title: GRAPE-Bench: When Vision Degrades, Does Video Reasoning Hold?

evidence_items.summary: Can a simple mirror expose the limitations of today's robotic manipulation policies? Inspired by the mirror self-recognition test in animal cognition, we investigate whether robot policies can reliably manipulate physical objects in scenes containing their reflections. We introduce RoboDojo-Mirror, a benchmark built on RoboDojo that preserves task objectives, success criteria, and policy checkpoints while comparing a mirror-free baseline with single-mirror, dual-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions. Across five policies spanning Vision-Language-Action models, World Action Models, and agentic policies, every mirror condition reduces aggregate success rates: averaged over the three conditions, the drop ranges from 10.8 to 56.7 percentage points across policies, and it reaches 62.5 points on the mirrored tabletop. Because a mirror is also a physical obstacle, we compare it against geometrically matched non-reflective panels; 50--88\% of mirror-specific failures occur without recorded robot--panel contact, so direct collisions alone do not explain the degradation. Trajectory and contact analyses instead reveal recurring behaviors consistent with phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real ones. Targeted diagnostics further characterize grasping near reflections, policy-dependent pushing progress, and physical-target interaction under main-camera occlusion. Real-robot experiments with π_{0.5} and FastWAM also show lower overall success rates under the upright-mirror and mirrored-tabletop conditions. These findings reveal a shared vulnerability to reflective environments across diverse robot policies and motivate reflection-aware evaluation of embodied intelligence. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/robodojo-mirror.
evidence_items.title: Embodied AI Fails the Mirror Test: How a Simple Mirror Breaks Robot Policies

evidence_items.summary: While text-driven body motion generation has matured, pure-hand synthesis remains bottlenecked by data. Existing datasets often treat hands as rigid end-effectors, lack fine-grained captions, or are too limited in scale to support robust generalization. We introduce RoMo Hands, an in-the-wild, text-paired dataset of ~542K sequences (884 hours, 95.5M frames at 30 fps) which is an order of magnitude larger than prior work. To ensure high-quality supervision, a stringent dexterity filter discards low-articulation sequences, focusing the distribution on complex bimanual movement. Each clip is paired with five captions at increasing granularities from global semantic tags to atomic finger states, organized under a hierarchical taxonomy. To bridge the gap between body and hand architectures, we propose a novel 393-D bimanual representation that adapts redundant body-motion paradigms to the high-DoF kinematics of hands. Systematic benchmarking of diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive generators reveals distinct trade-offs under these hand-specific adaptations, including a sharp divergence between semantic alignment and kinematic plausibility. Our dataset, representation, and benchmark establish a rigorous foundation for the next generation of dexterous motion synthesis. Project page: https://romodataset.github.io/romo-hands/.
evidence_items.title: RoMo Hands: A Large Scale Richly Organized Text to Hand Motion Dataset

evidence_items.summary: Spatial reasoning in hospitals requires tracking look-alike equipment, interpreting patient-relative directions, and judging passage widths, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of these abilities. We introduce Clinical3D-Bench, a simulated benchmark with 3,368 questions of eight types on egocentric walkthroughs of 373 hospital-room layouts. Layouts follow hospital design guidelines, answers are computed from the 3D scenes, and paired scene states test whether models change their answers when relevant evidence changes. Videos are photorealistic, and ten physicians screened the layouts. Among 35 multimodal large language models (MLLMs), the best open and proprietary models reach 45.7% and 53.6% macro accuracy, against 40.8% for an answer prior and 79.0% for physicians on a subset, and 27 of 32 open models score below 40% on two-way patient-relative directions. Fine-tuning on Clinical3D-45K, our 44,750-question training set, lifts two MLLMs 16-20 points above the best proprietary model. 3D maps given to the fine-tuned MLLM as input go largely unused: replacing them with another video's, even when they are ground truth, barely changes its accuracy. The proposed GeoJeV instead lets the MLLM compute with 3D: it reconstructs a scene memory from each video, selects 3D operations and their arguments from the MLLM's question state, and adds their evidence to its option scores. It achieves the highest accuracy of all evaluated models, narrowing the gap to physicians.
evidence_items.title: Clinical3D-Bench: Evaluating and Improving Spatial Intelligence of Multimodal LLMs in Hospital Environments

evidence_items.summary: Decision models, which output probability distributions over candidate labels instead of generating text, are increasingly used as classifiers and evaluators for inputs associated with real-world locations. However, it remains unclear whether they can leverage spatial context and whether their predictions are geographically biased. We introduce GeoDecisions, a multimodal benchmark for evaluating the spatial awareness and geographic bias of decision models. GeoDecisions comprises two tasks: (1) geo-aware image classification, and (2) location rating on objective and subjective topics. Evaluating six decision models against supervised task-specific models, we find that spatial awareness requires vision: textual coordinates alone provide insufficient context for classifying everyday photos and satellite images. We also find substantial geographic bias. On everyday photos, despite achieving higher accuracy, open-weight decision models exhibit more spatially clustered errors than supervised models. Moreover, across all five subjective topics, every decision model gives lower ratings to locations with lower socioeconomic conditions. Finally, we propose a training-free method that combines decision models with a location prior to improve their spatial awareness without substantially increasing performance bias. Our code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/GeoDecisions.
evidence_items.title: Seeing Is Locating: Spatial Awareness and Geographic Bias in Decision Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Visual creation demands expressive imagery together with precise control over text, layout, and structure. We introduce Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation, an agentic framework that connects these capabilities through Pixel as Code. Raster images are represented by learned discrete visual tokens, while structured artifacts use explicit programs. A shared generation-and-rendering interface connects these representations to visual feedback across images, vector graphics, webpages, and documents. A Nemotron-native harness coordinates planning and raster candidate selection, with targeted repair for editable structured and hybrid artifacts. To support this interface, we develop Nemotron-Labs-Image-Tokenizer, the autoregressive raster generator Nemotron-Labs-Image-30B-A3B, and the structured-code model family Nemotron-Labs-VisionCode. On approximately 178K images spanning six visual domains, our tokenizer improves reconstruction PSNR from 26.08 to 29.57 dB over Emu3.5 IBQ. It also provides 7.13x faster encoding and 10.93x faster decoding at batch size one on A100. In standalone evaluation, one Nemotron-Labs-VisionCode variant surpasses Kimi K3.1 Pro on the aggregate across Chart2Code, MMSVG, Design2Code, and Image2Struct. At the system level, the Nemotron-native configuration raises GenEval2 Soft-TIFA GM from 31.71 to 52.56 using the same raster generator. With our best setting, Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation achieves performance competitive with GPT Image 2 and Nano Banana Pro across most benchmarks with available comparisons.
evidence_items.title: Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation: Pixel as Code for Agentic Visual Creation

evidence_items.summary: Dense-embedding retrievers can fail adversarially: when a query is answered by a document A and reversed by a near-copy B that differs from A by a small meaning-changing edit (a "trap"), raw cosine over E5-Large-v2 places B in the top-10 for 82-100% of queries at a pool of 5,000. We study two things. First, a small learned projection W: R^1024 -> R^d (d in {11, 32}), trained by a deterministic recipe on a declared set of cases, that suppresses the trap: for the declared cases, HN@10 = 0.0000 (no trap in the top-10) in all twelve (domain, pool-size) settings across four independent domains (legal, medical, patent, financial) and pools up to 100,000, while the correct paraphrase is retained for 93-99% of cases, under exact nearest-neighbour search. Second, a boundary-conditioned accelerator that serves the projection at that scale: an acceleration of spectral graph retrieval (SpectRAG) that replaces a dense eigendecomposition with a boundary-value solve, holding HN@10 = 0.0000 at n = 100,000 in every domain and retrieving the ~300-query suite in 0.6-1.1 s (~2-4 ms per query on average). Because the lens's output is the stored representation (a few floats per document), a hardened, specialised index per domain or tenant is ~90x smaller and dimension-proportionally faster than the full embedding, making many small declared indexes a practical alternative to one large vector store. The claim is scoped to the declared cases on the measured pools, with no probabilistic bound; the correct-answer rate drops for a reworded query against an unchanged corpus (about 0.79, trap suppression still holding). A projection transfers only partly to other domains, which we report in full. The recipe, lenses, trap sets and evaluation harness are released under AGPL-3.0; the accelerator's implementation is a reserved commercial component, and every HN number is reproducible under exact search.
evidence_items.title: Small Learned Projections for Semantic-Reversal-Aware Retrieval with Spectral Acceleration: A Four-Domain Empirical Study

evidence_items.summary: We present KMed-31B, a medical large language model post-trained from an open-weight model for on-premises deployment with limited hardware. Post-training a model for diverse medical tasks remains difficult, because improving one kind of task can lower performance on another. We attribute this to differences between tasks in expected output and available feedback. Medical question answering and diagnosis prediction have reference answers, whereas clinical inquiry has no single correct response and is judged with rubrics. We therefore divide medical training tasks into four categories by these two properties, train one specialist per category with a reward that its feedback supports, and integrate the specialists into a single student with Multi-teacher On-policy Delta Distillation (MOPD^2). For clinical inquiry, we build Synthetic Health Dialogue, a simulated corpus of consultations with lay users and clinicians whose patient cases span common clinical presentations in primary care. Relative to its base model, KMed-31B raises HealthBench Hard from 22.95 to 41.87 and HealthBench Professional from 37.92 to 50.20 in non-thinking mode, and from 23.80 to 51.48 and from 41.97 to 59.18 in thinking mode, while its scores on four multiple-choice medical benchmarks are maintained or slightly improved. KMed-31B has the highest unadjusted HealthBench Hard score among the compared models, including proprietary ones, and scores higher on HealthBench Professional than every open-weight model we compare, including models with more than ten times as many total parameters. Applied to another base model, Qwen3.8-27B, the same training recipe also raises both HealthBench scores. We describe the training recipe, data construction, and settings in detail so that institutions requiring on-premises deployment can develop medical models from open-weight foundations.
evidence_items.title: KMed-31B Technical Report

evidence_items.summary: Autoresearch agents, which autonomously design, run, and refine experiments, are accelerating scientific progress, particularly in AI research. However, existing agents rely on harnesses that combine multiple mechanisms, making it difficult to determine how individual components contribute to performance. We systematically study harness design for long-horizon, self-evolving autoresearch agents along two dimensions: context management, which determines what an agent retains from its past attempts, and skill management, which governs how it stores and reuses lessons from those attempts. Across MLE-Bench and KernelBench with gpt-oss-120b, gpt-6-luna, and gpt-6-sol, we isolate the effects of individual harness design choices by evaluating each against a recency-truncation baseline within a shared agent framework. For context management, we find that preserving individually accessible records of past attempts is more effective than maintaining a rolling summary, with context folding performing best across all six settings and improving upon the baseline by up to 19.2%. For skill management, selectively discarding persistently unused lessons is more effective on average than consolidating them or promoting them to standing rules. Building on these findings, we combine context folding and skill deletion in MLEvolver, which achieves a 72.7% medal rate on MLE-Bench Lite and a 94% fast_1 score on KernelBench Level 3, substantially outperforming AIDE and OpenEvolve under the same inference budget. Overall, our study distills design principles for preserving experimental history and curating reusable lessons in autoresearch harnesses, paving the way for agents that turn accumulated experience into sustained progress.
evidence_items.title: Demystifying the Autoresearch Harness: How Context and Skills Shape Self-Evolving Agents

evidence_items.summary: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We further introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.
evidence_items.title: LingSante MedGuard Technical Report

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Optimization benchmarks play a fundamental role in assessing algorithm performance; however, existing artificial benchmarks often fail to capture the diversity and irregularity of real-world problem structures, while benchmarks derived from real-world problems are costly and difficult to construct. To address these challenges, we propose an evolutionary automatic benchmark generation framework that leverages a large language model (LLM) as a generative operator, termed the LLM-driven evolutionary benchmark generator (LLM-EBG). In this framework, the LLM serves as an evolutionary operator that generates and evolves benchmark problems within a flexible, expressive representation space. As a case study, we generate unconstrained single-objective continuous minimization problems represented as mathematical expressions designed to induce significant performance differences between a genetic algorithm (GA) and differential evolution (DE). Experimental results show that LLM-EBG successfully produces benchmark problems in which the designated target algorithm consistently outperforms the comparative algorithm in more than 80% of trials. Furthermore, exploratory landscape analysis reveals that benchmarks favoring GA are highly sensitive to variable scaling, demonstrating that the proposed framework can generate problems with distinct geometric characteristics that reflect the intrinsic search behaviors of different optimization algorithms.
evidence_items.title: An evolutionary framework for automatic optimization benchmark generation via large language models

evidence_items.summary: We propose an efficient content detection method generated by large language models (LLMs), referred to as Mahalanobis distance–based confidence score (MDCS)–based detection (MDCSD), that fully harnesses the universality of LLMs across multiple splits. Its essence lies in utilizing the MDCS of the text as the ultimate discriminative feature. The prerequisite for computing the MDCS is the efficient joint estimation of the precision matrices corresponding to multiple splits. We provide regularization techniques for constructing the joint estimator and offer corresponding computationally feasible optimization algorithms. The sparsity and consistency of the joint estimator are demonstrated. Based on offset Rademacher complexity, we further derive the optimal excess risk bound for the detection problem. Superiority of MDCSD is validated on the recently released Human ChatGPT Comparison Corpus data set. History: Accepted by Ram Ramesh, Area Editor for Data Science and Machine Learning. Funding: This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants W2511079, 72471010, 72250065, and 72325007], the Xiangjiang Laboratory Key Project [Grant 23XJ02004], and the Science and Technology Innovation Program of Hunan Province [Grant 2024RC7003]. Supplemental Material: The software that supports the findings of this study is available within the paper and its Supplemental Information ( https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/suppl/10.1287/ijoc.2024.0877 ) as well as from the IJOC GitHub software repository ( https://github.com/INFORMSJoC/2024.0877 ). The complete IJOC Software and Data Repository is available at https://informsjoc.github.io/ .

evidence_items.summary: Background: The physician global assessment (PhGA) is a core outcome measure in juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) but is incompletely captured, even in clinical registries. We developed a large language model (LLM) approach that extracts explicitly documented PhGA from clinical narratives and infers a score where none is recorded. To our knowledge, this is the first study to address both tasks. Methods: We linked charts from 306 children with JIA at one center to the Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatology Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry (2016-2024). A structured prompt was developed on 100 randomly sampled charts, then evaluated on 400 charts from patients not represented in the development set. Extraction used GPT-5.2 within a HIPAA-compliant Azure environment. Registry-recorded PhGA served as the reference standard, with discordances adjudicated by a pediatric rheumatologist blinded to both sources. Agreement was assessed by intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC(2,1)), exact match, and mean absolute error (MAE). Results: Against registry values, ICC(2,1) was 0.87 (95% CI 0.85-0.89; n=400), with 70.5% exact agreement and MAE 0.363. Agreement was near-perfect for explicit extractions (n=190; ICC 0.99; 95% CI 0.98-0.99) and lower for inferred scores (n=210; ICC 0.72; 95% CI 0.64-0.78). Large discordances (≥2 points) occurred in 7.3% of cases. Against the adjudicated standard, overall ICC(2,1) was 0.96 (95% CI 0.95-0.97), with 77.5% exact agreement and MAE 0.200. All 14 explicit discordances reflected mismatch between the registry and the clinical note, rather than extraction errors (adjudicated ICC 1.00). For inferred scores, ICC rose to 0.90 (95% CI 0.87-0.92). Residual disagreement was concentrated at the inactive/minimally active boundary. Conclusion: An LLM can reliably extract PhGA from clinical notes with high accuracy to support downstream clinical research, offering a scalable approach to mitigating missingness in patient registries.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model Extraction and Inference of Physician Global Assessment from Clinical Notes in Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

evidence_items.summary: Smart public spaces combine sensing infrastructures, digital services, responsive facilities, and physical spatial elements, producing experience evidence that cannot be adequately represented by questionnaires or isolated environmental indicators. This study develops a multimodal artificial intelligence model that evaluates comfort, perceived safety, spatial engagement, accessibility, and an integrated experience score from synchronized behavioral video, UWB trajectories, environmental sensing, and textual feedback. Data are collected from 120 participants completing four eight-minute spatial conditions in an instrumented campus plaza. Modality-specific encoders generate 128-dimensional representations, which are temporally aligned and integrated by a four-layer cross-modal Transformer with hierarchical regression heads. On participant-independent testing, the proposed model achieved an overall MAE of 0.044 ± 0.004, RMSE of 0.061 ± 0.005, R² of 0.905 ± 0.012, and Spearman ρ of 0.951 ± 0.008, significantly outperforming early-fusion and single-modality baselines (p < .001). Removing trajectory or textual information increased overall MAE to 0.061 ± 0.006 and 0.059 ± 0.005, respectively. The model also retained stable performance across crowd-density and lighting conditions, while SHAP analysis identified distinct modality contributions to each experience dimension.
evidence_items.title: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Based Evaluation Model for Smart Public Space Experience

evidence_items.summary: The comprehensive evaluation of college physical education teaching effects is critical for ensuring both student performance and instructional quality. This study proposes the AI-IoT Physical Performance Fusion System (AIPPF), which integrates multimodal wearable sensor data, vision-based pose estimation, and a CNN-Transformer fusion model for automated performance scoring. The system synchronizes physiological signals with biomechanical movement analysis to deliver real-time monitoring, movement error detection, personalized feedback, and scalable institutional integration. Experimental findings demonstrate that AIPPF achieves over 90% accuracy in evaluation compared to 65–85% for traditional and fuzzy evaluation models, reduces safety risks to 6–16% versus 30–40% in prior methods, lowers fatigue accumulation by 15–20%, and enhances student engagement scores to above 85%, reaching a maximum of 94% in gamified sessions. Computation efficiency was also improved, with response times of 35–50 ms, enabling real-time classroom application.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of College Physical Education Teaching Effects Based on Artificial Intelligence and IoT

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objective To evaluate ambient Artificial Intelligence (AI) scribe systems (AAS) across multiple domains using a rapid learning health system (LHS) approach, including provider satisfaction, efficiency, documentation quality, usability, and patient sentiment. Materials and Methods This LHS evaluation compared 2 AAS systems (Abridge and Nabla) among 100 providers over 90 days. Evaluation incorporated a cluster randomized crossover comparison, analysis of use and EHR-based workflow outcomes, and standardized simulated encounters to assess documentation quality and safety. Outcomes included provider satisfaction, efficiency, note quality, usability, and patient sentiment. Results In standardized simulated encounters, both systems achieved 76% note element accuracy with minimal risk for harm. In the randomized crossover comparison, Abridge demonstrated higher usability scores (78.5 vs 73) and was preferred 3:1 over Nabla, which had higher automated speech recognition error rates. Across 16 479 clinical encounters, AAS was used in 35.7% of visits. Total EHR time decreased by approximately 5 minutes per day; same-day chart closure increased by approximately 5% during the initial crossover period, but this effect was attenuated. Provider experience was positive (Net Promoter Score [NPS] 53). Discussion Both systems demonstrated comparable documentation accuracy and modest efficiency gains while improving clinician satisfaction. Despite similar performance, clinicians reported differences in usability and preference. Adoption below 40% reflected the trade-off between documentation support and verification burden. Conclusion Rapid, multidimensional evaluation within a LHS can assess AAS across domains of implementation, efficiency, clinician experience, and documentation quality and safety. Ongoing monitoring of efficiency, documentation quality, and use patterns is essential.
evidence_items.title: Rapid comparative evaluation of 2 ambient artificial intelligence applications in a learning health system

evidence_items.summary: AI transforms financial reporting via predictive anomaly detection, semantic analysis, and continuous auditing. The fractured literature between computer science and accounting lacks a unified framework. To correct this, a scoping review mapped global scholarship. Evaluating 562 Scopus records published before April 2026 exposed exponential growth between 2020 and 2025. Reflexive Thematic Analysis yielded four themes: algorithmic classification predicting distress; semantic quantification decoding narratives; continuous audits using robotic workflows; and ethical hurdles from transparency barriers. Bridging this gap demands grounding machine learning in accounting theories. Future operations must implement explainable AI, align with sustainable development goals, and obey regulatory standards.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Financial Reporting Systems

authors: Gaurav S. Mitkari, Trupti Y. Biradar, Aditya K. Tanpure

evidence_items.summary: Natural products (NPs) remain a valuable source of chemical diversity for pharmacological research and drug development. Their complex structures and biological activities have contributed to the discovery of medicines and inspired new therapeutic strategies. Nevertheless, conventional natural-product discovery can be slow and resource-intensive because researchers must address source selection, extraction, isolation, dereplication, structural elucidation, biological testing and subsequent optimization. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), natural-language processing, computer vision and graph-based methods, offers computational approaches to help manage these tasks. This review discusses the role of AI across the natural-product discovery pipeline, with emphasis on data integration, plant and microbial source exploration, biosynthetic gene-cluster analysis, metabolomics and spectral interpretation, activity and target prediction, virtual screening, network pharmacology, toxicity and ADMET estimation, and molecular design. It also describes commonly used databases and computational resources, outlines a practical AI-supported workflow, and considers opportunities for integrating experimental evidence with computational predictions. The benefits of AI include prioritization of candidate compounds, improved analysis of large and heterogeneous datasets, hypothesis generation and more systematic exploration of chemical and biological relationships. Important limitations remain, including dataset bias, inconsistent annotation, small sample sizes, overfitting, poor external validation, limited interpretability, reproducibility concerns and the need for experimental confirmation. Ethical, regulatory and biodiversity considerations are also discussed. AI is best regarded as a decision-support layer that complementsnot replacesphytochemistry, pharmacology, analytical chemistry and biological experimentation.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Natural Products Discovery

evidence_items.summary: Introduction: Skin cancers represent some of the most common cancers worldwide. Its incidence is constantly rising. Early detection is essential to reduce morbidity and improve survival. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI)-based software has increasingly been integrated into 2D/3D total-body-photography (TBP) systems, to support clinicians in diagnosing cutaneous lesions. Objectives: To evaluate VIDIX 4.0 diagnostic performance using histopathology as the reference standard and assess the ability of the DEXI score to discriminate between malignant and benign lesions. Methods: This monocenter retrospective study included 204 lesions from 165 patients who underwent VIDIX 4.0 videodermoscopy, followed by excision and histopathological examination. Diagnostic performance was evaluated in terms of sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and accuracy, with 95% confidence intervals calculated using the Wilson method. Malignant and benign lesions were compared after excluding actinic keratoses. DEXI scores were analyzed using Kruskal–Wallis and Mann–Whitney U tests with Holm adjustment. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis assessed DEXI discrimination using the area under the curve (AUC) with 95% confidence intervals. Results: VIDIX sensitivity was 93.3% for nevi, 81.8% for basal cell carcinoma (BCC), 63.2% for melanoma, 44.4% for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), 33.3% for actinic keratosis (AK), and 61.1% for seborrheic keratosis (SK). For malignant versus benign lesions, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were 80.3%, 92.7%, and 88.9%, respectively. DEXI scores differed significantly among histopathological categories (P<0.0001), showing good discrimination between malignant and benign lesions (AUC, 0.939; 95% CI, 0.896–0.974).
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of an Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Videodermoscopy System for Cutaneous Lesion Classification: A Retrospective Study

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) holds great promise in radiotherapy. However, prospective evaluation and robust assessment frameworks for AI contouring and planning tools are lacking, casting doubt on the quality and cost-effectiveness of some AI radiotherapy solutions and hindering wider clinical deployment. ARCHERY, an international, prospective multi-cancer basket trial, seeks to undertake a large-scale evaluation of AI-assisted contouring and planning for cancers of the head and neck, prostate and cervix for patients in diverse country settings. We describe the evaluation approach led by the UK Radiotherapy Trials Quality Assurance (RTTQA) Group which, through literature appraisal, established protocol-defined reference standard contour and planning parameters and, following a scoping review and consensus discussion, developed evaluation definitions to enable robust and consistent assessment. This approach demonstrates a strong example of AI radiotherapy study methodology and tool assessment, and serves as a foundation for adoption, adaptation and development in future AI radiotherapy studies.
evidence_items.title: Defining an evaluation framework for radiotherapy trials which use artificial intelligence- lessons from the ARCHERY trial

evidence_items.summary: This chapter examines how immersive technologies and artificial intelligence can enhance accessible tourism experiences for people with disabilities. Building on literature on tourism constraints and the tourism value chain, it first discusses physical, informational, communicative, cognitive, attitudinal, and psychological barriers that shape travel participation. It then evaluates the accessibility roles of virtual reality, augmented reality, extended reality, metaverse environments, robot-supported systems, and AI-based smart tourism platforms across pre-travel planning, on-site experience, remote participation, and post-travel feedback. The chapter argues that these technologies can support destination preview, real-time guidance, multimodal communication, personalization, remote access, and service improvement. However, it also emphasizes that technology should complement, not replace, accessible infrastructure, trained personnel, ethical data governance, and participatory design involving people with disabilities.
evidence_items.title: Immersive Technologies and Artificial Intelligence for Accessible Tourism

evidence_items.summary: This chapter explores how artificial intelligence reshapes assessment design in higher education, using Cantonese as a second language as a distinctive lens. Cantonese's tonal and sociolinguistic complexity provides a rigorous case for evaluating AI's role in oral proficiency testing. The discussion highlights the shift toward adaptive, learner-centred formats that move beyond standardised methods. Drawing on Hong Kong's higher education practices, it demonstrates how integrating Automatic Speech Recognition, Large Language Models, and Text-to-Speech enables contextualized tasks, real-time feedback, and alignment with ACTFL and CEFR frameworks. It also addresses challenges of transparency, cultural sensitivity, and human-in-the-loop mediation. Ultimately, AI-driven assessment design fosters flexible, inclusive, and pedagogically robust approaches across multilingual higher education.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Assessment Design for Cantonese Education

evidence_items.summary: Abstract A new gyrokinetic code, TEK , was benchmarked in simulating energetic particle (EP) driven toroidal Alfvén eigenmodes (TAEs) in the simple tokamak configuration chosen by the ITPA-EP group for code benchmarking purposes. Linear benchmark has been well established by other codes, whereas nonlinear benchmark for this case is lacking. This paper presents, besides the linear benchmark, nonlinear results for both single- n and multiple- n simulations ( n is the toroidal mode number). The nonlinear results are in good agreement with an analytical theory on zonal field beat-driven by Alfvén eigenmodes, partially verifying the correctness of the nonlinear simulations. The saturation level and the resulting EP transport are examined. This provides data for future inter-code nonlinear benchmarking. In TEK , all species (electrons, thermal ions, EPs) are treated on the same footing using the gyrokinetic model (with electrons in the zero Larmor radius limit). The electromagnetic cancellation problem is mitigated by using the mixed-variable pullback method. Numerical details related to electromagnetic gyrokinetic simulation are discussed.
evidence_items.title: Linear and nonlinear benchmark of gyrokinetic simulation of energetic particle driven toroidal Alfvén eigenmodes in ITPA TAE benchmark case

evidence_items.summary: Commuting origin–destination (OD) estimation increasingly combines incomplete passive mobility data with census margins, surveys, and traffic counts, yet whether each calibration step improves fidelity depends on control reliability and how well model assumptions match commuting structure. This study examines these conditions in a synthetic simulation benchmark set in a 40-zone, Jeddah-inspired geography. Sixty synthetic commuting matrices represent gravity-based demand, employer–housing links, and barrier-defined communities. Ten observation scenarios produce 6000 observation sets, reconstructed by uniform expansion, census iterative proportional fitting (IPF), prior blending, and hard or reliability-weighted screenline fitting. Census IPF raises mean cell R2 from 0.790 to 0.923 for gravity demand under baseline capture bias, but reduces accuracy once census error exceeds about 0.06 log-SD under mild capture bias. Prior blending improves gravity demand yet underestimates imposed employer links by 36%. Hard screenline fitting recovers barrier structure but costs 0.031 in R2 under noisy counts; reliability weighting retains the barrier gain and limits that loss to 0.004. Interval procedures include 41–81% of true cells; a bias-aware parametric bootstrap gives the best interval scores but still misses most intrazonal flows. The benchmark locates transition regions rather than universal rankings and does not estimate observed Jeddah commuting.
evidence_items.title: When Does Calibration Improve Commuting OD Reconstruction? A Jeddah-Inspired Synthetic Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Background Unsupervised multi-omics workflows can yield stable partitions within one analytical framework while assigning patients differently across frameworks. We benchmarked this distinction in gastric cancer under shared feature identities and matched patient perturbations. Results Five protocol-frozen primary integration tracks were benchmarked in 352 TCGA-STAD primary gastric cancers with matched mRNA, microRNA, copy-number variation, non-silent mutation, and DNA methylation data; a second Cancer Integration via Multikernel Learning (CIMLR) preprocessing scheme was examined post hoc . Patient-dependent scaling, integration, and clustering were refitted in the same 100 prespecified 80% patient perturbations at K = 2–6. K = 2 was the only resolution without a cluster containing &lt;10% of patients in any primary track or perturbation. Mean within-track pairwise adjusted Rand indices ranged from 0.078 to 0.955, whereas mean agreement among primary tracks within the same perturbation was 0.175. K = 3 increased mean cross-track agreement to 0.263 but produced two small-cluster perturbations in primary CIMLR. Thus, no tested K yielded a universally stable discrete patient partition. Reference microsatellite instability (MSI) status was associated with four of five K = 2 primary partitions and all five primary partitions at K = 3. MLH1 promoter methylation and cytolytic activity were associated with four of five K = 2 partitions, whereas six-gene interferon-gamma and 18-gene T-cell-inflamed scores were associated with all five. Within-perturbation feature reselection and related-modality exclusion for principal component analysis (PCA), similarity network fusion (SNF), and non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) retained method dependence and most biological associations, with method-specific exceptions.
evidence_items.title: A fixed-feature perturbation benchmark of unsupervised multi-omics integration in gastric cancer
Improving Flood Extent Segmentation with SAR-Derived Polarimetric Indices and Transfer Learning on the STURM-Flood Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Antibody-antigen complex prediction remains difficult because the surface recognized by a specific antibody is often uncertain, and model confidence may not distinguish alternative poses. We developed APEs (Agentic Prediction of Epitopes for Structure Prediction), an agentic system that retrieves public evidence, interprets predicted antibody and antigen structures, and produces ranked residue-level epitope hypotheses. For retrospective evaluation, web retrieval was restricted to sources released before each CASP target entry date. Across eight CASP16 and six released CASP17 targets, the top-ranked patch reached residue precision of at least 0.5 for nine of 14 targets. We then used the predicted epitopes to steer additional Protenix-v1 sampling and to compare steered finalists with the highest ipSAE unsteered model. The retrospective best selection across three independent router calls increased mean DockQ from 0.306 to 0.375; DockQ increased from 0.089 to 0.679 for H2321 and from 0.005 to 0.379 for H2346. These results show that publicly available evidence specific to the target antibody-antigen complex can serve as an inference-time signal for epitope localization, guided complex sampling, and model selection. We also release predictions for CASP17 targets whose experimental structures had not been released when the predictions were finalized, providing a prospective test of APEs (https://github.com/CSSB-SNU/ape).
evidence_items.title: APEs: Agentic Prediction of Epitopes to Guide Antibody-Antigen Structure Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Students miss deadlines because the information about tasks is spread out across email, the learning management system (LMS) and the institutional ERP and there is no tool that checks the information against the time a student actually has. This paper introduces CollegeOS, an agentic planning framework that senses academic tasks, ranks them with a four-signal priority score, packs a day-by-day study schedule into a capacity model reduced by the student’s real class timetable, and repairs the plan when conditions change. The framework is by construction constraint-safe: a deterministic scheduler enforces deadlines and daily capacity as hard constraints, while an optional large language model (LLM) can only provide bounded priority boosts and can never change feasibility. The connector for the NorthCap University ERP provides the attendance and timetables, which feed the capacity model and attendance-aware boosts. We evaluate the system against an earliest-deadline-first (EDF) baseline over 40 simulated semesters. Repair-mode replanning reduces mean plan churn from 0.899 to 0.813 (the 95% confidence intervals do not overlap), while on-time completion (50.2% vs. 51.0%) is indistinguishable from the baseline in the saturated workload regime tested. We report these results openly, along with a weight ablation and the known limitations, and identify a feasibility-aware scheduler as the next step.
evidence_items.title: A Constraint-Safe Agentic Framework for Academic Task Planning Using ERP-Aware Capacity Modelling

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents an agentic artificial intelligence framework that detects, diagnoses and resolves hold transactions, which are stuck or failed transactions, in integrated hospital pharmacy environments. Large health systems often run order entry, medication processing, billing, stock and inventory, laboratory, blood bank and automated dispensing software from different vendors, and holds arise at the interfaces where no single vendor sees the whole transaction. Analysts resolve holds manually today, so backlogs build up and stock records drift from physical reality. The research problem is how to automate the repetitive part of this work without weakening audit, inventory accuracy or patient safety. Using a design science approach, the paper develops a taxonomy of five hold causes, a five agent architecture based on a monitor, analyze, plan, execute and knowledge control loop, a tiered autonomy policy with approval gated reprocessing, and an artificial intelligence governance model. A 30 day simulation with 20 replications and a sensitivity analysis evaluate the design. Under stated assumptions, about 82 percent of holds are resolved automatically and mean handling time falls from about 43 to 11 minutes, but the human escalation queue stays bounded only above a break even of about 80 percent automatic resolution. The work indicates that governed agentic automation is a promising option for multivendor hospital pharmacy operations, provided that automatic resolution and false fix rates are confirmed through the staged pilot protocol proposed here.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI for Autonomous Detection and Resolution of Hold Transactions in Integrated Multi-Vendor Hospital Pharmacy Systems

evidence_items.summary: Agent harnesses today manage context on the model's behalf: when the window fills, the harness triggers a compaction that summarizes the history. We study the alternative, model-driven context management, in which the model itself decides when and what to compact through a context API. We gave models control over their own context in \nooa, NVIDIA's open source agent harness, and compared the two strategies on document research and machine learning engineering across context budgets from 8K to 512K tokens. Models that use the context API effectively reach higher accuracy, often with fewer input tokens, especially at tight budgets: GPT 6.1 nearly triples its score at a 32K budget on OfficeQA Pro v2 (21\%~rightarrow~56\%), and Kimi gains with up to 41\% fewer input tokens. Models differ widely, however, in how often they use the API, how aggressively they compact, and when they start compacting, and prompt changes shift that timing. Finally, we show that inference engines can make model-driven edits cheaper: by reusing the KV cache of the unchanged suffix after an edit, we cut prefill compute by up to 15\% per request with no measurable change in accuracy. Together, these results point to a new co-design frontier: models trained to manage their own context, served by inference engines that support KV cache editing.
evidence_items.title: Letting Models Manage Their Own Context: Where We Stand

evidence_items.summary: A growing body of recent work addresses the retargeting of human hand-object demonstrations to robotic hands. To train whole-robot policies, however, the retargeted motions must be kinematically feasible and physically executable, and be produced efficiently at scale. We present DexEngine, a simulation pipeline that turns human manipulation data into train-ready, physically executable arm-hand trajectories. DexEngine first places each clip's hand-object motion where the arms can reach it, finds an arm motion that follows the human hands, and then corrects the motion in physics simulation with residual reinforcement learning. From nine human hand-object datasets, we generate about 5,200 clips for each of four dexterous hands, augmented into 65,000 trajectories (116 h) and 325,000 episodes (578 h) in total. Even with arms attached, DexEngine tracks objects more accurately than prior floating-hand methods and runs over 10x faster than RL-based ones. Policies trained on our data far outperform those trained on the same clips without physics correction or with the arms attached after a floating-hand correction, showing that fine-tuning data need physics correction. Mid-training on our data further improves them at equal fine-tuning budget, in simulation and on a real robot.
evidence_items.title: DexEngine: Scaling Human Demonstrations into Physically Executable Whole-Robot Data

evidence_items.summary: Diffusion models have shown strong potential for image matting by transferring generative priors learned from large-scale pretraining. However, existing approaches largely rely on latent diffusion models, whose compressed representations and VAE-based reconstruction introduce a mismatch with the high-frequency precision required for matting. We present PixelMatte, a framework that adapts pretrained pixel-space diffusion transformers for high-fidelity image matting. We show that strong image-conditioned matting capabilities can be acquired even from a pure text-to-image model without paired image-to-image pretraining. Our approach reuses the backbone's native patch embedding to jointly process the input image, trimap, and noisy alpha matte as spatially aligned tokens, enabling direct pixel-space prediction without additional condition encoders or adapters. With pixel-accurate synthetic supervision and real-image fine-tuning, PixelMatte predicts alpha mattes in a single forward pass. Two lightweight calibration modules, LayerShift and High-Pass Refiner, further improve regional opacity accuracy and boundary fidelity. Experiments across four benchmarks and two distinct pixel diffusion backbones demonstrate substantial improvements over existing methods, reducing SAD and gradient errors by 24-44% relative to RenderMatte on P3M-500-NP and AM-2K, while achieving competitive performance on AIM-500 and RenderMatte-2K. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of pixel-space generative priors for precision-sensitive image matting. Project page: https://white-yc.github.io/pixelmatte/.
evidence_items.title: High-Fidelity Image Matting with Pixel-Space Diffusion Transformers

evidence_items.summary: Flow-based generative policies offer expressive action modeling for embodied control, yet achieving efficient one-step generation under reward-driven policy optimization remains challenging. In particular, evolving action distributions during online reinforcement learning may introduce inconsistencies between instantaneous-velocity learning and interval-averaged action generation. To address this challenge, we propose iMFPO, a one-step generative policy optimization framework with decoupled velocity learning and drift-aware velocity alignment. A shared interval-conditioned actor supports instantaneous-velocity supervision and interval-averaged action generation. JVP-corrected velocity regression is jointly optimized with reward-driven policy objectives, with action-level guidance from a frozen PPO teacher during training. At inference, iMFPO directly generates actions through interval-averaged velocity prediction, achieving one-step control without iterative flow integration. Across Go2, G1, H1, and Spot, zero-latent evaluation yields mean returns of 35.69, 34.44, 416.23, and 29.86. On Go2, action-generation latency drops from 15.57 ms to 0.41 ms relative to 64-step RFPO. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/iMFPO. Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/iMFPO.
evidence_items.title: iMFPO: Improving Mean Flow Policy Optimization with Drift-Aware Velocity Alignment for Embodied Control

evidence_items.summary: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet visual corruption can disrupt the resulting policies. We introduce HOG-WAM, which adds future Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) as structural supervision derived directly from demonstration images. An auxiliary HOG diffusion transformer (DiT) module reads RGB features through asymmetric attention, allowing its objective to shape the visual representation used for control. The module is used only during training and removed at inference, preserving FastWAM's RGB-to-action architecture. We evaluate four controlled observation corruptions through a visual-corruption extension of RoboTwin, termed RoboTwin-Plus; HOG-WAM achieves the highest success among the compared policies under all four. Mixed-noise success increases from 78.86% to 82.86% relative to FastWAM, with comparable performance on clean scenes. On LIBERO Plus, overall success increases from 74.49% to 75.26%, with the largest gain under sensor noise, from 74.14% to 78.89%. Across four Franka tasks, average success increases from 40% to 59% under clean observations and from 17% to 24% under noisy observations. A representation ablation favors combining RGB observations with auxiliary HOG prediction over replacing RGB with HOG. These findings support future-gradient prediction as complementary supervision for visually robust control, with larger absolute gains on physical tasks than in simulation. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/HOG-WAM.
evidence_items.title: HOG-WAM: Improving Visual Robustness through Future Gradient Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Robots should adapt to unfamiliar environments and acquire new skills through interaction, then execute those skills efficiently with practice. Vision-language-action policies provide efficient control, but often need additional human demonstrations to handle unfamiliar settings; reasoning agents can discover solutions using broad prior knowledge and robot-control APIs, but repeated deliberation and repair are costly. Inspired by human learning through reasoning and practice, we propose RoboEvo^2, a framework for recursive harness-policy co-evolution. In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, policy failures guide a coding agent to search complementary Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes, consolidating verified solutions into reusable skills, routing strategies, and experience memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, verified trajectories provide supervised training, while Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD) teaches the policy to favor successful corrections over failures from the same starting state. The improved policy provides stronger motor skills for subsequent search, while its remaining failures redirect harness evolution, closing the reciprocal loop. Through recursive co-evolution without additional human demonstrations, RoboEvo^2 improves standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% on LIBERO-PRO, with similar gains and reduced agentic costs on RoboTwin C2R. Further experiments demonstrate autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment harness transfer, and 95.0% hybrid success on the Unitree G1-D. Our models and code will be publicly released.
evidence_items.title: RoboEvo^2: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via Harness-Policy Co-Evolution

evidence_items.summary: Accurate 3D surface reconstruction from unposed images remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision. Recent feed-forward pointmap methods eliminate the need for camera poses but inherently produce discrete, sparse representations. In this paper, we present a generalizable pipeline that directly recovers continuous, high-fidelity 3D surfaces from unposed images by seamlessly integrating pointmap- and ray-based representations. Our approach first extracts explicit geometric priors using a pre-trained pointmap model. A query-view-centric selection module then identifies geometrically relevant reference views via a robust surfel voting mechanism. Next, a cross-attention regressor bridges target query rays with reference features to estimate a continuous coarse surface. Lastly, a raylet-based module aggregates local 3D features to carve out high-frequency details and analytical normals. Trained as a single foundation model on 9 diverse datasets, our method demonstrates exceptional zero-shot generalization on 6 unseen datasets, clearly surpassing state-of-the-art baselines in geometric accuracy and detail preservation.
evidence_items.title: FoundSurface: Feedforward Ray-Based 3D Scene Surface Reconstruction from Unposed Images

evidence_items.summary: Understanding large-scale 3D urban scenes requires representations that capture both multi-scale geometric structures and complex spatial relationships. However, existing 3D vision-language methods primarily emphasize global semantic alignment or object-level representations, leaving structured relational modeling underexplored within unified contrastive and generative frameworks. In this paper, we present 3D CoCa v3, a scene-graph-enhanced contrastive and generative framework for urban 3D scene understanding. Our framework features a Pyramid Vision Encoder for multi-scale geometric representation learning and a language-model-based decoder with question-guided caption retrieval and visual cross-attention. We further introduce MSG-based relational descriptions to enrich contrastive 3D-language alignment with structured spatial relationships. To support semantic and relational supervision, we construct City3D-9.6K, a multi-view urban vision-language dataset with aligned visual-geometric observations, scene captions, and scene graphs. Extensive experiments on City-3DQA demonstrate that 3D CoCa v3 achieves 88.35% and 64.79% overall top-1 accuracy on the sentence-wise and city-wise splits, surpassing 3D CoCa v2 by 20.88 and 3.57 percentage points, respectively. Furthermore, 3D CoCa v3 achieves the best performance on GeoEval3D, demonstrating its effectiveness in urban spatial reasoning and geometric understanding. Code is available at https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/3DCoCav3.
evidence_items.title: 3D CoCa v3: Contrastive Learners with Scene Graphs for Urban Scene Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Generating PPTX presentations is a structured task that requires semantic planning, visual composition, precise layout, and editability, motivating collaboration among specialized agents. However, programmatic methods offer editability but often produce rigid designs, while image-based methods provide visual richness but flatten content into difficult-to-edit pixels. A hybrid system can combine these strengths, but must coordinate interdependent decisions across content, layout, and appearance. To address this challenge, we propose SlidesWeaver, a hybrid multi-agent system that coordinates language and vision agents through shared deck- and slide-level states. Specifically, it uses staged multimodal commitment, diffusion-based composition planning, and two generation schedules for different priorities between composition freedom and accurate text preservation, while preserving native text and geometry. Across 1,728 generations spanning 24 system-model configurations, SlidesWeaver achieves consistently superior overall quality across all evaluated dimensions while maintaining structural control, editability, and practical generation efficiency.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Code and Pixels: Co-Generating Editable and Visually Rich Presentations
